session_19.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_19.text: My father has left-sided hemiplegia after a stroke. I help him every day with passive joint range-of-motion training and right-hand grip strength exercises. As a doctor who is not a rehabilitation specialist, I want to confirm whether the movements are standard, and how to manage the frequency and intensity so that it is safe and effective?

session_19.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_19.text: During passive movement, each joint should be moved slowly through the full range of motion, avoiding forceful pulling, twice a day for 15-20 minutes each time. Grip strength training starts with making a fist and releasing, 10-15 reps per set, 3-4 sets per day, adjusted according to your father's response—stop immediately if pain or elevated blood pressure occurs. It is recommended to record blood pressure and fatigue after training.

session_19.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_19.text: It is necessary to record blood pressure and fatigue. In addition, how long is the golden period for rehabilitation? What abnormal signals should we watch out for?

session_19.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_19.text: Three to six months after stroke is the golden recovery period, but improvement is possible within a year with consistent training. session_20.text: Hard-pen calligraphy first three days: Day 1, practice horizontal strokes (long horizontal, short horizontal) and vertical strokes (hanging-needle vertical, dewdrop vertical). Day 3, practice dots (left dot, right dot) and rising strokes. Copy each day for 20 minutes, then review. You can also record videos and ask Teacher Zheng for feedback; I will keep track of your progress too. Stick with it for a week and you will see changes.

session_21.text: My father has just completed early rehabilitation for a neurological disease. I would like to know the specific methods and precautions for home training to avoid secondary injury.

session_21.text: What you need are active and passive training movements for the affected limb, daily training frequency and intensity, and key points for safety monitoring, right?

session_21.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_21.text: Recommended 2-3 times a day, 15-20 minutes each session, with slow, steady movements. Active training includes fist clenching and finger extension; passive training includes wrist flexion, extension, and rotation. Watch for facial color and heart rate; stop immediately if dizziness or pain occurs. Rehabilitation progress includes increased joint range of motion and improved muscle strength. If sudden weakness or slurred speech occurs, seek emergency medical care.

session_25.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_25.text: My father is doing standing and walking training after a stroke. I'd like to learn how to safely assess his fatigue threshold to prevent falls, and what manual techniques can promote neuroplasticity?

session_25.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_25.text: It is recommended to use the Borg Rating of Perceived Exertion (RPE) scale to assess fatigue. Measure blood pressure and heart rate before training; pause if systolic blood pressure >180 or diastolic >100. Walking training should be done in 5-10 minute sessions, divided into 2-3 sets, with 2 minutes of rest between sets. To prevent falls, fix the walker height (level with the greater trochanter of the femur) and arrange a barrier-free passage. To promote neuroplasticity, mirror therapy and symmetrical bilateral limb movement training can be used, 2 times a day for 15 minutes each time.

session_25.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_25.text: Understood. I've recorded the gait angle and muscle strength changes, but how can these data be connected to the rehabilitation therapist's home care?

For nutrition, ensure daily protein intake of 1.2–1.5 g/kg body weight. To prevent joint contractures, passively move all joints 2 times a day, with 10 full-range movements for each joint.

session_27.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_27.text: My father was just discharged from the hospital today and returned to the old house in Luoyang. In the afternoon, I consulted a rehabilitation therapist at the community center and did the first slow walking and finger exercises. As a doctor, I want to confirm: if my father feels mild pain during training, should we pause or reduce the intensity? How should we adjust the daily training volume according to his tolerance?

session_27.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_27.text: It is recommended to follow the "no pain" principle: if mild soreness or fatigue appears, you can reduce the intensity (for example, reduce the number of slow walking round trips to one and halve the grip exercises), but if there is real pain, stop immediately and rest. Daily training can be divided into 2–3 sessions, each no more than 20 minutes, increasing gradually. Pay attention to your father's facial expression and breathing, and use his ability to perform the movements comfortably as the standard.

session_27.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_27.text: Understood. Also, my father is taking aspirin and antihypertensive drugs. Should rehabilitation training be staggered with medication times? Are there any special dietary precautions?

session_27.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_27.text: It is recommended that training be arranged 1-2 hours after taking medication to avoid peak drug concentration affecting blood pressure or increasing bleeding risk (for aspirin). For diet, low-salt, low-fat, high-protein foods (such as fish and soy products) and foods rich in dietary fiber (such as oatmeal and vegetables) are recommended to control blood pressure and promote nerve repair. Avoid high-sugar and greasy foods, and drink more water to prevent constipation.

session_27.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_27.text: Today I picked up Dad from the hospital and returned to the old house in Luoyang. Mom made hulatang soup and huimian noodles. The family talked about my childhood memories of setting off fireworks and buying zodiac commemorative coins. It felt especially happy.

session_27.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_27.text: This is truly a precious moment: father's recovery and family reunion bring a warmth that is deeply moving. The story about the commemorative coin sounds very interesting, and you can feel the calm and joy in your heart.

session_27.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_27.text: Mhm, Dad talked about the details of taking my brother and me to set off fireworks. I put food on his plate and told him to eat slowly. At that moment, I felt all the hard work was worth it.

session_27.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_27.text: The little moments between you and your father are priceless. This joy of reunion should be cherished. After returning to Zhengzhou, remember to take care of yourself so the family can continue to feel at ease.

session_27.text: This moment is so precious—your father's smile is a positive sign of recovery, and the photo also carries the warmth of the neighborhood. Do you want to keep this feeling to yourself, or consider sharing it on Moments and other social platforms to record your mood and spread warmth?

session_29.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_29.text: COPD vs. asthma: COPD has persistent airflow limitation (smoking history, irreversible); asthma has intermittent episodes (allergy history, reversible) + positive bronchodilator test. A 2-hour block of study is enough; in the morning, 1.5 hours for difficult points + 0.5 hours for practice questions, and the same rhythm in the afternoon. Before bed, use mindful breathing to relax for 5 minutes to avoid excessive tension.

session_30.text: Yes, I especially want to know about job prospects, time costs, and whether studying rehabilitation while preparing for the attending physician exam has any conflicts.

session_30.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_30.text: Rehabilitation medicine and internal medicine are highly synergistic; your respiratory medicine knowledge gives you a strong advantage in pulmonary rehabilitation. I suggest three steps: 1) First obtain the added qualification of rehabilitation physician (1–2 years of further training can meet the requirement); 2) When preparing the application, use the framing of 'department service extension' and emphasize how internal medicine–rehabilitation synergy benefits the department's performance; 3) The content for the attending physician exam overlaps with the basics of rehabilitation medicine, so you can study them in parallel.

I would like to apply for a six-month rotation in the rehabilitation department, and when I come back, I can lead the department to develop respiratory rehabilitation services and improve overall service quality." session_31.text: Today I'm reviewing the cardiovascular system. I always confuse the ECGs of angina pectoris and myocardial infarction, and I'm also unclear about the principles of drug selection for heart failure. Could you help me sort it out?

session_31.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_31.text: Okay. In angina, common ECG findings are ST-segment depression (stable angina) or transient ST-segment elevation (variant angina), whereas ST-elevation myocardial infarction presents with persistent convex upward ST-segment elevation with pathological Q waves. Heart failure medications by stage: stage A/B use ACEI/ARB plus beta-blockers to prevent remodeling; stage C add diuretics to control symptoms, and digitalis if necessary; stage D requires inotropes or device therapy. Do you need me to further detail the differential points or risk stratification?

session_31.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_31.text: Yes, especially the indications for thrombolysis and intervention in acute ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction, and the specific timing of drug selection for heart failure staging. Could you explain it more systematically?

session_31.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_31.text: For STEMI within 12 hours of onset, emergency PCI is the first choice; if the patient cannot reach it within 120 minutes, thrombolysis may be performed. Heart failure stages: Stage A with high-risk factors, use ACEI/ARB; Stage B asymptomatic heart failure, add beta-blockers; Stage C symptomatic, add diuretics + aldosterone antagonists + digitalis; Stage D refractory, requires heart transplantation or left ventricular assist device. I suggest you make a comparison table and mnemonics to reinforce.

session_32.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_32.text: Yu Xiaowen: When I review my heart failure notes, I'm a bit confused about the preferred choice between ARB and ACEI in different NYHA classes. How should LVEF and symptom weighting be combined with risk stratification? Could you help me sort it out?

session_32.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_32.text: Don't worry, this is a commonly tested point. ACEI/ARB are first-line for all HFrEF (LVEF ≤ 40%), recommended for NYHA class II-IV, but ACEIs have stronger evidence (e.g., the SOLVD trial). ARBs are used for ACEI intolerance (e.g., cough, angioedema). Risk stratification is mainly based on NYHA class (symptoms) and LVEF (objective measure): NYHA class III-IV plus LVEF < 35% indicates high risk, requiring consideration of ICD or CRT. Memory aid: ACE first, ARB as backup; LVEF ≤ 40, NYHA determines high risk.

session_32.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_32.text: Yu Xiaowen: Got it. Then in what situations should beta-blockers and aldosterone antagonists be used with caution?

session_32.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_32.text: Beta-blockers should be used with caution in acute heart failure, severe bradycardia, and asthma; aldosterone antagonists should be used with caution in hyperkalemia (serum potassium >5.5) and severe renal insufficiency (eGFR <30). When the two are combined, electrolytes and blood pressure need to be monitored. Clinical decision: first use diuretics to reduce edema, then ACEI/ARB plus beta-blockers, then add aldosterone antagonists. This stepwise medication approach is safer and more effective.

session_33.text: During passive stretching, protect the shoulder joint and avoid exceeding 90 degrees to prevent subluxation. session_33.text: This afternoon I reviewed the respiratory system and did 40 practice questions with a 72% accuracy rate. I want to focus on understanding the typical blood gas analysis changes during acute asthma attacks, and the difficulties in distinguishing COPD acute exacerbation from asthma attacks.

session_33.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_33.text: In the early stage of an acute asthma exacerbation, hyperventilation causes respiratory alkalosis (PaO2↓, PaCO2↓, pH↑). As the condition worsens, airway obstruction causes PaCO2 to rise again or even respiratory acidosis. Key points for differentiation: COPD is more common in middle-aged and elderly patients with a smoking history and persistent dyspnea, while asthma is mostly episodic wheezing with a positive bronchodilator test.

session_45.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_45.text: For a low-grade fever, physical cooling is the first choice: wipe the forehead and limbs with a warm damp towel. For nasal congestion, you can inhale steam (breathe in steam from a cup of hot water) or rinse the nose with saline. For a sore throat, drink warm honey-lemon water or gargle with light salt water. Cold medicine containing acetaminophen can reduce fever, but avoid repeated use. If the dizziness worsens tomorrow or the high fever persists, you need to see a doctor. Rest more tonight and keep the room humid.

session_45.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_45.text: I was previously taking compound paracetamol and amantadine. Do I need to switch medication? Is soaking my feet useful?

session_45.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_45.text: Compound paracetamol and amantadine hydrochloride contains acetaminophen and can reduce fever, so there is no need to change medication, but do not take it with other fever reducers. Soaking your feet can help promote circulation and relieve fatigue, but be careful that the water temperature is not too high (around 40°C) and the duration is 15–20 minutes. If you sweat after soaking your feet, dry off promptly and keep warm to avoid catching a cold.

session_45.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_45.text: My father is in the recovery period after a myocardial infarction and has slight edema in his ankles. I want to know whether this is cardiogenic edema or caused by reduced activity. Also, I plan to help him with passive joint exercises and walking a few steps with a walker tomorrow. Is this plan safe?

session_45.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_45.text: Your father is 56 years old and in the recovery period after a myocardial infarction. The lower limb edema needs to be differentiated: if it is pitting edema, worsens in the afternoon, and is accompanied by shortness of breath, it suggests a cardiogenic cause; if it is light in the morning and heavy in the evening and improves with activity, it may be poor venous return. At present, the edema is mild. It is recommended to start with a low-salt diet and elevating the lower limbs, and observe the pressing rebound. Passive joint movement and walking with a walker are feasible when blood pressure and heart rate are stable (resting heart rate <100, systolic blood pressure 90-130 mmHg), but avoid exertion. Each session should not exceed 10 minutes, and monitor for chest tightness and shortness of breath.

session_45.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_45.text: I understand. So what specific passive joint mobility exercises are there? How should the walker height be adjusted? Also, at what level of swelling should rehabilitation be paused and medical attention sought?

session_45.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_45.text: Passive joint range-of-motion: from distal to proximal, ankle pumps (10 seconds each of plantarflexion and dorsiflexion, 5 reps per set), knee flexion/extension, hip adduction/abduction, 2-3 times a day, with gentle force. Walker height: when standing, the handles should be level with the wrist crease, and the elbows flexed 15-20 degrees. Indications to stop and seek medical attention: swelling worsens to obvious pitting after pressing (>2mm), or the appearance of shortness of breath, chest pain, or coughing up pink frothy sputum.

session_56.text: If I directly cite a rate from the literature, do I need to rephrase it? For example, the original says 'accounts for 30%', can I write 'the usage rate is 30% (12/40)'?

session_56.text: If the original text does not provide a denominator, I suggest noting the data source and stating, 'According to XX study, the medication use rate is 30%.' session_58.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_58.text: Of course. For missing data, multiple imputation or listwise deletion is commonly used, depending on the proportion and mechanism of missingness. The Cox proportional hazards assumption can be tested with Schoenfeld residuals; if P>0.05, it is satisfied. Censoring in KM curves is usually indicated by vertical tick marks (plus signs), and the risk table shows the number of remaining subjects at each time point, helping to interpret the reliability of the curve.

session_58.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_58.text: If the assumption is not met, consider stratified Cox regression or adding time interaction terms. The KM curve focuses on displaying survival probability trends and uses the log-rank test for comparison between groups; at the same time, pay attention to whether the censoring distribution is balanced. I suggest you ask Dr. Li with these points tomorrow, and it will be more efficient.

session_60.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_60.text: I understand your concerns. Mirror therapy is recommended 2–3 times a day, 15–20 minutes each time. The key is to have your father focus on watching the movement of the healthy foot and imagine the affected side moving in sync. Mental practice can be combined with passive massage: first guide him to imagine with his eyes closed for 5 minutes, then follow with gentle massage. Be careful to avoid excessive fatigue; the criterion is that your father feels no pain.

session_60.speaker: Yu Xiaowen

session_60.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_60.text: Emotionally, I suggest setting aside 10 minutes each day for a 'progress review' and using data (such as walking distance from 100 meters to 150 meters) as positive reinforcement. Electrical stimulation may be considered, such as transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS), as an aid when muscle strength is below grade 2, but it requires evaluation by a physician. Hydrotherapy is very safe; a water temperature of 32-34°C is recommended, 20 minutes per session, with attention to slip prevention. Consult the attending physician before trying any new therapy.

session_60.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_60.text: Understood. I'll first try the mirror therapy frequency you suggested for a week, and adjust the way I communicate emotions. I'll decide on hydrotherapy after the assessment.

session_60.text: Very good. I suggest recording progress every 3 days with a balance score (e.g., BBS), and take care to avoid secondary injury: keep walkways in the home clear of obstacles during training, and your father should wear non-slip shoes. If there is stinging pain or dizziness, stop immediately. Wish you a smooth recovery.

session_70.text: I just reviewed the potassium supplementation formula for patients with complicated heart failure. I'm going on rounds with Dr. Li this afternoon and I'm afraid of calculating it wrong. In this formula, the initial serum potassium is 3.0 mmol/L, potassium is supplemented at 0.4 mmol/kg, and body weight is 60 kg. Should the supplement be 0.4*60=24 mmol? Is the unit mmol of potassium chloride?

session_70.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_70.text: Yes, the potassium supplementation formula is usually expressed in millimoles (mmol) of potassium chloride. For an initial serum potassium of 3.0 mmol/L, the amount to supplement is 0.4 mmol/kg × 60 kg = 24 mmol. But note: ① The target serum potassium is recommended to be 4.0-4.5 mmol/L; ② It needs to be adjusted based on renal function, urine output, and diuretic use to avoid the risk of hyperkalemia; ③ Clinically, 10% potassium chloride solution is commonly used, with 1 g containing 13.4 mmol of potassium; calculate how many grams you need.

session_70.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_70.text: If a patient has low urine output or is taking spironolactone, should the potassium supplement dose be halved? Also, Teacher Li mentioned key points about anticoagulation. Could you explain how to coordinate electrolytes and anticoagulation using a similar case?

session_70.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_70.text: Yes, if urine output is low or a potassium-sparing diuretic (such as spironolactone) is used, the potassium supplement should be reduced to 50%-70% of the original plan, with close monitoring of serum potassium. A similar case: a 60 kg heart failure patient with serum potassium 3.2, on furosemide and spironolactone. Supplement potassium at 0.3 mmol/kg, i.e., 18 mmol. At the same time, assess the INR (if on warfarin) or direct anticoagulant doses to avoid bleeding. Anticoagulation and potassium supplementation are not closely related, but note that hypokalemia can easily induce arrhythmias, so anticoagulation should be more cautious. You can explain it this way to Dr. Li this afternoon.

session_76.speaker: Yu Xiaowen

session_76.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_76.text: Yes, a p < 0.05 in Levene's test indicates unequal variances, so use the corrected t value in the second row. Remember the mnemonic: 'Equal variances look at the first row, unequal look at the second; if p is less than 0.05, the difference is significant.'

session_85.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_85.text: I just talked with the director about transitioning to rehabilitation medicine. He suggested I publish a paper in a core journal and said he would help arrange for me to shadow Director Li in the rehabilitation department. session_85.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_85.text: What you currently need is a systematic path from thesis topic selection to clinical shadowing learning, including how to use the case resources of general internal medicine to enter the rehabilitation field, right?

session_85.text: Yes, especially which one is easier to get started with between case reports and review articles, and what to focus on observing during clinical shadowing.

session_85.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_85.text: I suggest prioritizing case reports—rehabilitation medicine journals such as the Chinese Journal of Rehabilitation Medicine are quite receptive to case reports. You can start with common stroke and post-fracture patients in general internal medicine and record the efficacy of early rehabilitation intervention. During clinical shadowing, focus on observing Director Li's assessment process, rehabilitation goal setting, and communication style with patients; after each shadowing session, organize 3 key observations.

session_85.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_85.text: What does the writing framework for a case report generally look like? Also, I have a lot of night shifts now—how can I squeeze out time to complete these plans?

session_85.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_85.text: A case report usually includes an introduction, case description, discussion, and conclusion, with a length of 2,500–3,500 characters; the core is to highlight the uniqueness and effectiveness of rehabilitation intervention. In terms of time management, it is recommended to set aside 30 minutes each day for literature reading or writing (for example, during gaps in night shifts), use fragmented time to record key points from cases, and also confirm with the department director whether you can adjust shifts during daytime clinic observation.

session_86.text: My father is 56 years old. Tonight he said his knee was uncomfortable, so I helped him walk a bit. As a doctor, I would like to understand the possible causes and home care options.

session_86.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_86.text: Your father's condition may be knee osteoarthritis or meniscal degeneration, and it needs to be judged based on specific symptoms. Would you like to start with daily protection, exercise rehabilitation, or indications for medical treatment?

session_86.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_86.text: First, daily protection and appropriate exercises, such as methods to strengthen the quadriceps, as well as the timing for hot and cold compresses.

session_86.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_86.text: Suggestion: 1. Apply a cold compress for 15 minutes per session for acute pain, and a hot compress for 20 minutes per session for chronic stiffness. 2. Do straight-leg raises and wall sits (knees not beyond toes) every day, 10 reps per set, 3 sets per day. 3. Avoid weight-bearing activities such as squats and mountain climbing, and wear a knee brace to support the patella. 4. If symptoms persist for more than 2 weeks or are accompanied by swelling, it is recommended to visit the orthopedics/rehabilitation department. Glucosamine can be used as a supplementary aid, but its effect varies from person to person.

session_91.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_91.text: My father is 56 years old and has limited mobility after a cerebral infarction. I have booked daily physical therapy at Zhengzhou Jihe Rehabilitation Center starting April 5. I would like to know whether the specific training content, duration, and intensity are suitable for him, and what care and monitoring need to be coordinated at home?

session_91.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_91.text: Your father is in the sequelae phase after a cerebral infarction; the golden period for rehabilitation is the first 6 months. Physical therapy usually includes balance training, joint mobility exercises, and muscle strength recovery. Each session is recommended to last 45-60 minutes, and the intensity should be increased gradually based on tolerance. You have already made an appointment with a professional institution; the key is family cooperation: daily assisted standing and walking practice, home modifications to prevent falls, a low-salt and low-fat diet, and monitoring of blood pressure, mood, and whether limb numbness worsens.

session_91.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_91.text: Thank you! So how exactly can we do assisted training at home? Are there any nutrients to supplement in the diet, such as vitamins or protein?

session_91.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_91.text: Home-assisted training can be done 3–4 times a day, with 15–20 minutes per session of sit-to-stand exercises, passive range-of-motion exercises for the affected joints (within a pain-free range), and slow walking with support. For diet, it is recommended to increase high-quality protein (eggs, fish) and B vitamins while avoiding high salt and fat. It is advised to use a simple scale (such as the Fugl-Meyer motor function score) weekly to record progress. If dizziness, chest tightness, or other symptoms occur, stop immediately and contact the physician.

session_91.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_91.text: You want to balance empathy and principles, maintaining both gentleness and decisiveness in a high-pressure medical environment and family caregiving, right?

session_91.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_91.text: Yes, for example, in my father's rehabilitation training, I often soften the plan because I can't bear to see him struggle. How can I carry it out firmly without hurting feelings?

session_91.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_91.text: You can try setting clear rehabilitation milestones and use the approach of 'Let's finish this set together, then rest for 5 minutes,' which both respects his feelings and anchors the goal. In doctor-patient communication, use 'I understand your concerns, but for the sake of recovery, let's try this plan together' to build trust.

session_92.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_92.text: I just finished learning about skewed distributions. The median is more representative of central tendency than the mean, but I don't quite understand the specific reason. Can you explain?

session_92.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_92.text: Okay. In a skewed distribution, extreme values significantly pull the mean, while the median is unaffected by extreme values and reflects the central position more stably. Take hospital length of stay, which you are familiar with, as an example: most patients are discharged after a short stay (e.g., 3 days), but a few stay long-term (e.g., 30 days). The mean gets pulled up (e.g., 5.5 days), while the median might be only 3 days, better representing the typical patient's length of stay.

session_92.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_92.text: I see. So in actual research papers, if the data are heavily skewed, should the median be reported instead of the mean?

session_92.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_92.text: Yes. A general recommendation is: if the absolute value of the skewness coefficient is greater than 1 or there are obvious outliers in the data, report the median and interquartile range as a priority. In medical research, the median is commonly used for variables such as length of hospital stay, cost, and disease duration. At the same time, combine box plots or histograms to show the distribution shape and enhance persuasiveness.

session_101.text: I just ran a one-sample t-test in SPSS using case data: the effect of a certain antihypertensive drug on systolic blood pressure. I started with Analyze → Compare Means → One-Sample T Test, but I'm not sure whether the data format needs one row per subject. Also, how should I write the conclusion in the paper for the results t=-2.45, p=0.018, 95%CI[-5.3, -0.7]?

session_101.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_101.text: Your operation steps are correct. The data format is one participant's measurement value per row. Interpreting the results: t=-2.45 indicates the sample mean is lower than the test value; p=0.018 <0.05 rejects H0, so the antihypertensive drug is considered to effectively lower systolic blood pressure. The 95% CI [-5.3, -0.7] indicates that the average reduction ranges from 0.7 to 5.3 mmHg. The conclusion of the paper can be written as: The one-sample t-test showed that after taking the antihypertensive drug, systolic blood pressure was significantly lower than 140 mmHg (t=-2.45, df=29, p=0.018, 95% CI -5.3 to -0.7).

session_101.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_101.text: I see. Do I still need to report the effect size? SPSS doesn't give it directly. How do I calculate it manually?

session_101.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_101.text: It is recommended to report Cohen's d = mean difference / standard deviation, reflecting effect size. Formula: d = Mean Difference / SD. In your case, the mean difference is -3; if SD = 6, then d = -0.5, which is a medium effect. In the paper, you can add: Cohen's d = -0.5, indicating moderate clinical significance. In an exam, if the question requires it, you must report it; otherwise, it is optional.

session_106.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_106.text: Okay. The rehabilitation plan can set phased small goals: for example, increase leg raises by one set each day this week (from 3 sets to 4), and extend walking time by 2 minutes. For emotional support, try the "positive feedback method" — after each exercise, point out specific progress details (such as "the calf raise angle is 10 degrees higher than the day before yesterday"), while distracting him with topics he is interested in, such as recalling stories from his youth. Also, I suggest you record daily progress, and when you walk farther with him on the weekend, compare the data to build his confidence.

session_106.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_106.text: I am a resident physician. I taught myself SPSS to do a paired-sample t-test and want to confirm whether my operation and understanding are correct. For example, should the data entry format be one row per pair, and then click Analyze → Compare Means → Paired-Samples T Test?

session_106.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_106.text: Yes, the paired-samples t-test requires data from repeated measures or matched designs, with each pair of data on one row; the SPSS path is correct. In the output, focus on the t-value, degrees of freedom (df), and two-tailed p-value. Usually p < 0.05 indicates a statistically significant difference. Also note that the effect size (Cohen's d) can help assess clinical significance.

session_106.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_106.text: What is the core difference between that and the independent samples t-test? Sometimes I'm not sure whether to use paired or independent.

session_106.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_106.text: Key distinction: the paired t-test is applicable to before-and-after measurements on the same group of subjects (e.g., before and after treatment) or matched pairs (e.g., case-control), emphasizing that the data are not independent; the independent t-test is applicable to two independent samples (e.g., experimental group vs control group). It is recommended to check whether the data are paired/correlated - if so, use the paired test; otherwise, use the independent test. In operation, the independent t-test is in the Independent-Samples T Test menu, and you need to define the grouping variable.

session_106.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_106.text: Got it. Then I'll practice more with the clinical data. Thanks!

session_106.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_106.text: You're welcome. I suggest using the department's real data (such as blood pressure values before and after medication) to practice repeatedly and compare with the result tables output by SPSS. If you have any specific questions about interpreting the results, feel free to come and discuss again.

session_111.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_111.text: I admitted a pneumonia patient today. I want to compare his white blood cell counts before and after treatment with data from previous similar cases. Should I use an independent samples t-test or a chi-square test in this situation?

session_111.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_111.text: You are dealing with a comparison of two independent sets of quantitative data (new patients vs. previous cases). The t-test is suitable for quantitative data that are normally distributed and have equal variances; the chi-square test is used for categorical variables. It is recommended to first check whether the white blood cell count satisfies normality (e.g., Shapiro–Wilk test). If the sample size is small or the distribution is skewed, consider the non-parametric Mann–Whitney U test.

session_111.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_111.text: Understood. But if I want to compare the treatment effectiveness rates (effective/ineffective) of two groups of patients, should I use the chi-square test? Also, what are the standards for presenting statistical results in a paper?

session_111.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_111.text: Yes, efficacy comparison uses the chi-square test for a 2x2 table. Note that when the sample size is <40 or the expected frequency is <5, Fisher's exact test or Yates' correction should be used. In papers, it is usually written as “χ²=value, P=value”, along with percentages, for example, “the treatment group had an effective rate of 85% and the control group 60%, a statistically significant difference (χ²=5.23, P=0.022)”. In the SPSS output, pay attention to the chi-square value, degrees of freedom, and asymptotic significance.

session_136.text: For the paper revision, I need to change the t-test to a chi-square test. I'm not sure about the specific applicability conditions and the SPSS operation steps. Could you help me sort it out?

session_136.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_136.text: The chi-square test is used for categorical variables (such as sex and diagnostic results), while the t-test is used for continuous variables (such as blood pressure values). If your outcome variable is categorical data, choose chi-square. SPSS operation: Analyze → Descriptive Statistics → Crosstabs, put the row variable and column variable in, click Statistics, check Chi-square, and run. Note that the sample size should be no less than 40 and the expected frequency should be no less than 5.

session_136.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_136.text: Understood. My data are the recovery statuses (yes/no) from the two-year follow-up, which are categorical variables. How should I interpret the chi-square value in the results, and what are the key points to note when explaining the method change to the journal?

session_136.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_136.text: When interpreting, pay attention to the significance of the Pearson chi-square value (p<0.05 indicates a statistically significant difference). When reporting to the journal, briefly state that the t-test was originally used and then changed to chi-square based on the variable type (categorical variables), and attach the SPSS output tables to ensure the method selection matches the variables.

session_136.text: Today I used Anki to review the differentiation between cerebral hemorrhage and cerebral infarction, but some key points are still easy to confuse. session_136.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_136.text: Of course. On CT, cerebral hemorrhage appears as a hyperdense lesion, commonly seen in hypertension; cerebral infarction appears as a hypodense lesion, commonly seen in cardioembolism or atherosclerosis. In terms of treatment, cerebral hemorrhage requires blood pressure control and surgical decompression, while cerebral infarction requires intravenous thrombolysis (within 4.5 hours) or mechanical thrombectomy. Memory aid: "Hemorrhage is hyperdense, lower the pressure; infarction is hypodense, thrombolyze quickly." Would you like me to elaborate on each differentiating point?

session_136.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_136.text: This mnemonic is really practical! Can you also compare the characteristics of neurological deficits and the time of onset?

session_136.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_136.text: Cerebral hemorrhage often strikes suddenly during activity or emotional agitation, presenting with severe headache, vomiting, and impaired consciousness; cerebral infarction often begins during rest or sleep, with symptoms progressing gradually, and hemiplegia and speech disorders are common. Onset during sleep strongly suggests infarction. I suggest you review with the table. Do you need me to generate a comparison table?

session_137.text: I'm going hiking on Shaoshi Mountain in Songshan tomorrow. I'd like to confirm the recommended route, tomorrow's weather in Zhengzhou and Dengfeng, and the safety precautions I need to note.

session_137.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_137.text: Recommended classic route for Shaoshi Mountain: Sanhuangzhai → Shaolin Temple, about 10 kilometers in total, moderate difficulty, nice scenery but some steep steps. Tomorrow, May 18, in Dengfeng the weather will be cloudy turning overcast, 18–28°C, with possible showers in the afternoon. It is recommended to wear quick-dry clothing plus a waterproof shell jacket. Safety: protect your knees; use knee pads and trekking poles when going up and down steps. A first aid kit is ready. session_137.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_137.text: Knee protection: warm up fully before hiking (wall sit 30 seconds x 3 sets), rest 5 minutes after every 40 minutes of walking, and when going downhill shift your center of gravity slightly backward, keep your knees slightly bent, and avoid fully straightening them. If pain worsens, immediately use the elastic bandage in the first-aid kit to apply pressure and immobilize the knee, reduce weight-bearing, and consider returning the same way from Sanhuangzhai (shorter distance). Preventing getting lost: download offline maps on your phone in advance (2bulu or Amap), stay on the main trail, and check your location with Sun Yue every half hour. If you are out of contact for more than 30 minutes, call the scenic area rescue number 0371-62800000.

session_138.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_138.text: Set out at 6 this morning and climbed Mount Song with my good friend Sun Yue. Finally reached the 1,492-meter Junji Peak! I almost gave up on the Sky Ladder section, but luckily she encouraged me. At the summit, I shouted toward the valley and felt months of stress melt away. Now I'm home soaking my feet, feeling really fulfilled.

session_138.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_138.text: You not only want to share the joy of summiting, but also hope to let this energy of 'pushing boundaries' settle into motivation for your future work and life, right?

session_138.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_138.text: Right! At the summit I wrote 'Broaden the Boundaries,' but I don't know how to apply this mountaineering spirit to daily life, especially when residency work is so busy.

session_138.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_138.text: You can break down the climb into small goals: like climbing a heavenly ladder, divide each day's thorny tasks into 100 steps, and give yourself a small reward after each section. Next time you feel you can't hold on during a night shift, recall the feeling of looking down from the summit and tell yourself that you've already reached Junji Peak, so you can finish this stretch too.

session_138.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_138.text: I hiked for over 6 hours with 800 meters of elevation gain today. Now my whole body is sore, especially my thighs and back. I might be on duty tomorrow. Are there any quick recovery methods?

session_138.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_138.text: Delayed-onset muscle soreness is very common after high-intensity hiking. It is recommended to do gentle static stretching now (hold each movement for 15-30 seconds) and avoid intense stretching. You can use a foam roller to gently roll over the front of the thighs and the calves, avoiding the joints. Apply a warm compress tonight for 15 minutes to promote circulation, supplement protein and electrolytes, and ensure 7-8 hours of sleep. If the soreness is obvious tomorrow, consider short-term use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen, but be mindful of fasting status and allergy history.

session_138.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_138.text: Thank you. So should I take a hot bath first now? Also, my knee feels a little tight. Do I need to wear a knee brace?

session_138.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_138.text: Soaking in a hot bath can relax muscles, but the water temperature should not be too high (around 40°C), and the duration should be controlled to 15-20 minutes. Tightness in the knee may be joint fatigue or mild inflammation. It is not recommended to wear a knee brace immediately to avoid dependence. You can first do static stretching of the quadriceps and hamstrings. If walking still causes discomfort tomorrow, consider using a sports knee brace. In addition, check for local redness, swelling, heat, and pain; if present, be alert to inflammation.

session_141.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_141.text: My father is in the recovery phase of a cerebral infarction and has difficulty moving. Today I saw a demonstration of a lower-limb rehabilitation robot with a stride length of 35 cm and a step frequency of 80 steps/min. Is this device suitable for him?

session_141.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_141.text: Lower-limb exoskeleton robots are generally suitable for patients at Brunnstrom stage III or above. If your father has reached this stage, the adaptive training mode (from passive to resistive) can improve gait in a targeted way. It is recommended to first evaluate his muscle strength and balance ability.

session_141.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_141.text: So what exactly should I do for the rehabilitation medicine rotation? Li Wei suggested I go, but I'm not clear about the path and schedule.

session_141.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_141.text: You can apply to the head of the neurology department for a short-term rotation (usually 1-3 months), focusing on rehabilitation assessment, robot indications, and the collaborative process with the neurology department. At the same time, pay attention to medical insurance policies; some provinces and cities have already covered rehabilitation robot therapy.

session_141.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_141.text: My father is in the recovery stage of a cerebral infarction, with muscle strength below grade 3. He can sit independently but needs help to stand. Today I showed him a rehabilitation robot video, and he is worried about the cost. session_141.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_141.text: At Grade A tertiary hospitals in Zhengzhou, a single session of lower-limb rehabilitation robot training costs about 200-400 yuan, and medical insurance does not yet cover this (it is not included in Henan Province's rehabilitation catalog). However, for patients with muscle strength below grade 3 who can sit independently, the assisted standing training mode can be used, making it suitable for early intervention. It is recommended to try it once or twice first to evaluate the effect.

session_141.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_141.text: I've learned about the cost and medical insurance situation. My father is conservative by nature and has concerns about new technology. How can I explain the value of the robot to him in simple terms so he is willing to try it?

session_141.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_141.text: You can use the analogy: ‘The robot is like a personal rehabilitation coach, precisely assisting your standing practice and reducing the risk of falls.’ Emphasize that a short-term trial (rental or trial lesson) requires no long-term investment, and share the case of a similar patient who recovered the ability to walk within three months. At the same time, if you accompany him during practice, it will increase his sense of security.

session_142.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_142.text: Tonight I reviewed the flashcards on anemia and leukemia, but I still have questions about distinguishing iron-deficiency anemia from thalassemia. Can you help me sort out the key points?

session_142.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_142.text: Okay. Main distinguishing points: iron deficiency anemia is microcytic hypochromic, with decreased serum iron and ferritin, and increased total iron-binding capacity; thalassemia is also microcytic hypochromic, but serum iron is normal or increased, and hemoglobin electrophoresis shows abnormal hemoglobin (e.g., elevated HbA2, HbF). Clinically, family history and regional characteristics are relevant.

session_142.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_142.text: I understand, thank you. Also, I always get confused about the FAB classification of acute leukemia. Can you briefly list it?

session_142.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_142.text: The FAB classification divides acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) into L1, L2, and L3, and acute myeloid leukemia (AML) into M0 through M7, of which M3 is acute promyelocytic leukemia, and DIC must be watched for. Focus on remembering the characteristics of each type, such as M6 erythroleukemia and M7 megakaryocytic leukemia.

session_153.text: I just watched a wheel-throwing video on Xiaohongshu. I'm a bit confused about the key points of "centering" and "opening." Could you explain in detail the basic steps and common mistakes of wheel throwing? I mainly do hand-building and am not familiar with the pottery wheel yet.

session_153.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_153.text: Centering is the key to throwing on the wheel: wrap both hands around the clay ball, press evenly toward the center with the base of your palms, brace your elbows against your thighs to steady your arms, and the clay ball spins into a concentric cone. When opening, press your thumb vertically down to leave the bottom thickness, then expand outward at a steady speed. Common mistakes are uneven pressure causing the clay to go off-center, and opening too deeply which can easily collapse. It is recommended to practice centering for 10 minutes before attempting to open.

session_153.speaker: Yu Xiaowen

session_153.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_153.text: The studio usually provides clay and basic tools; it's recommended to bring your own apron and towel. Beginners should use porcelain clay or red terracotta, which are more ductile and less likely to collapse. Safety: roll up sleeves and tie back long hair to avoid getting caught in clothing or equipment; set the pottery wheel to low speed first, then increase speed once you're proficient. session_154.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_154.text: I'm writing a paper on orthopedic rehabilitation and need to use propensity score matching (PSM) to balance baseline data. Can you first briefly explain its principles and applicable scenarios?

session_154.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_154.text: PSM is a method for eliminating confounding bias in non-randomized studies. It uses logistic regression to calculate the probability of each sample receiving treatment (the propensity score), then matches the treatment group and control group based on the scores. It is suitable for observational studies or retrospective data, for example, comparing the effects of two surgical approaches. The difference from logistic regression is that PSM matches first and then analyzes, while logistic regression directly controls covariates.

session_154.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_154.text: Got it. Then how can I quickly implement PSM in SPSS? Also, I have data from several previous papers and need to do a comparative analysis with them. Do you have any strategies?

session_154.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_154.text: In SPSS, you can use the PS Matching extension plug-in (needs to be downloaded). Steps: 1) Define matching variables and exact matching criteria; 2) Set the caliper value (0.02-0.05); 3) Perform matching and check balance. For literature comparison, it is suggested to first unify inclusion criteria and outcome indicators, and use a forest plot to show the similarities and differences in effect sizes. In the discussion section, focus on explaining reasons for differences (such as population, follow-up time, and methodology). When submitting, pay attention to the target journal's requirements for word count (usually 5,000-8,000 words) and figure/table formats. The Cover Letter should emphasize innovation and clinical significance.

session_154.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_154.text: Thank you! I'll organize my thoughts this evening and try SPSS again tomorrow. Can you be more specific about the key points for writing a Cover Letter? For example, how to attract the editor's attention at the beginning?

session_154.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_154.text: In the opening sentence of the cover letter, state the core contribution of the study, for example: “We present a propensity score–matched analysis comparing [procedure A] vs [procedure B] in [population], demonstrating significantly better [outcome] with comparable safety.” Then explain that it fits the journal's scope and declare that it has not been submitted elsewhere. End by expressing expectations for peer review. It is recommended to keep it within 200 words.

session_162.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_162.text: Agent, I almost prescribed 50 mg of Plendil (felodipine) just now. Luckily my supervising teacher reminded me. I need to confirm the usual dose, maximum dose, common side effects, and interactions with other drugs for Plendil to avoid making the same mistake again.

session_162.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_162.text: For Plendil (felodipine), the recommended starting dose is 5 mg once daily, the maintenance dose is 5-10 mg once daily, and the maximum dose is 20 mg once daily. Common side effects include headache and peripheral edema (especially ankle), usually dose-related. When used in combination with other antihypertensive drugs (such as beta-blockers), attention should be paid to the risk of hypotension; when used with CYP3A4 inhibitors (such as ketoconazole), the dose should be adjusted. Would you like to know about adjustment plans for a specific patient?

session_162.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_162.text: Yes, I am admitting a 65-year-old female patient with mild abnormal liver function (ALT 60 U/L) and no other medications. Is a starting dose of 5 mg appropriate for her? Are special adjustments needed?

session_162.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_162.text: For patients with mild liver function abnormalities, it is recommended to start with 2.5 mg once daily, adjust every 2 weeks based on tolerance and blood pressure response, and a maximum dose of no more than 10 mg. Plendil is mainly metabolized by the liver; hepatic impairment can increase plasma concentration. At the same time, monitoring for ankle edema is recommended, and combination with an ACEI/ARB may be considered to reduce this side effect. If severe headache or hypotension occurs, the drug should be discontinued promptly for evaluation.

session_162.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_162.text: Understood. I'll start with 2.5 mg and regularly recheck liver function and blood pressure. Also, I had insomnia last night and am worried it will affect my daytime concentration. Are there any quick strategies to improve focus?

session_162.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_162.text: Your plan is reasonable. I suggest marking the starting dose in the medical order and setting a reminder. As for focus, you can try briefly closing your eyes and taking deep breaths for 2 minutes, using peppermint essential oil to refresh yourself, or scheduling a 15-minute nap. Also, I suggest avoiding blue light before bed tonight, and you can combine that with progressive muscle relaxation to improve sleep. Medical work requires sustained focus; if necessary, you can communicate with your supervisor to adjust your shift.

session_162.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_162.text: Today I did a 10-minute basic meditation for the first time. I feel my chest isn't as tight, but my mind keeps wandering. What can I do to be more focused?

session_162.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_162.text: It is normal for your mind to wander, so do not blame yourself. You can try the 4-7-8 breathing technique: inhale for 4 seconds, hold your breath for 7 seconds, and exhale for 8 seconds, letting your breath become the anchor of focus. Every time you bring your thoughts back is progress in practice.

session_162.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_162.text: Okay, I've remembered this breathing technique. Also, do I have to sit cross-legged when meditating?

session_162.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_162.text: Not necessarily. Sit on a chair with both feet flat on the floor, or put a cushion behind your back and lean against the wall. The key is to keep the spine straight and relaxed. Also, during work breaks during the day, you can do one or two minutes of breathing exercises to build the habit.

session_162.text: Today while writing medical orders, I almost got the dosage wrong, and Teacher Li reminded me. Although I corrected it in time, I've been feeling guilty all along. I talked to my best friend in the evening, but I still can't let it go.

session_162.text: I understand you. This kind of lingering fear and guilt really takes time to process. The fact that you were able to accept it humbly and resolve to improve your sleep at the time was already very professional. Do you want me to help you calm down, or give you some psychological adjustment advice?

session_162.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_162.text: Hmm, I always worry that the teacher will think I'm not careful enough, and I hate myself for getting nervous so easily.

session_162.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_162.text: Treat this mistake as a warning rather than a denial. I suggest you write a brief reflection diary, recording the cause of the error and how to correct it, and also do a few minutes of mindful breathing tonight—while inhaling, silently say 'I allow myself to make mistakes,' and while exhaling, silently say 'I learn from this.' This can ease self-blame and also help you sleep.

session_162.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_162.text: Thank you. Mindful breathing sounds good; I'll try it right now.

session_162.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_162.text: The fact that you are willing to take action shows that you are very resilient. Remember, perfection is a process, not a result. You are already good enough. Good night, tomorrow will be better.

session_164.text: Next Wednesday at 3 p.m., I have a talk with my supervising teacher Li Wei. I want to ask for career planning advice, but I am not sure how to phrase it so that it is both candid and professional. Can you help me organize a framework for the conversation?

session_164.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_164.text: Sure. Teacher Li Wei is rigorous and very busy. I suggest focusing on three core areas: clinical skill improvement (for example, difficulties in managing typical cases you're currently encountering), research opportunities (how to participate in projects or publish papers), and career development path (specific steps to take the attending physician exam in three years). Start by thanking him for his guidance, then honestly express your motivation and confusion, for example, 'I have some questions about clinical practice and would like your advice.' Avoid negative complaining.

session_164.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_164.text: This framework is good. But specifically for psychological stress management, how should I bring it up without seeming weak? For example, sometimes after being on duty my efficiency is low and I feel like I can't keep going.

session_164.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_164.text: It can be turned into a growth-oriented question: ask 'How did you balance work pressure and continuous learning in your early career?' or 'What did you do to adjust during periods of career burnout?' This both shows self-awareness and reflects a proactive approach to seeking solutions. Teachers will appreciate this positive attitude.

session_164.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_164.text: Today I wrote in my diary, 'Accept vulnerability and recover from fear.' In the early morning I panicked over a typo at work, but later gradually calmed down through mindful breathing and confiding in my friend Wu Min. session_166.text: My father just finished his first mirror therapy session. I'd like to understand more professional clinical details, such as the suitability of patients at different stages, common mistakes, and how to quantify the effects.

session_166.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_166.text: I see. What stage is your father at after the stroke? How are his cognitive status and limb function (such as active movement and sitting balance)? This will help me determine the best time window for mirror therapy and adjust the treatment plan.

session_166.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_166.text: He is in the recovery period, with left-sided hemiplegia. He can sit up independently, but his right hand has no active movement. I worry whether cognitive impairment will affect the outcome.

session_166.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_166.text: Mirror therapy has a relatively low cognitive threshold, but severe spatial neglect must be ruled out. It is recommended to first perform an MMSE screening (a score >20 is usually feasible). The training frequency is 15 minutes per day, combined with routine PT, to avoid fatigue. The effect can be evaluated weekly using the Fugl-Meyer upper extremity section.

session_166.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_166.text: How should mirror therapy and conventional training be integrated? Are there any recent high-quality studies supporting this?

session_166.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_166.text: Suggested sequence: first do 5 minutes of routine joint exercises, then 15 minutes of mirror therapy, and finally 10 minutes of functional training. A 2024 RCT (n=80) showed that 20 minutes of daily mirror therapy combined with routine rehabilitation improved FMA scores by an average of 12.3 points after 4 weeks, outperforming the routine-only group (8.1 points). A dressing mirror can be used as equipment, and a simple head-mounted display could also be considered.

session_168.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_168.text: Okay. In this case, palpitations and pulse deficit suggest atrial fibrillation, but if the ventricular rate is around 150 beats/min and regular, 2:1 conduction in atrial flutter should be suspected. Flutter waves (F waves) in atrial flutter appear sawtooth-like in leads II, III, and aVF with a rate of 250-350 beats/min, while atrial fibrillation shows fine f waves and is absolutely irregular. For management, radiofrequency ablation is the first choice for atrial flutter (success rate >90%); for atrial fibrillation, anticoagulation should be based on the CHA2DS2-VASc score. If Dr. Li's case is confirmed as atrial flutter, cardioversion or ablation should be considered rather than rate control alone. The latest guidelines recommend that synchronized cardioversion is safer when atrial flutter is accompanied by a rapid ventricular rate.

session_183.text: I just ran a logistic regression on stroke rehabilitation in SPSS. The results include OR values and P values, but I'm not sure whether the model fit is reasonable. How should this be presented in a paper?

session_183.speaker: Yu Xiaowen

session_183.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_183.text: First check whether the P value of the Hosmer-Lemeshow test is >0.05, then list the OR values and confidence intervals of significant variables, and compare similarities and differences with similar studies in the discussion; if the sample size is sufficient, consider subgroup analysis by age or disease duration to strengthen the robustness of the conclusions. For tables, use three-line tables and annotate variable assignments and the reference group.

session_183.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_183.text: As a neurologist, I bought low-fat milk, oatmeal, ejiao cake, and flat peaches for my father during his stroke rehabilitation. Is ejiao cake really beneficial for stroke recovery? Is the nutritional combination reasonable?

session_183.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_183.text: Ejiao cake is mainly made of ejiao, sesame, etc. It nourishes blood and yin, but lacks evidence-based support for stroke rehabilitation and has high sugar content, so it is not recommended for regular consumption. Low-fat milk provides high-quality protein and calcium, and oatmeal is rich in dietary fiber, making a reasonable combination. During the rehabilitation period, it is recommended to increase fish, soy products, and dark-colored vegetables to ensure adequate intake of high-quality protein.

session_183.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_183.text: Got it, I plan to stop taking the ejiao cake. My father's walking has improved, but he still needs attention. Could you elaborate on the precautions for home rehabilitation training and blood pressure and lipid management?

session_183.text: Rehabilitation training: balance exercises 2–3 times a day (standing against a wall, single-leg support), combined with speech function training (reading aloud or naming picture cards). Blood pressure target <140/90 mmHg; for blood lipids, pay special attention to LDL-C <1.8 mmol/L. Remove rugs and install handrails at home to prevent falls. You may consult the rehabilitation department to develop a personalized plan.

session_185.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_185.text: This morning I was shadowing in the outpatient clinic, and Dr. Li Wei showed me a CT and MRI of a patient with lacunar cerebral infarction, with typical small round low-density foci in the basal ganglia. I would like to systematically organize this part of the knowledge. Could you help me supplement the differential diagnosis and the latest treatment guidelines?

session_185.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_185.text: Lacunar cerebral infarction is common in the basal ganglia, thalamus, and brainstem. On imaging, it presents as small round or oval low-density lesions with a diameter of <15 mm. Differential diagnosis should focus on excluding leukoaraiosis (usually symmetric and diffuse) and enlarged perivascular spaces (along the course of blood vessels). For treatment, the 2023 AHA/ASA guidelines recommend antiplatelet therapy (aspirin/clopidogrel) combined with statin lipid-lowering in the acute phase, and long-term secondary prevention requires controlling blood pressure and blood glucose.

session_185.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_185.text: Got it. What indicators are mainly used in prognosis assessment? Also, I want to include this case in the first draft of my paper. What should I pay attention to?

session_185.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_185.text: Prognosis assessment focuses on the number and location of lesions and the control of vascular risk factors. A single lacunar infarction in the basal ganglia region usually has a good prognosis, but when multiple lesions are present or the thalamus and brainstem are involved, the risk of cognitive impairment increases. In the paper draft, you can describe the imaging features (location, size, margins), combine them with clinical manifestations (such as asymptomatic or mild motor dysfunction), and cite the latest guidelines to support treatment decisions.

session_197.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_197.text: This morning while doing practice questions, I marked a question on digitalis toxicity but didn't have time to look into it. Could you explain in detail the pathological mechanism and typical clinical manifestations of toxicity? Including blood concentration monitoring and indications for stopping the drug.

session_197.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_197.text: Okay. The mechanism of digitalis toxicity is mainly the inhibition of myocardial Na-K-ATPase, which leads to increased intracellular sodium and in turn promotes sodium-calcium exchange, causing calcium overload and delayed afterdepolarizations. Typical manifestations: gastrointestinal symptoms (anorexia, nausea), neurological symptoms (yellow vision, blue vision, headache), and arrhythmias (ventricular bigeminy, non-paroxysmal junctional tachycardia, atrioventricular block). A blood concentration >2 ng/ml warrants caution, but clinical correlation is needed; indications for discontinuation include new arrhythmias or worsening gastrointestinal or neurological symptoms.

session_197.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_197.text: Understood. Let me confirm the specific treatment steps: besides stopping the drug and supplementing potassium, which antiarrhythmic drugs are used, and when should digoxin antibody Fab fragments be used?

session_197.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_197.text: Treatment process: 1. Stop the medication immediately (digitalis and diuretics); 2. Correct hypokalemia (supplement potassium to around 4.5) and hypomagnesemia; 3. Antiarrhythmic treatment: use lidocaine or phenytoin sodium for ventricular arrhythmias, and avoid direct-current cardioversion (which can easily induce malignant arrhythmias); 4. Digoxin antibody Fab fragments are used for severe toxicity (serum potassium >5.0, bradycardia with hemodynamic instability, severe ventricular arrhythmia), with the dose calculated according to the digoxin body load.

session_202.text: I have compiled the wrong questions on thrombolytic therapy for acute cerebral infarction, but I still have questions about the choice between rt-PA and urokinase and the thrombolytic time window. Could you help me sort it out?

session_202.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_202.text: Yes, I also think that assessing the risk of hemorrhagic transformation after thrombolysis is very important. In particular, is an NIHSS score greater than 25 a contraindication? And what are the key points for managing complications?

session_202.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_202.text: NIHSS > 25 is a relative contraindication for rt-PA due to the high risk of bleeding. Complication management: for intracranial hemorrhage, stop thrombolytic drugs immediately and give cryoprecipitate or tranexamic acid; for vascular reocclusion, antiplatelet therapy may be considered. It is recommended to remember these key points in combination with typical cases.

session_203.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_203.text: I just reviewed the TOAST classification for cerebral infarction and the predictors of hematoma expansion in intracerebral hemorrhage. I made up a mnemonic and want you to check if it's accurate. For the TOAST classification, I used 'big-heart-small' — large-artery atherosclerosis, cardioembolism, small-artery occlusion. For hematoma expansion predictors, I made up 'swirl sign, island sign, blend sign; early expansion serves as a warning.' Is this right?

session_203.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_203.text: Your mnemonic summarizes the key points, but the TOAST classification has other subtypes (other determined etiology and undetermined etiology); 'large-cardio-small' only covers the first three. I suggest completing it as 'large-cardio-small-other-undetermined', or only using it to distinguish the three most common categories. The predictors of hematoma expansion are partly correct; the swirl sign, island sign, and blend sign are typical signs on non-contrast CT, but note that 'early' usually refers to within 6 hours of symptom onset. Do you need me to help you refine the differentiating imaging features of each subtype?

session_203.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_203.text: Yes, I'm a bit confused about the two subtypes 'other etiologies' and 'unknown causes,' especially since the imaging findings are easily mixed up. Could you help me analyze them?

session_203.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_203.text: For other identified causes (such as moyamoya disease and vasculitis), imaging often shows infarction in atypical vascular territories, or is accompanied by vessel wall abnormalities. The undetermined type requires exclusion of all the above and often presents as multiple, bilateral infarctions in different vascular territories. The mnemonic can be supplemented: other causes show abnormal vessels; undetermined type comes as multiple and bilateral. It is recommended to combine non-contrast CT, MRI, and vascular imaging for comprehensive assessment.

session_204.text: I am a resident doctor at Zhengzhou Central Hospital, considering switching from internal medicine to neurology and rehabilitation medicine. session_204.text: Understood. session_204.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_204.text: I suggest you schedule a brief informal talk with the department director now, bringing the thrombolysis cases and plans you have organized, and expressing your interest in neurorehabilitation. If the director supports it, first apply for a short-term rotation (1-2 months). This will both build experience and lay the foundation for later certification. session_204.text: DWI-FLAIR mismatch is the gold standard for determining whether onset was less than 4.5 hours ago; your decisive decision this time shows solid imaging skills. For family communication, I suggest using the vivid metaphor "time is brain," while emphasizing close monitoring for 24 hours after thrombolysis, which can reduce the family's concerns. It's also great that you turned the recording into case notes; later you can directly use them as the "clinical case" section of a paper, and it would be more complete with an additional comparative case analysis.

session_209.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_209.text: According to the latest guidelines: for CAP, empirical treatment commonly uses macrolides (such as azithromycin) to cover atypical pathogens, and in severe cases combines with β-lactams (such as ceftriaxone). For HAP, drug-resistant bacteria need to be considered; mild to moderate cases use anti-pseudomonal β-lactams, and severe cases or those at high risk of resistance use carbapenems (such as meropenem). Macrolides are mainly used for CAP outpatients or mild hospitalized cases, while carbapenems are used for severe cases or infections caused by ESBL-producing bacteria.

session_209.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_209.text: Understood. Then after the drug susceptibility results come out, how should medication be adjusted based on the results? Especially for drug-resistant bacteria such as MRSA or Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

session_209.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_209.text: Susceptibility results guide de-escalation therapy: for CAP, after using macrolides, if the pathogen is identified, switch to narrow-spectrum drugs; for HAP, if MRSA is cultured, choose vancomycin or linezolid; if Pseudomonas aeruginosa is susceptible, ceftazidime or carbapenems can be used; if resistant, combine with aminoglycosides or ciprofloxacin. Also adjust the dosage according to liver and kidney function.

session_216.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_216.text: I've recently been experiencing frequent soreness and stiffness in my neck and shoulders, especially after sitting for long periods or night shifts. I am 24 years old and a doctor. I usually get massages, apply heat packs, and do yoga, but the effects don't last long. Are there more scientific ways to relieve and prevent this?

session_216.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_216.text: Based on your description, it may involve myofascial pain syndrome or early cervical strain. Which specific advice would you like me to give: office environment adjustments, stretching exercises, frequency of heat therapy, or indications for seeking medical attention when necessary?

session_216.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_216.text: Both, I think, especially posture adjustments during daily office work and stretches suitable for doctors, and also how to tell whether an MRI is needed?

session_216.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_216.text: Recommendations: 1) Raise the screen to eye level, keep elbows at 90 degrees, and do 5 minutes of neck lateral flexion and extension stretches every 45 minutes; 2) apply a warm compress for 15 minutes before bed, do yoga 2-3 times a week, and add deep neck flexor strengthening exercises (e.g., chin tucks); 3) if arm numbness, severe headache, or symptoms lasting more than 2 weeks occur, consider an MRI to rule out cervical spondylosis. Recommended pillow height: 8-12 cm.

session_218.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_218.text: I just submitted my department transfer application and will move to the rehabilitation department next month. Could you help me systematically sort out the work model and research directions of the rehabilitation department? Especially how to combine clinical work and research.

session_218.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_218.text: The daily work of the rehabilitation department includes assessments (such as the Fugl-Meyer Scale), developing rehabilitation plans (PT/OT/ST), and common cases include post-stroke rehabilitation and post-orthopedic surgery rehabilitation. Recommended research directions include neurorehabilitation (e.g., motor relearning mechanisms), rehabilitation robotics, and standardization of assessment methods. My suggestion is that at the beginning of your rotation, you first spend a week learning basic assessment techniques, while reading the 6th edition of Rehabilitation Medicine and articles from the journal Neurorehabilitation over the past five years, and pay attention to clinical data collection points.

session_218.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_218.text: Thanks, that's very clear. My undergraduate research foundation is weak. In the first week after my rotation, what exactly should I start with?

session_218.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_218.text: First-week priorities: ① Each day, accompany the supervising teacher to see 3–5 newly admitted patients and record assessment data; ② Attend the department research meeting on Thursday afternoon and raise one clinical question; ③ Use evenings to learn R basics and the reliability and validity analysis of the Fugl-Meyer scale. This will quickly build a bridge between clinical work and research.

session_218.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_218.text: I am a resident physician. Recently my shoulders and neck have often felt tired. Before getting up in the morning, I applied a heat pack; after doing Baduanjin, I felt more relaxed. But in the evening after showering at home, my shoulders became sore again. I would like to ask about more effective relief methods and daily health care advice.

session_218.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_218.text: Your condition is typical neck and shoulder muscle tension caused by prolonged sitting and high-intensity mental work. Baduanjin is a good active relaxation, but micro-exercises during work breaks may be more critical. Would you like me to share quick stretching techniques for a doctor's work pattern, or details such as heat compresses and sleeping posture?

session_218.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_218.text: That's right, and I especially want to know how to incorporate Baduanjin into work breaks, and whether simple moves like the double-chin tuck are useful.

session_218.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_218.text: Recommendations: ① Every 45 minutes at work, do a set of “chin tucks” (retract the chin for 5 seconds, repeat 5 times) and “shoulder circles”; ② In Baduanjin, the move “Shake the head and wag the tail to dispel heart fire” emphasizes leaning back and rotational force; you can do it twice at noon; ③ For the heat patch, apply it for 6–8 hours before bed, and avoid using it for more than 12 hours during the day; ④ Adjust the pillow to a height that keeps your chin parallel to the bed surface when lying on your back. Do you think these options are workable?

session_218.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_218.text: Can you explain in more detail the technique for generating power in "shaking the head and wagging the tail"? When I do it, I always feel the range of motion isn't enough.

session_218.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_218.text: Key points: Stand with your feet twice shoulder-width apart, bend your knees and squat while placing both hands on your knees. Lower your head and round your chest, twist your waist to the left and back, and let your head sweep in a downward arc from the left side across the chest to the right side, feeling the thoracic spine twist segment by segment. Do the same to the right and back. The key is to be led by the tailbone, not just turning the neck. In addition, coordinate with abdominal breathing and exhale when turning your head. You can do it slowly first to find the feeling of spinal rotation.
