session_219.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_219.text: Next week I will participate in a joint consultation on a case of headache of unknown cause. I need materials on the differential diagnosis between low-pressure headache and cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, especially the differences in imaging features. Could you help me summarize them?

session_219.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_219.text: Okay. Intracranial hypotension headache on MRI often shows diffuse dural thickening and enhancement, brain sagging, and venous sinus dilation; cerebral venous sinus thrombosis manifests as loss of flow void signal in the venous sinus, T2 hyperintensity, and associated cerebral parenchymal edema or hemorrhage. Key distinguishing points: lumbar puncture pressure measurement (low intracranial pressure ≤60 mmH₂O vs normal or elevated) and DSA/CTV examination.

session_219.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_219.text: Then what are the core recommendations in the latest guidelines for managing these two diseases? For example, how to distinguish them before surgery, and whether a routine lumbar puncture is needed?

session_219.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_219.text: Latest recommendation: If MRI is atypical, lumbar puncture with pressure measurement and cerebrospinal fluid analysis should be prioritized. Once low intracranial pressure headache is confirmed, an autologous blood patch can be used; cerebral venous sinus thrombosis requires anticoagulant therapy. Before consultation, it is recommended to prepare: blood D-dimer, MRV or CTV imaging, and a detailed history of positional headache.

session_219.text: I'm transferring from the neurology department to the rehabilitation department. I'm currently reading Fundamentals of Rehabilitation Medicine in the evenings. session_219.text: Recommend Rehabilitation Medicine (edited by Li Jian'an) as an advanced textbook, and the Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation video course (e.g., on Bilibili or medical MOOC platforms). For clinical tools, focus on mastering assessment scales such as FIM, the Berg Balance Scale, and MMT, and become familiar with the introductory operations of exercise therapy and physical agent therapy. It is suggested that you combine your neurology experience, first focus on neurological rehabilitation, and set up a daily 30-minute skill checklist study.

session_219.text: You can search for "Basic Rehabilitation Medicine (Chinese University MOOC)" or the "Neurorehabilitation Therapy Technology" series of courses; some include practical demonstrations. In addition, the website of the Rehabilitation Branch of the Chinese Medical Association has clinical guidelines and operation videos.

Outside of family and work, keep a 10-minute review every evening. This way, you can steadily build professional confidence.

session_225.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_225.text: Are you asking about the specific operational differences between active and passive modes in PNF techniques, and how to choose the appropriate mode based on Brunnstrom staging?

session_225.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_225.text: Yes, and also the similarities and differences with the Bobath technique and its practical application in community rehabilitation.

session_225.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_225.text: In the PNF diagonal spiral pattern, the active mode is performed by the patient independently to promote neuromuscular re-education; the passive mode is guided by the therapist to improve ROM and relaxation. Brunnstrom stages I-II mainly use passive movement, stages III-IV use assisted active movement, and stages V-VI use resistance. Unlike Bobath, PNF emphasizes spiral diagonal movement, while Bobath focuses on inhibiting abnormal tone. In community rehabilitation, simplified patterns can be used, such as seated upper-limb diagonal push-pull exercises, with attention to safety.

session_227.text: My father has a history of cerebral infarction, and commercial medical insurance was rejected. Can you recommend any feasible medical security options? For example, Huimin Insurance or special insurance for chronic diseases?

session_227.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_227.text: Henan Huimin Insurance (Zhongyuan Yihui Insurance) can be purchased with pre-existing conditions. It does not cover hospital expenses related to a previous cerebral infarction, but other diseases can be reimbursed normally, with an annual premium of several dozen yuan. In addition, you can look into chronic-disease cancer-prevention insurance on platforms such as Shuidi and Qingsong; some products can cover people in the stable period after cerebral infarction.

session_227.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_227.text: So does Huimin Insurance not cover medical expenses from a recurrence of cerebral infarction at all? And is there a time limit for enrollment?

session_227.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_227.text: Yes, Henan Huiminbao does not cover hospitalization expenses caused by the five agreed-upon pre-existing conditions (including cerebral infarction) and their complications, but other diseases are normally covered. The enrollment window is usually January to March each year; for specifics, follow the official notices of “Yujianbao”. If you miss it, you can consider the national version of Huiminbao (such as ZhongAn Minhuibao), which likewise requires no health declaration.

session_227.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_227.text: I'm studying the ASIA classification in rehabilitation medicine, and I'm confused about how sacral sparing distinguishes between complete and incomplete injuries. Can you explain it?

session_227.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_227.text: Sacral sparing refers to the presence of saddle sensation (S4-S5 dermatomes) or voluntary anal sphincter contraction. If sacral sparing is present, the injury is incomplete (ASIA B/C/D); if completely absent, it is complete (ASIA A). What exactly is the question you got stuck on?

session_227.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_227.text: It was a question about sensory level determination. I couldn't tell the difference between 'neurological level' and 'sensory level,' which caused me to choose the wrong judgment about sacral sparing.

session_227.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_227.text: Neurological level refers to the most caudal segment of the spinal cord with normal function (sensory and motor), while sensory level is based only on sensory examination. If the sensory level is lower than the motor level, the neurological level is usually taken as the higher one. When determining sacral sparing, the key is whether there is a response to perianal stimulation — you can mark the S4-S5 region with a red pen, corresponding to the saddle area test point in the practice questions.

Common abnormalities on the additional cervical spine AP and lateral X-ray from today’s checkup include loss of the physiological cervical curvature, mild bone spurs, or narrowing of the intervertebral disc space. For the pillow height, use about one fist high when sleeping on your back and one and a half fists high when sleeping on your side, and choose memory foam material; 4. For exercise rehabilitation, swimming is recommended (freestyle/breaststroke), and avoid sports that use unilateral force, such as badminton. After the formal report is issued, we can judge whether a cervical spine MRI is needed based on the specific situation.

Rehabilitation physicians are responsible for diagnosis, treatment planning, and medication adjustment; therapists are responsible for carrying out PT/OT/ST and other training. I suggest you participate more in team rounds at the beginning and actively learn hands-on skills from therapists. To qualify as an attending physician in rehabilitation medicine, you need to take the national unified examination. You can prepare in advance using the textbook 'Rehabilitation Medicine'.

session_232.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_232.text: Suggest you give priority to fulfilling your bridesmaid promise to Wang Fang (because it is confirmed and carries deeper responsibility), while being honest with Zhang Jing about the schedule conflict and making a compensatory gesture: for example, participating in one of her wedding segments via livestream on the day, recording a blessing video for her in advance, and taking her out for a meal after the wedding to explain the reason. session_233.text: When I play ball, my teammates say I look like I'm executing KPIs, and recently when running I only focus on pace and calories. How can I shift from a 'getting the task done' mindset to truly enjoying exercise?

session_233.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_233.text: You can try three tips: 1) For workout check-ins, only record feeling words (such as 'light' and 'excited'); 2) Schedule one 'no-data' relaxed rally per week, agreeing with your practice partner to focus only on the flow of rallies; 3) Practice mindful breathing when receiving serves, bringing your attention back to bodily sensations instead of the score.

session_233.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_233.text: These sound very practical, especially "no-score sparring." But when you encounter a partner who wants to chase results, how do you keep your own pace?

session_233.text: You can communicate clearly in advance: use 'I want to practice controlling my landing point today' as an excuse to turn confrontation into cooperative practice. At the same time, draw on rehabilitation medicine principles — make 'listening to body signals' the primary goal, and when the other person speeds up the pace, allow yourself to pause for 10 seconds to reset your breathing.

session_235.text: This afternoon I confessed to Wang Fang about the wedding. She said with red eyes, "Why didn't you tell me earlier?" I... felt really awful, but I also felt a little relieved after getting it out.

session_235.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_235.text: Your emotions right now are complex—there is both guilt and heaviness after confessing, as well as relief and a desire to repair the friendship. Do you want me to help you sort through these feelings, or talk about the comfort that reconciliation brought while doing pottery tonight?

session_235.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_235.text: Yes, she smiled during pottery and said she understood me but needed time... I'm worried—can our friendship really go back to how it was before?

session_235.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_235.text: From what you described, Wang Fang is willing to accept your candor and make pottery together, which shows she values this relationship. It is normal to need time to process things; a frank wound will instead heal more strongly because of sincerity. You did the right thing. Respecting her pace is the best repair.

session_235.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_235.text: Hmm... Actually, I know the road ahead is still long, but at least I can sleep soundly tonight. Thank you for listening to me.

session_235.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_235.text: You're welcome. The brave step you took has already begun to mend the rift. Get some good rest. Tomorrow you can bring her a cup of honey citron tea; silent care is also warm. Good night.

session_235.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_235.text: Today I completed two pieces at the Shenghuali Pottery Studio—a cup engraved with “W.F.” and a small double-happiness bowl. They were successfully fired, and I feel especially happy!

session_235.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_235.text: It sounds like you not only completed your work but also spent a meaningful time with your colleague Wang Fang. Would you like to share some details about the creative process or that sense of accomplishment?

session_235.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_235.text: Yes, Wang Fang was very clumsy when she first made pottery, but Master Zheng guided her patiently. I designed the letters on the carved cup. The double-happiness small bowl almost cracked while kneading the clay, but in the end both succeeded, and we were both very excited.

session_235.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_235.text: This kind of perfect finish from process to result is truly gratifying—your pottery has made great progress, and you repaired the relationship through cooperation. A double joy worth commemorating. I suggest taking photos of the piece. Next time, you can try combining the two techniques to create a more complex shape, such as a small bowl with engraved characters.

session_235.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_235.text: Tonight, after I confessed to Wang Fang, she said she needs time to process it. I'm a bit worried there will be a rift in our friendship. Can you give me some specific action suggestions to repair the relationship?

session_235.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_235.text: It is recommended that you proactively invite her for coffee tomorrow, first express understanding of her feelings, then specifically ask what help she needs with wedding preparations, such as accompanying her for a makeup trial or finding a venue, and show sincerity through concrete actions.

session_235.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_235.text: Would directly asking her out put pressure on her? Would giving her a meaningful gift be better?

session_235.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_235.text: A gift can ease the pressure. I recommend giving her a bracelet or a custom photo album, along with a handwritten card. Write about how much you value your friendship and your wedding commitment, and add, ‘We can talk again when you’re ready.’

session_237.text: So you hope to combine the tactile sensations, focus, and symbolic meanings of zodiac culture in pottery creation to improve the mood of elderly stroke patients? I suggest clarifying the mechanisms from two dimensions—neural plasticity and cultural psychology—and referring to existing controlled experimental designs for handicraft therapy.

session_237.text: Yes, that's the direction. How exactly should the pilot be designed? Are there any recommended types of literature or experimental paths?

session_237.text: A pretest-posttest control design can be used, with the intervention group attending Chinese zodiac-themed pottery classes twice a week (such as making zodiac plates), and the control group receiving routine rehabilitation training. The outcome measures should include the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale and prefrontal lobe activity measured by fNIRS. Recommended references include papers from the past five years in Arts in Psychotherapy on craft therapy and stroke rehabilitation, as well as Wang Jisheng's research on Chinese localized psychological interventions.

session_240.text: Xiaowen is organizing the annual meeting notes at home tonight. She still has questions about how VR-specific training protocols and neuroplasticity mechanisms can guide clinical rehabilitation timing. I hope you can help me clarify these two key points.

session_240.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_240.text: Okay, VR technology typically uses head-mounted displays and haptic feedback gloves. Task-oriented training (such as grasping and reaching) designed for 45 minutes daily for 4 weeks can significantly improve upper-extremity Fugl-Meyer scores. Neuroplasticity emphasizes early high-intensity training (the golden period 3-6 months after onset) and task-specific training, promoting synaptic remodeling through long-term potentiation mechanisms.

session_240.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_240.text: Got it. So how can I integrate neuroplasticity theory into home rehabilitation guidance, based on my own poster research on home-based rehabilitation intervention?

session_240.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_240.text: It is recommended to design 20 minutes of daily home task training under family supervision (such as physical operations simulating VR), using environmental cues and timely feedback to enhance neuroplasticity. Also recommend reading the literature on scales for home supervision in Neurorehabilitation.

session_240.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_240.text: My friend and I plan to volunteer at an elderly care home on August 31. The initial plan includes finger exercises, clay modeling, and music interaction. session_240.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_240.text: You are particularly concerned about the elderly person's physical safety, worried about the difficulty of the finger exercises and the cleaning issues with clay. I can design a set of low-risk finger movements and recommend safe, easy-to-clean clay materials. Would you like me to first give specific exercise suggestions for the finger movements?

session_240.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_240.text: Yes, let's start with your suggestions for the finger exercises. Also, I'd like to hear your opinion on the overall activity time allocation, such as how to avoid fatigue for the elderly.

session_240.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_240.text: It is recommended to divide the finger exercises into three groups: Group 1: make a fist and open the hand (slowly, 5 times); Group 2: finger opposition pinching (alternate thumb with index finger, middle finger, etc.); Group 3: wrist rotations (3 circles clockwise and 3 counterclockwise). Rest 30 seconds between groups. Overall flow: warm-up 5 minutes (relaxation breathing) → finger exercises 10 minutes → clay pinching and sculpting 15 minutes → music interaction 10 minutes → sharing and relaxation 5 minutes. Keep the total time to 45 minutes to avoid fatigue.

session_243.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_243.text: Right, I'm struggling to decide whether transparent glaze or celadon glaze would be more effective. Also, how exactly do you moisten the piece before glazing? Are there standards for firing temperature and time?

session_243.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_243.text: Transparent glaze clearly shows the carved lines, while celadon glaze makes the patterns softer and more rustic. It is recommended to test small samples first. Before glazing, gently wipe the bisque with a damp sponge until it is slightly moist, and avoid over-moistening. For firing, a medium temperature of 1200–1240°C is recommended, with the heating rate controlled within 100°C/h, a 20-minute soak, and natural cooling. To reduce bubbles, you can first bisque-fire at 800°C and then apply the glaze.

session_243.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_243.text: My father has recovered well after his cerebral infarction; now he can walk slowly with a cane. I want to help him do more systematic home training, such as transitioning from cane-assisted walking to walking independently, and increasing balance and lower limb strength. session_243.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_243.text: Gradually add seated calf raises (3 sets of 15 reps per day), wall sits (knees slightly bent, hold for 30 seconds, repeat 5 times), and standing on one leg while holding onto something for support (10 seconds each time, 5 sets per side). Monitor your heart rate to keep it ≤120 beats per minute. Stop immediately if dizziness or pain occurs. Recommended 3-5 times per week, 20-30 minutes each session.

session_243.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_243.text: These exercises sound practical, but my father's endurance is average. How should the training frequency and intensity be flexibly adjusted? Also, sometimes his left foot drags a bit. Are there any techniques to correct his gait?

session_243.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_243.text: The intensity should be such that your father does not feel fatigued after training. Start with 15 minutes per session and gradually increase the time. For foot drop, try leg-raising exercises: seated with a resistance band hooked around the toes, 3 sets of 10 reps daily; when walking, remind him 'heel first, then toes,' and family members can gently tap the affected ankle to help with foot placement.

session_244.text: I just finished a learning log on early rehabilitation pathways for stroke, incorporating my father's personal experience. I'd like to hear your views on "early intervention" and "active participation"—do they align with clinical consensus?

session_244.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_244.text: Your summary is spot on. Early intervention usually refers to starting rehabilitation within 24-72 hours after vital signs are stable, emphasizing that active participation is better than passive treatment. Could you share which stage in your father's case impressed you the most?

session_244.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_244.text: During my father's recovery, the rehabilitation therapist encouraged him to actively practice standing rather than relying solely on the electric tilt table. I thought it was slow at the time, but now I can see it worked better. Is this active participation the optimal choice?

session_244.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_244.text: Yes, active exercise can activate neuroplasticity and prevent disuse syndrome. If task-oriented training (such as reaching and weight shifting) had been combined at that time, balance might have improved faster. When observing tomorrow, you can pay attention to such strategies.

session_244.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_244.text: Understood. During tomorrow's ward observation, I will focus on the design of active training. Thank you for your feedback—it gives me more confidence in the sentence circled in red in my father's notes.

session_244.text: Your sense of mission is exactly what rehabilitation medicine needs. Put this insight into practice, and you will become a very good doctor. Feel free to continue the discussion anytime.

The book's reflections on the end of life really touched me, especially combined with the patients I encountered in the rehabilitation department during the day. session_244.text: The rehabilitation department documentation system usually includes dedicated assessment scale modules (such as FIM and the Barthel Index), and its medical record templates also focus more on describing functional recovery. A common operational difficulty is that the scales have many scoring items and are easy to miss. It is recommended to first familiarize yourself with the two menus 'Assessment Records' and 'Rehabilitation Treatment Form'.

You can ask the supervising teacher in advance for a paper version of the department's commonly used rating scales to familiarize yourself with the order of items; after logging in, first check the shortcut key list in 'System Help'.

session_249.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_249.text: Today I learned underglaze painting. What is the approximate water content ratio in the brush belly during the water separation technique? I didn't see clearly when my master demonstrated.

session_249.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_249.text: When applying the wash, the belly of the brush should hold about 80%–90% water—full but not dripping. If the water content is too high, the color will be pale and diffuse; if too low, the stroke will be dry and sluggish. For the curved surface of the vase you are practicing, you need to reduce the water content appropriately to prevent runs.

session_249.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_249.text: What about the "tearing-hair" technique? How should the brush angle and force be controlled when painting chicken feathers?

session_249.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_249.text: For the fur-tearing method, lightly sweep with the side of the brush, keeping the brush tip at a 10-15 degree angle to the surface. Move the brush quickly and steadily. First draw the main trunk, then tear out fine hairs layer by layer. It is recommended to try a few strokes on a scrap blank, and only work on the final piece once you feel familiar with the technique.

session_254.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_254.text: Today I learned about mirror therapy and want to create a home training plan for my father, who has impaired hand function after a stroke. He is in the chronic phase with fine motor disorders of the hand. How exactly should this be done at home? How should the mirror be placed, how many times a day, and how long each session?

session_254.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_254.text: To understand your needs, I need to know his current joint range of motion and muscle strength, especially finger flexion and extension and grip ability, as well as whether there are any signs of pain or fatigue, in order to give personalized advice.

session_254.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_254.text: His fingers can flex reasonably well, but extension is significantly limited. Muscle strength is about grade 3, with no pain. He can voluntarily make a fist but opens it slowly, and fails fine motor tasks such as pinching small objects.

session_254.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_254.text: Recommendation: Put the mirror in the median sagittal plane. The healthy side performs gripping, finger opposition, and extension movements, and the affected side imitates them simultaneously. Twice a day, 15 minutes each time, to prevent fatigue. In the early stage, start with fist clenching and progress to finger opposition, gradually increasing the difficulty. You can use a tablet to record the healthy side as a mirror substitute. Observe breathing and heart rate. If you feel irritable or the movements become distorted, rest immediately. Avoid compensation on the affected side. Mild swelling is normal; if pain persists, stop.

session_256.text: Last night's shift I had planned to review the shock chapter, but I was interrupted frequently by patients and barely got to read. Now I'm really anxious about falling behind... Is there any way to review efficiently in fragmented time?

session_256.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_256.text: I understand your frustration. It's hard to concentrate when the night shift keeps getting interrupted. For fragmented time, I suggest you focus on using the mobile question bank to do multiple-choice questions, 5-10 minutes at a time. You can also pre-record audio lessons and listen during shift handovers or commutes. Start with weak chapters, such as shock, and repeatedly listen and do the corresponding questions, so you can use short-term memory more efficiently.

session_256.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_256.text: Listening to audio and doing practice questions does work, but I can never remember the key points—I'm all over the place. Is there a more systematic review strategy? For example, how to plan the weekly review content?

session_256.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_256.text: I suggest you make a weekly plan by system module, for example, this week only review shock and heart failure. Spend 10 minutes before bed every day using a mind map to sort out the framework, and use night shift breaks to focus on the 20 high-frequency questions in that module. If you get interrupted, don't panic; just mark “to review later” next to the question number and make it up when you rest. On weekends, take half an hour to do a mock test and consolidate weak points. This way it is both systematic and flexible.

The review structure is suggested to have four parts: research background (aging and rehabilitation needs), neural mechanisms of ceramic art, existing clinical evidence (including Master Zheng's case), and research gaps and future directions.

session_282.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_282.text: Shoulder-hand syndrome often occurs 1-3 months after stroke, manifesting as swelling and pain in the affected hand and increased skin temperature. Early intervention includes proper limb positioning and avoiding excessive stretching. Physical therapy recommends alternating hot and cold soaking and centripetal wrapping techniques. Occupational therapy focuses on active assisted training such as gripping a ball, while joint range of motion needs to be monitored.

session_282.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_282.text: What is the specific procedure of the centripetal wrapping manipulation? How can it be combined with occupational therapy?

session_282.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_282.text: Centripetal wrapping: wrap a 1-2 mm diameter cord from the fingertips toward the wrist, releasing each finger immediately after wrapping. Repeat 3-5 times to reduce edema. Immediately after finishing, perform hand functional activities such as wringing a towel or picking up beans to promote sensorimotor integration. Clinically, adjust frequency according to the stage: in Phase I, focus on reducing swelling; in Phase II, add anti-spasticity training.

session_309.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_309.text: I have just finished the first draft of the hospital anniversary speech, using as the main thread my experience of accompanying my father through rehabilitation after his cerebral infarction and then finding my career direction. It is about 1,200 words. But after reading it, I feel the emotional expression is not direct enough and the logical transitions are not smooth enough. Can you help me see how to improve the structure, wording, and emotional elevation?

session_309.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_309.text: I understand your needs. To make the speech move the hospital anniversary audience, my suggestions: 1) Structurally divide it into an opening (introducing your father's story), a main body (two to three stages from confusion to growth), and a conclusion (gratitude and blessings); 2) Add direct emotional expression at key turning points, such as 'At that moment I understood the meaning of rehabilitation'; 3) Refine a memorable closing line, such as 'Light up life with rehabilitation.' Keep the duration within 5 minutes, with a medium-slow speaking pace. Do you need me to provide sample revisions for specific paragraphs?

session_309.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_309.text: Right, especially the opening and closing parts. I'm a bit unsure about the direct expression of emotion. Could you help me revise a few examples?

session_309.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_309.text: Okay. For the opening, I suggest changing it to: 'In the winter of 2018, the moment my father collapsed from a stroke, I held his cold fingers and knew for the first time how important rehabilitation was. Five years later, I stand here in a white coat—this is the starting point of my becoming a rehabilitation doctor.' For the closing line: 'The hospital taught me medicine, my father taught me perseverance, and the rehabilitation department gave me a name—doctor.' This way it naturally integrates the hospital culture, and the emotional progression is clearer.

session_315.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_315.text: Dr. Liu Qiang taught me the practical details of neural mobilization today, but I'm still worried that I'll make mistakes in tomorrow's clinical procedure. Can you help me systematically sort out the key points?

session_315.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_315.text: It seems you need confirmation of the indications, contraindications, and specific techniques of neural mobilization (such as force, angle, and duration), as well as methods for adjusting based on patient feedback. Right?

session_315.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_315.text: Yes, especially the mobilization methods for the median and ulnar nerves, and the steps to take when the patient experiences pain.

session_315.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_315.text: Okay, according to clinical guidelines, first assess neural tension. For median nerve mobilization, use a combination of shoulder abduction, forearm supination, wrist extension, and finger extension; glide slowly to the end feel and hold for 10 seconds. For the ulnar nerve, use shoulder external rotation, elbow flexion, wrist extension, and finger flexion. The intensity should be based on a mild pulling sensation without pain; repeat 10-15 times per side, 2-3 sets per day. If radiating pain or worsening numbness occurs, stop immediately and reduce the angle, and record the response. Common mistakes are overstretching and not communicating in advance; be sure to explain and obtain cooperation before the procedure.

session_315.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_315.text: I have just finished the draft for tomorrow's talk, themed "How Doctors Can Take Care of Themselves While Taking Care of Others," combining my father's rehabilitation experience with my own journey as a doctor. session_315.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_315.text: It sounds like a powerful speech! The case of your father's recovery is compelling in itself. I suggest you slow down when describing specific details (such as his struggles or moments you accompanied him) to let your true feelings flow naturally. session_315.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_315.text: Using the yoga insight as the closing of the whole piece is clever and not abrupt. I suggest adding a transition sentence before turning to it, such as "But the way to guard yourself is sometimes hidden in the most ordinary experiences," to make the logic smoother. Overall you have done very well; stay confident, and you will surely move the audience when you share it.

session_315.text: I just took a breathing meditation yoga class, and my neck and shoulders are much more relaxed. I want to incorporate breathing techniques into clinical work, such as before ward rounds or when seeing anxious patients. Are there any practical short-term tips?

session_315.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_315.text: It is recommended to try the 4-7-8 breathing method: inhale for 4 seconds, hold for 7 seconds, and exhale for 8 seconds; repeating it three times takes only about one minute. It is suitable for use before ward rounds or in idle moments while handling medical records, and it can quickly calm the nerves.

session_315.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_315.text: This is very good, but wouldn't taking deep breaths during ward rounds or patient consultations be too obvious? Is there a more suitable, discreet method?

session_315.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_315.text: It can be naturally incorporated into the gaps of daily work: for example, doing 30 seconds of abdominal breathing while washing hands, or closing your eyes during shift handover and consciously focusing on your breath. The key is to set triggers in fixed scenarios, such as phone reminders, and stick with it for 2-3 weeks to form a habit.

1. Precontemplation: no intention to change, need to raise awareness
2. Contemplation: have intention but no action, need to stimulate motivation
3. Preparation: begin small actions, need to make a plan
4. Action: actively changing, need support and consolidation
5. Maintenance: maintain behavior, need to prevent relapse

Key points of motivational interviewing:
- Express empathy: understand the client through reflective listening
- Develop discrepancy: help the client see the gap between current situation and goals
- Avoid arguments: do not force change, guide the client to self-discovery
- Support self-efficacy: strengthen the client's confidence in change
- Roll with resistance: allow setbacks and adjust strategies

session_319.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_319.text: I just finished throwing and scoring the rabbit zodiac ceramic plate in a heated room at 15-20°C and 45% humidity, and I'm worried it will crack from drying too quickly. How should I control the drying speed of the semi-finished piece? What practical tips are there for carving the scroll grass pattern when trimming?

session_319.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_319.text: Understood. Your core needs are to prevent the ceramic plate from cracking during the drying and trimming stages, while improving the precision of the scroll grass pattern carving. Suggestions: cover the edges with a damp towel and spray water every 2 hours, keeping the surface moist for 3-4 days; judge dryness by touching – it should feel slightly cool and not sticky. When trimming, hold the carving knife at an angle of about 15-20 degrees, cut in one direction from outside to inside, and for details, first lightly trace the outline and then deepen it.

session_319.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_319.text: Does the damp towel covering it need to stay wet continuously? Do I need to take care of it at night while sleeping? Also, the lines of the scrolling grass pattern tend to break at the turns. Is there a way to prevent that?

session_319.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_319.text: During the day, use a spray bottle to evenly mist the towel every 2-3 hours; at night, replace the wet towel with a slightly damp plastic bag over the pottery plate (leave small holes for ventilation) to prevent evaporation from being too fast. Cracking or chipping at turns is usually caused by carving too quickly or using uneven force. Suggestion: slow down before the turn, switch to a finer carving knife (such as a trimming knife) and carve gradually from the inside of the outline toward the outside, letting the wrist drive the blade rather than using force from the arm.

session_320.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_320.text: I'm reviewing thrombolytic therapy for myocardial infarction. The indications, contraindications, and the use of alteplase are a bit fuzzy. Can you help me sort them out?

session_320.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_320.text: Are you looking to focus on the golden time window for thrombolysis, drug selection, or management of reperfusion arrhythmias after successful thrombolysis?

session_320.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_320.text: The golden time window and reperfusion arrhythmia are what confuse me the most. Please explain them. Also, the comparison with emergency PCI.

session_320.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_320.text: The golden time window for thrombolysis is within 3 hours of symptom onset for the best effect; it is still effective within 6 hours. Reperfusion arrhythmias commonly include premature ventricular contractions or accelerated idioventricular rhythm, which are usually benign, but there is a risk of ventricular fibrillation requiring defibrillation. Compared with PCI: thrombolysis is faster and more convenient, but PCI has a higher recanalization rate and a lower bleeding risk, and is suitable for those with contraindications or a high risk of severe bleeding. I suggest you make a comparison table.

session_320.text: I just saw a Xiaohongshu photo of crackle glaze paired with sky-blue - it's beautiful. My rabbit plate is earthenware clay, fired at about 1200°C, and not yet glazed. session_320.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_320.text: Are you planning to use sky blue as the base glaze or the top glaze? Can the studio control the reduction atmosphere? If you want clear texture, you might consider a matte or semi-matte glaze to avoid reflections interfering with the details.

session_320.speaker: Yu Xiaowen

session_320.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_320.text: The plan is feasible: first apply a sky-blue base glaze with even thickness, let it dry, then apply a crackle glaze (not too thick). Firing in a reducing atmosphere makes the sky blue more translucent. It is recommended to apply a thin layer of white engobe locally on the base glaze before applying the crackle glaze, creating a contrast of light and dark to highlight the crackle pattern; alternatively, use a transparent crackle glaze with a small amount of sky-blue colorant to simplify the process. It is suggested to test a small sample first.

session_321.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_321.text: After taking iron supplements for three weeks, my anemia has improved significantly, but I always have stomach discomfort. I am considering switching to taking them every other day. Is that reasonable? Also, are there any ways to reduce stomach irritation?

session_321.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_321.text: Taking iron supplements every other day can reduce gastrointestinal side effects, and studies show no significant difference in efficacy for iron deficiency anemia. It is recommended to take them with meals or immediately after meals, and to avoid taking them with coffee or tea. At the same time, vitamin C (such as orange juice) can be added to promote absorption. Monitor hemoglobin changes over a period of about 4–6 weeks; if symptoms persist, consider switching to a sustained-release formulation.

session_321.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_321.text: Okay, how exactly should I take vitamin C? I'm worried that taking it every other day might affect the previous treatment results.

session_321.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_321.text: Taking vitamin C 200mg along with the iron supplement is fine, or eat one kiwi/orange after a meal. Taking it every other day yields similar total absorption to taking it daily, but you need to make sure you take it regularly once every 2 days. Your previous records show that your hemoglobin has risen, indicating that it is effective. After the adjustment, continue to observe for 2 weeks. If the stomach discomfort is significantly reduced, you can maintain the current regimen.

session_321.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_321.text: I just reviewed unstable angina and did some practice questions but got several wrong. I'd like you to systematically walk me through the differential diagnosis, risk stratification, and latest treatment guidelines.

session_321.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_321.text: Okay. Unstable angina belongs to acute coronary syndrome. The key is to differentiate it from stable angina (trigger factors, duration, relief by nitroglycerin) and acute myocardial infarction (persistently elevated troponin, ST-segment elevation/pathological Q waves on ECG). For risk stratification, the TIMI score (≥5 is high risk) and the GRACE score are recommended to guide the timing of intervention. The core of treatment is dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + clopidogrel/ticagrelor), anticoagulation (heparin/low-molecular-weight heparin), intensive statin therapy, and beta-blockers (if no contraindications). Indications for revascularization include high-risk stratification or failure of medical therapy. Do you need me to analyze your wrong questions specifically?

session_321.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_321.text: Yes, what confuses me most is how to distinguish between dynamic ECG evolution and ST-segment changes in unstable angina. Also, how exactly should the timing of intervention be chosen?

session_321.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_321.text: Unstable angina ECG typically shows transient ST-segment depression or T-wave inversion (appearing during chest pain and resolving after relief), while myocardial infarction shows ST-segment elevation or persistent depression with Q wave formation. session_329.text: I just finished 20 neurorehabilitation case analysis questions and got 3 wrong. session_329.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_329.text: You want to analyze clinical decisions for these two error-prone points from the perspectives of pathophysiology and evidence-based practice, so as to avoid similar mistakes, right?

session_329.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_329.text: Right, for example, what are the specific contraindications for early rehabilitation intervention in stroke? I also get confused about identifying and managing autonomic dysreflexia after spinal cord injury.

session_329.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_329.text: Contraindications to early rehabilitation after stroke include: progressive elevation of intracranial pressure, blood pressure ≥200/110 mmHg, active bleeding, or hemodynamic instability within 48 hours after thrombolysis or thrombectomy. Autonomic dysreflexia in spinal cord injury is common in injuries above T6, with triggers such as bladder distension; typical manifestations include sudden hypertension with headache, facial flushing, and profuse sweating. The trigger should be removed immediately and blood pressure monitored; nifedipine may be used if necessary.

session_329.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_329.text: Got it! So what is the evidence-based basis for adjusting the rehabilitation plan? For example, if I meet a patient two weeks after a stroke with increased muscle tone but stable vital signs, should I continue rehabilitation or adjust it?

session_329.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_329.text: Stable vital signs are the prerequisite for continued rehabilitation. Increased muscle tone needs to be assessed for whether it affects function. If spasticity affects movement, the plan can be adjusted to include passive stretching and baclofen, but early rehabilitation should not be stopped. The core evidence-based basis is the AHA/ASA guidelines: within 24-48h after stroke, if the condition is stable, bedside rehabilitation can be started, except for contraindications. I suggest you compare the key decision points of different stages when practicing questions later.

session_336.text: I'm using Barthel index data from 14 stroke rehabilitation patients to make a waterfall chart. Although it's more intuitive than before, the colors and labels feel not professional enough, and I want it to clearly show the stages of functional improvement. Any suggestions for optimization?

session_336.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_336.text: I suggest using gradient blue for the early stage (0-30 points) to show rapid improvement, orange for the middle stage (30-60 points) to show steady improvement, and green for the late stage (60 points and above) to show the plateau. Data labels should directly annotate the change values, and key turning points (such as week 2) should be highlighted with arrows or notes. This both distinguishes the stages and meets the concise, standardized formatting requirements of medical journals.

session_336.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_336.text: The point about using colors to distinguish stages is very practical. What should I pay attention to when adding annotations? For example, how can the text better echo the results section of the paper?

session_336.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_336.text: Annotations should be concise, such as “marked functional improvement in Week 2 (+25 points),” and should correspond to the paragraph in the paper describing staged rehabilitation outcomes. It is suggested to place the waterfall chart in the Results section, title the chart “Barthel Index Trend,” directly mark key turning points on the chart, and use one or two sentences in the main text to summarize the change pattern, avoiding repetition.

session_336.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_336.text: I just finished reading an article on stroke rehabilitation adherence in the Chinese Medical Journal and extracted three core arguments: family support, patient beliefs, and the medical environment. I want to organically integrate them into the introduction of my paper, leading to my research based on local rehabilitation department data. How should I connect them logically? What structure do you recommend?

session_336.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_336.text: It is suggested to adopt a "funnel-style" introduction structure: first broadly introduce the importance of rehabilitation adherence, then focus on the literature evidence of the three influencing factors (family support, patient beliefs, medical environment), point out the shortcomings of existing research (such as the lack of localization or comprehensive analysis of a certain factor), and finally introduce your research to fill this gap. For logical coherence, you can proceed along "society-psychology-system," from external support (family) to internal motivation (beliefs) to external environment (medical care), with natural transitions.

session_336.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_336.text: This approach is very clear. But when writing the introduction specifically, how can I naturally transition from literature citations to my own research? In particular, what are some common ways to write transition sentences?

session_336.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_336.text: Common transition sentences include: "Although the above factors have been widely discussed, quantitative analysis targeting the local rehabilitation department patient population is still lacking." "Based on this, this study intends to use local rehabilitation department data from x month to x month of xxxx, systematically evaluating the interaction between family support and patient beliefs on adherence." Note that you need to paraphrase the literature conclusions in your own words, avoid direct copying, and just cite the source when quoting. This both highlights the necessity and naturally introduces your research angle.

session_341.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_341.text: I just applied a transparent glaze to the textured clay board for the grip ball used in my father's rehabilitation. Master Zheng said the glaze should not be too thick, and to increase the firing temperature by five degrees. Can you explain in detail what the ideal thickness of the transparent glaze is? Relative to what temperature is the five-degree increase, and what is the principle?

session_341.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_341.text: The ideal thickness of a transparent glaze is generally 0.2–0.3 mm; if it is too thick, it will easily cover up texture details. Master Zheng suggested raising the temperature by five degrees, which usually means a slight increase based on a medium-temperature kiln (e.g., 1180–1220°C), for example from 1200°C to 1205°C. This slightly increases glaze fluidity, helping it cover evenly without blurring the texture. For textured surfaces like a grip ball, a slow temperature rise (100–150°C per hour) is recommended, with a 10–15 minute hold at the maximum temperature to balance gloss and clarity.

session_341.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_341.text: The glaze I added is about 0.2 mm, so it should be fine, right? For firing, just raise the temperature by five degrees to 1205°C as Master Zheng said?

session_341.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_341.text: 0.2 mm is the ideal range. If it is applied evenly without obvious buildup, the texture effect will be very good. Raising the temperature by five degrees to 1205°C is a reasonable operation, but it is recommended to first place a test piece in the same kiln batch (using a waste blank coated with the same glaze thickness) to visually verify the final result and ensure everything is foolproof.

session_343.text: According to the common pottery process, transparent glaze usually needs bisque firing (about 800°C) before glazing; otherwise the clay body is too brittle and fragile. For thickness, dipping evenly for 2-3 seconds or brushing 1-2 layers is enough—too thick a layer is prone to running or bubbling. I suggest you bring the dried clay slab, sponge, and tweezers tomorrow, as well as a schedule that connects your morning and evening plans with the Sun Yue Bookstore date.

session_343.text: After bisque firing, it is recommended to gently wipe the surface with a damp sponge to remove loose dust and prevent the glaze from crawling. In addition, don't forget to wear gloves when glazing to prevent oil from your hands from affecting adhesion. You can organize the steps into a checklist: ① Check the clay slab's dryness ② Bisque fire (if the studio has one ready) ③ Clean ④ Dip glaze / brush glaze ⑤ Trim excess glaze from the bottom.

session_344.text: I just delivered the ceramic slab with the grip-ball texture to the studio. Master Zheng praised the glaze and suggested adding anti-slip massage bumps after firing to help my dad's rehabilitation. How exactly should I add them? What materials should I use? Could you explain the steps and precautions?

session_344.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_344.text: It is recommended to use food-grade silicone for the raised dots. No second firing is needed; they can be glued directly onto the raised areas of the glazed surface. The dots should be about 8 mm in diameter, 15 mm apart, and 3-5 mm high to enhance the grip. After curing, test the anti-slip performance. If it needs to be increased, ceramic particles mixed with resin can be used. In terms of rehabilitation effects, the raised dots can stimulate the acupoints and muscles of the hand, and combined with the texture of a grip ball, they can improve grip strength training.

session_344.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_344.text: I see. Does that bump actually help much with spinal cord injury rehabilitation? Are there similar successful cases?

session_344.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_344.text: Clinical studies show that similar tactile stimulation can promote neural remodeling and improve fine motor skills of the hand. Refer to the case of silicone massage ball gloves used in the rehabilitation department; regular gripping training can improve grip strength by 20%. Note that training should be done 15-20 minutes daily to avoid fatigue.

session_344.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_344.text: My parents got vaccinated this afternoon. My mother was nervous but it went without a hitch, and now the observation period is over. As a doctor, I still worry about potential adverse reactions, such as fever and local pain. Also, given my father's history of spinal cord injury, are there any special precautions?

session_344.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_344.text: I understand that your parents have just been vaccinated, your mother is feeling anxious, and your father has a history of spinal cord injury. Are you mainly concerned about handling common adverse reactions, the interval between concurrent medications, and special risks for patients with chronic diseases?

session_344.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_344.text: Yes, especially whether my father should stop taking mecobalamin tablets and vitamin B12? And at what fever temperature should he take medication?

session_344.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_344.text: Mecobalamin and vitamin B12 usually do not affect the vaccine reaction, so there is no need to stop taking them. If the temperature exceeds 38.5°C or there is severe discomfort, acetaminophen can be used; for local redness and swelling, apply a cold compress first and then a warm compress. It is recommended to observe for 48 hours, paying special attention to whether your father has any abnormal neurological symptoms.

session_344.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_344.text: I just cleaned out the family medicine cabinet and found three boxes of expired cold granules, povidone-iodine that had been opened for more than three months, and two boxes of my father's expired neurotrophic medications. I made a shopping list: ibuprofen, Vitamin C Yinqiao tablets, new povidone-iodine, band-aids, gauze and tape. My father said he has already bought vitamin B12 and Neurotropin, so no need for mecobalamin tablets. Can you help me check whether the list is reasonable? Especially since my father has a history of spinal cord injury, are there more suitable neurotrophic alternatives?

session_344.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_344.text: Your list is quite comprehensive, but here are a few optimization suggestions: 1) Ibuprofen is suitable for pain relief and fever reduction, but acetaminophen can be chosen if you are planning pregnancy or have a gastric ulcer; 2) Vitamin C Yinqiao tablets contain multiple ingredients and are prone to deterioration after opening, so pay attention to sealing and the expiry date. It is recommended to stock single-ingredient vitamin C tablets instead, as they are more stable; 3) Povidone-iodine has a validity period of 1 month after opening, and yours has been opened for more than 3 months, so it must be replaced; 4) For your father’s neurotrophic support, vitamin B12 and Neurotropin have effects similar to mecobalamin tablets, but Neurotropin is a compound preparation, so it is recommended to consult a doctor about whether it needs to be combined with mecobalamin. Do you want me to compare the applicable scenarios of these medications in detail?

session_344.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_344.text: Yes, I want to know which is more suitable as a home essential: ibuprofen or fever patches? Also, what exactly is the difference between the vitamin B12 and Neurotropin my father bought and mecobalamin tablets?

session_344.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_344.text: 1) Fever patches for physical cooling are suitable for low-grade fever below 38.5°C; ibuprofen is suitable for moderate to high fever (>38.5°C) or pain. It is recommended to keep ibuprofen at home, and an electronic thermometer is more practical. 2) Vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin) needs to be converted for absorption; methylcobalamin is the active form and has better nerve repair effects. Neurotropin contains neurotrophic factors and is suitable for spinal cord injury, but the dosage needs to be evaluated by a doctor. It is recommended that your father keep the current plan and consult the doctor at the next follow-up about whether to switch to methylcobalamin or use combination therapy.

session_345.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_345.text: The key difference between atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter is that in atrial fibrillation, P waves disappear and are replaced by f waves (rate 350-600 beats/min), while atrial flutter shows sawtooth F waves (250-350 beats/min). Mnemonic: 'Atrial fibrillation has fine, irregular f waves; atrial flutter has sawtooth, regular F waves.' For example, beta-blockers are used in atrial fibrillation to control ventricular rate, and synchronized cardioversion is the first choice for atrial flutter.

session_350.text: It sounds like an experience that was both fulfilling and heartwarming. Are you hoping someone can share in the sense of fulfillment from completing the exhibition and the joy of preparing a gift for a friend?

session_350.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_350.text: Master Zheng suggested I try making a series of the twelve Chinese zodiac animals, but I don't know which animal to start with, and how should I design the features of different animals?

session_350.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_350.text: It is recommended to start with the zodiac sign 'Rat' because its small size and flexible form are suitable for practicing hand-building techniques. The long tail and round ears can be emphasized, and a plain and elegant celadon glaze can be used to reflect the unity of the series. Subsequent pieces can proceed in zodiac order, with each work incorporating the cultural symbolism of the corresponding animal, such as the diligence of the ox and the might of the tiger.

session_350.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_350.text: The rat is indeed easy to handle, but I want to do something challenging, like a dog. How should I express a sense of loyalty? And in terms of technique, is wheel throwing or hand-building better?

session_350.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_350.text: For dogs, it is recommended to emphasize a lying or looking-back posture, using coiled clay strips to build muscle lines and express loyalty. In terms of technique, hand-pinching is recommended for small animals (mice, rabbits); medium ones (dogs, sheep) can combine slab construction; large ones (dragons, horses) use wheel-throwing and assembly. For the series, a matte glaze is recommended throughout to enhance texture.

session_350.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_350.text: Matte glaze is a great idea! But I'm usually busy with work. How should I plan my time to finish twelve pieces?

session_350.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_350.text: It is recommended to make a monthly plan: focus on completing one or two pieces each month, set aside 2 to 3 hours on weekends for concentrated creation, and use about 1 hour in the evenings on workdays for design sketches or small components. Set the goal of completing a series exhibition in about a year, so you have motivation without affecting your work. Would you like help making a specific schedule?

session_351.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_351.text: I'm making a series of Chinese zodiac ceramics, and I want to create a light amber glaze like aged white tea to achieve a warm, smooth texture. The book mentions iron oxide and manganese oxide, but I don't know how to control the exact proportions and glaze thickness. Can you give me some practical advice?

session_351.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_351.text: Suggested base formula: 3-5% iron oxide, 0.5-1% manganese oxide, with transparent or opaque glaze as the base. Apply the glaze twice, each time about 0.5mm thick, and fire at 1230-1260°C in a reducing atmosphere. First make test pieces to adjust the ratios; for example, 4% iron oxide plus 0.8% manganese oxide may be close to the light amber color you want.

session_351.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_351.text: How exactly do you operate in a reduction atmosphere? And if I want a warmer, matte finish, should I adjust the temperature or the glaze composition?

session_351.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_351.text: A reduction atmosphere is achieved by controlling the oxygen level in the kiln, for example by reducing air intake or adding silicon carbide. If you want a matte, warm finish, you can lower the iron oxide content to 2-3%, add 3-5% zinc oxide or talc, and reduce the firing temperature by 10-20°C. It is recommended to first make 3-5 test pieces for comparison.

session_353.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_353.text: You can communicate using the framework 'current situation → future goals → specific questions': first present your financial status and rehabilitation expenses, then explain your savings goals, and then directly ask about fund risks and fee allocation optimization. session_353.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_353.text: Hello doctor. I've recently been taking iron supplements, red meat, and liver, and my dizziness and fatigue have basically disappeared, and I have much more energy. I'd like to confirm whether my current diet plan is scientific. Since I'm preparing for the attending physician exam and my brain is working hard, do I need to make adjustments?

session_353.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_353.text: Very good. Your improvement shows that the iron supplement is very effective. The current plan is scientifically sound, and I suggest you continue with it. During the exam preparation period, you can add B vitamins (such as whole grains and leafy greens) and Omega-3 (such as deep-sea fish and walnuts), which help with brain function and reduce fatigue. You can try adding a small handful of walnuts to your breakfast and pairing lunch with a serving of steamed fish.

session_353.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_353.text: Okay, I often eat light tofu and hulatang in the evening. Is this combination okay? Are there more recommended recipes for exam preparation?

session_353.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_353.text: Tofu and hulatang are light and good, but hulatang is high in salt, so moderation is recommended. For exam preparation: breakfast oatmeal + egg + kiwi; lunch multigrain rice + steamed fish + broccoli; dinner tofu soup + chicken + stir-fried spinach. For snacks, yogurt or protein bars are options to ensure protein and vitamin intake.

session_353.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_353.text: I just read the chapter on texture and glaze color matching in "Introduction to Advanced Pottery". I want to design a vase with relief patterns, but I'm not sure how to combine paddling and carving techniques to create a natural texture effect. Do you have any suggestions?

session_353.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_353.text: You can try using the paddling technique to shape the basic form first. When the clay body is half-dry, use a carving knife or homemade tools to carve shallow relief patterns, then use a sponge dipped in water to gently refine the edges. This will make the texture more natural. Also, there happens to be a handicraft market around this time, so keep an eye out for the antique-textured pieces exhibited there; they might give you inspiration and glaze color references.

session_358.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_358.text: Today I shadowed Director Wang. When he was developing a rehabilitation plan for a patient with spinal cord injury from a car accident, he first asked the patient, 'What are the most inconvenient things in your daily life?' and then made a function-oriented plan rather than focusing only on indicators such as muscle strength and sensation. I had just read the chapter 'The Clinical Gaze' in The Birth of the Clinic, and I felt a resonance between the two. Could you help me sort out the essential difference between being 'function-oriented' and being 'indicator-oriented'?

session_358.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_358.text: You want to connect Director Wang's practice with Foucault's theory from the perspectives of medical humanities and clinical thinking, and explore how to cultivate this 'function-oriented' insight in daily life?

session_358.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_358.text: Yes, I really want to understand: why is focusing on the patient's account of 'the most inconvenient thing' more effective than only looking at indicators? How can this 'clinical gaze' be applied to the daily diagnosis and treatment of resident physicians?

session_358.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_358.text: The essential difference is that indicator-oriented approaches focus on objective measurements (such as muscle strength grading) and can easily overlook the patient's actual daily-life difficulties; function-oriented approaches start from the patient's chief complaints and life scenarios, directly linking rehabilitation goals to daily activities (such as toileting and walking). Director Wang's interviewing skill is an embodiment of the 'clinical gaze'—by listening to the patient's description of their impairments, she constructs an individualized functional profile. You can try asking more often during consultations, 'How does this problem affect your daily life?' and record the patient's functional needs to gradually develop this perspective.

session_358.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_358.text: Got it! I'll try using this approach when questioning patients during ward rounds tomorrow. Also, the book mentions that "the gaze" is a power relation. Director Wang's approach seems to weaken the doctor-patient power difference and focuses more on cooperation. Can you add more about the "clinical gaze" and patient subjectivity in The Birth of the Clinic?

session_358.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_358.text: Foucault argued that the traditional gaze objectifies patients, whereas Director Wang's approach, starting from the patient's functional needs, actually grants the patient subjectivity, involves the patient in goal setting, and balances the power relationship. I suggest you reread the inquiry-observation-description cycle in Chapter 2 and think about how to transform the clinical gaze from one-way observation into two-way dialogue in your own practice. This will deepen your understanding of the humanistic dimensions of rehabilitation medicine and help you formulate your next personal growth plan.

session_359.text: I started taking an iron supplement in mid-November and kept a food diary. I noticed improved energy and better complexion, but I'm not sure whether it's entirely due to the iron supplement. I'd like to ask for a scientific interpretation and follow-up advice.

session_359.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_359.text: Tonight, a snowy night, I soaked my feet and reread the chapter on the 'medical gaze' in Foucault's The Birth of the Clinic. Snow fell outside the window, and Winterreise played on a loop indoors—this immersion made the detachment of the 'gaze' and the weight of history feel especially real. How much of Foucault's description of the evolution of medical discourse power do you think still remains in contemporary doctor-patient relationships?

session_359.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_359.text: You seem to be not just sharing your reading experience, but also exploring how the 'medical gaze' has continued from its birth in the 18th century into modern clinical practice, especially its implications for your field of rehabilitation medicine. Foucault's 'gaze' implies a binding of power and knowledge. In contemporary doctor-patient communication, doctors still often unconsciously occupy a hegemonic position of 'viewing'—but your reflection itself is already a loosening of that structure. Did the stillness of the snowy night and the loneliness of 'Winterreise' strengthen the power of this critical thinking?

session_359.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_359.text: Indeed, the structure Foucault critiqued 30 years ago is still being reproduced today — doctors hold the power of terminology and diagnosis, and patients become objects of the gaze. As a rehabilitation physician, I often think about how to inject dialogue into the ‘gaze.’ The line in the book, ‘Clinical medicine was born from the gaze of death,’ is especially striking. How do you understand this sentence’s meaning in the contemporary era?

session_359.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_359.text: Foucault's original point was that anatomy transformed death into a scientific understanding of life, thereby giving rise to the medical 'gaze.' In a contemporary sense, it reminds us: the more advanced medical technology becomes, the more we must guard against the tendency to 'objectify' patients. The 'dialogical' aspect you mentioned may be the antidote - rehabilitation medicine emphasizes function and participation, and naturally requires breaking the one-way gaze. Next time we can discuss the chapter on 'discourse power,' or the concept of 'bodily discipline,' which intersects with your field. Reading on a snowy night is truly a moment where pathology and poetry are interwoven.

session_362.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_362.text: I've been on an iron-rich diet for two months. I felt good after a 5 km morning run today, but I want to assess whether the improvement in my anemia is scientifically sound. What should I pay attention to before going to the hospital for a routine blood test tomorrow?

session_362.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_362.text: A routine blood test usually requires fasting for 8-12 hours; it is recommended that you refrain from food and water tomorrow morning. In addition, avoid strenuous exercise as it may affect the results. Your morning run today is fine, but don't do extra exercise before the test. No other special preparation is needed.

session_362.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_362.text: Fasting — I understand. After the complete blood count results come out, how do we judge whether the anemia has improved? Are additional tests needed?

session_362.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_362.text: Focus on hemoglobin (Hb), red blood cell count (RBC), and serum ferritin. If Hb is close to the normal range, it indicates improvement. If it is still low, it is recommended to add an iron metabolism panel and vitamin B12 and folate levels to rule out other types of anemia. Continue iron supplementation in the diet, paired with vitamin C to promote absorption.

session_362.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_362.text: This morning I ran 5 kilometers in minus 1 degree Celsius in 32 minutes, with a pace of 6 minutes 24 seconds per kilometer. I felt a real sense of accomplishment! Also, I noticed that my anemia has improved. Is it related to running?

session_362.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_362.text: Congratulations on your winter morning running breakthrough! Regular aerobic exercise can indeed promote blood circulation and red blood cell production, which has a positive effect on improving anemia. It is recommended to keep it up, but pay attention to monitoring your heart rate and fatigue level. In winter running, pay special attention to staying warm and maintaining your breathing rhythm.

session_362.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_362.text: What specific mechanisms help anemia recovery? How should I optimize my pace and heart rate?

session_362.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_362.text: Running can increase plasma volume and the oxygen-carrying capacity of red blood cells, while also stimulating bone marrow hematopoiesis. Pace optimization can be combined with heart rate zone training (recommended to maintain 140-155 bpm). In winter, short-distance interval running can improve efficiency. Maintain 3-4 sessions per week and gradually increase intensity to avoid overtraining affecting recovery.

session_363.text: Hello Doctor, today (2025-12-29) I had a follow-up complete blood count. Hemoglobin is 125 g/L, and ferritin is normal, so the anemia has been corrected. I'd like to know how to maintain this going forward, and what to pay attention to in terms of diet and exercise.

session_363.speaker: Yu Xiaowen's Assistant
session_363.text: Congratulations on your lab results returning to normal! You want to consolidate your health and prevent relapse, right? It is recommended to continue a balanced diet, eating red meat or animal liver 1-2 times a week (for example, the spinach and pork liver soup your mother makes), paired with fruits and vegetables rich in vitamin C to promote iron absorption. Iron supplements can usually be stopped, but you need to pay attention after your period.

session_363.speaker: Yu Xiaowen
session_363.text: I usually like running and badminton. How should I control the exercise intensity? And do I need regular follow-ups?

qa.question: (Question time: 2025-12-31)In January 2025, my father suffered a sudden cerebral infarction at noon on the 15th. What specific changes occurred in my exercise patterns before and after my father's illness? How do these changes reflect the shift in the focus of my life?

qa.question: (Question time: 2025-12-31)What patterns were there in my learning engagement in April? And how does it relate to my career development?

The second track was preparation for the attending physician examination: it began on April 8 after being reminded by my supervising teacher. On April 14, I made a detailed monthly plan, then started reviewing the cardiovascular system on April 24, and consolidated it through literature reading on April 30. In addition, medical humanities reading ran through the whole month, including "Being Mortal", "Better", the literary fiction work "The Night Submarine", and multiple book club discussions (such as co-reading "Lean In", the Wutong Tree Book Club, Fan Deng Co-reading, Nonviolent Communication discussions, and discussions of a women's power reading list), which broadened my clinical perspective. This pattern was closely related to professional development: statistical competence directly serves scientific research papers and clinical data analysis and is the key to academic improvement; preparation for the attending physician examination is a necessary step for professional title promotion and is directly linked to career advancement (during which I also participated in a first aid skills competition to maintain clinical competence); humanities reading strengthens doctor-patient communication and understanding of bioethics, improving overall quality. The three learning tracks jointly point to a growth path that integrates clinical work, research, and the humanities.

During the same period, I developed interests in handicrafts (pottery on the 11th) and exercise (morning run on the 15th). In the second half (days 16–31), the focus shifted to research output and career development: from the 22nd to the 27th, I completed multivariate logistic regression analysis; on the 29th, I reported to Li Wei and received the suggestion to submit to a youth forum; on the 30th, I attended an intensive preparation class for the attending physician qualification exam; on the 21st, I observed a lower-limb rehabilitation robot. Interests continued to expand, with activities such as mountain climbing (hiking at Songshan on the 18th) and baking (French dessert class on the 24th). There were three key turning points: on May 6, I signed up for medical English and SPSS learning, marking the start of systematic research skill improvement; on May 13, my presentation in the department's case discussion was recognized by the director, boosting my career confidence; on May 20, I exchanged ideas with Zhao Ming on rehabilitation technology and art therapy, stimulating new thinking about the integration of rehabilitation technology and the humanities.

session_1.text: I currently can run 10 km in 1 hour 10 minutes, with a weekly mileage of about 30 km, and I want to systematically prepare for a half marathon next year. session_1.speaker: Feng Haoran's Assistant
session_1.text: It is recommended to use a 12-week cycle. The first 4 weeks are the base phase: weekly mileage gradually increases from 30 km to 40 km, pace kept at 5:30–6:00/km, with one core strength session per week. The middle 4 weeks are the strengthening phase: add one interval run (e.g., 400m × 6 @ 5:00) and one tempo run (8 km @ 5:10), and increase weekly mileage to 45–50 km. The last 4 weeks are the peak and taper phase: LSD (long slow distance) increases from 12 km to 20 km, then reduce volume by 30% in the final two weeks. Injury prevention: two dynamic stretching sessions per week, and ice the knees after runs.

session_9.text: I just attended the Fintech Summit, and I have many questions about the application of blockchain in ABS and risk management for robo-advisory. Could you help me sort out the key points?

session_9.speaker: Feng Haoran's Assistant
session_9.text: Do you pay more attention to technical details, such as the risk control mechanism of smart contracts in portfolio rebalancing, or the compliance path at the application level and the differences from traditional investment advisors?

session_9.speaker: Feng Haoran
session_9.text: I want to understand both aspects in depth. Especially the specific application of blockchain in supply chain finance ABS, and how robo-advisors shift from passive allocation to active risk management.

session_9.speaker: Feng Haoran's Assistant
session_9.text: In supply chain finance ABS, blockchain uses a distributed ledger to achieve asset transparency, and smart contracts automatically execute repayment and risk trigger conditions. Robo-advisor 2.0 introduces real-time market sentiment indices and dynamic rebalancing thresholds, replacing the traditional fixed allocation model. My suggestion is: first understand the underlying logic, then run simulation tests based on your client's asset portfolio.

session_9.speaker: Feng Haoran
session_9.text: I just discussed an idea with my childhood friend — building an 'industry sentiment index' using public financial reports and news sentiment, for high-net-worth clients to reference. How do you think this concept can be implemented?

session_9.speaker: Feng Haoran's Assistant
session_9.text: Sounds very promising. Would you like me to help you sort out data source selection, index construction methods, or evaluate its differentiating value for the existing investment advisory services?

session_9.speaker: Feng Haoran
session_9.text: Both are needed, especially how to quantify news sentiment, build a backtesting mechanism, and present value to clients. I want to do an internal evaluation first, then decide whether to report to my supervisor.

session_9.speaker: Feng Haoran's Assistant
session_9.text: I suggest three steps: 1) Screen highly correlated financial report indicators (such as revenue growth rate, gross margin changes); 2) Use sentiment analysis models to quantify news sentiment (e.g., a financial sentiment dictionary based on BERT); 3) Construct a weighted index, then use historical data to backtest its correlation with industry gains and losses. In terms of differentiation, it can be positioned as a 'forward-looking sentiment warning', complementary to existing technical analysis.
