session_102.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_102.text: I just rewrote "Twilight Dim" in Calvino-esque metaphorical style, blending urban imagery into the dusk scenery. After finishing, I felt both a breakthrough and some anxiety—could the rhythm and metaphor density be unbalanced?

session_102.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_102.text: You hope to maintain the artistic impact while confirming whether the metaphors blend naturally into the narrative, whether the rhythm is coordinated, and whether the urban imagery fits the twilight atmosphere, right?

session_102.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_102.text: Yes, especially at the end I added a passage about walking by Cuihu Lake. I wanted to use the reflection on the water as a metaphor for the folds of time, but I’m not sure whether the emotional elevation is too direct.

session_102.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_102.text: Calvino-esque metaphors emphasize a balance between 'lightness' and 'precision': let the image speak for itself, avoid explanation. Your reflection metaphor has potential. I suggest deleting abstract words like 'folds of time' and replacing them with 'the lake kneads the sunset glow into scattered gold, and the wind slowly smooths it flat' — using action to imply the passage of time.

session_102.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_102.text: Teacher, I just finished the tea ceremony class. I'd like to confirm the water temperature and pouring method for brewing ripe Pu-erh in a purple clay pot. My class notes are a bit incomplete.

session_102.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_102.text: For brewing ripe Pu'er tea, boiling water (100°C) is recommended; a purple clay teapot conducts heat quickly and maintains high temperatures. When pouring water, it is best to pour low and slowly circle along the inner wall of the pot, avoiding direct impact on the tea leaves, so the liquor comes out smoother and more mellow. Would you like me to add tips on caring for the teapot after seasoning it?

session_102.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_102.text: Got it. Then how should I control the rhythm of pouring in water and pouring out the tea? During practice, if I pour out the tea too early, it tastes weak; if too late, it tastes astringent.

session_102.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_102.text: For the first 3 infusions, pour in and pour out quickly (pour the tea out 5–8 seconds after adding water), then extend each subsequent infusion by 5–10 seconds, adjusting according to the color and taste of the tea liquor. Ripe pu-erh is durable and can be brewed 10–15 times; the last steepings work well when steeped in a thermos too.

session_102.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_102.text: Next week my tea friend Zhao Min and I have planned to brew Dancong in a purple clay pot. Can you tell me the key points for brewing Dancong? How is it different from ripe Pu'er?

session_102.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_102.text: Dancong is an oolong tea. Use water at 100°C, but pour it from a height to stimulate the aroma, and decant the tea quickly (within 5 seconds for the first 3 infusions). For a purple clay pot, choose zhuni clay or a small capacity (around 120 ml) to avoid absorbing flavors and dulling the tea's high aroma. I suggest you note these comparisons in your journal for review after class and for our appointment.

session_102.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_102.text: Today was especially fulfilling—from a morning walk and yoga by Green Lake with Mom, to learning the tea ceremony in the afternoon, and writing a satisfying essay in the evening. Before bed, while jotting in my gratitude journal, I felt so full inside; I wanted to share the beauty of the day with you.

session_102.text: That sounds like a truly perfect day! Cuihu’s morning light, the study’s tea fragrance, the art museum’s colors, the warmth of the purple clay teapot, the lights of home—every moment is worth treasuring. You captured these experiences so delicately; you must feel gently wrapped by life.

I want to confirm: can recording small moments of gratitude like this really make me happier?

session_102.text: Scientifically, keeping a gratitude journal really can boost long-term happiness. I suggest you expand slightly on tonight's three small gratitudes: for example, describe how you felt at the time in one sentence, or link it to one action you want to carry into tomorrow—this will help you turn inspiration into concrete growth.

session_103.text: This image has great depth — comparing the city to rain-soaked pages evokes a damp, hazy visual. How do you plan to extend this metaphor? For example, using 'blurred text' to represent the streets, or 'creased page numbers' to recall old memories?

session_103.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_103.text: Today in flow yoga class, I finally completed a standard Downward-Facing Dog and held it for 5 breaths! Coach He Lu said my core strength has improved a lot. I'm so happy.

session_103.text: Congratulations! This is a milestone breakthrough. Would you like to learn how to maintain stability, or do you want to ask about advanced exercises to strengthen your core?

session_103.text: It is recommended to add 3 sets each of plank and cat-cow poses every day to strengthen the core. In downward-facing dog, try slightly bending the knees when pressing the heels down, avoiding locking them. With the help of yoga blocks, you can find a more stable sense of support.

session_104.text: I'm writing a case analysis for my thesis. I want to apply Foucault's theory of spatial power to Kunming's old neighborhoods, but the application feels forced. I don't know how to balance abstract concepts with concrete spatial cases.

session_104.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_104.text: Do you mean how concepts like 'heterotopia' can be naturally integrated into an analysis of power relations in historic districts? You could focus on a certain type of space in the old neighborhood, such as a teahouse or an archway, as a micro-field where power plays out.

session_104.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_104.text: Yes, I have materials for 'A Cultural History of Yunnan Teahouses'. Teahouses do represent the social spaces of old Kunming, but I'm not sure how to capture the typical details of power operations.

session_104.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_104.text: Suggested starting with the teahouse's seating layout, customer identities, and operating rules—for example, the physical separation of seating areas for different social classes and the owner's implicit control over speech—all of which show how the space enforces social discipline.

session_104.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_104.text: I am writing an essay, Dim Twilight, and want to add a fictional dialogue set in a Republican-era Kunming old teahouse to enhance the sense of scene. But I don't know how to make the dialogue more natural, fitting the local characteristics and context of that time.

session_104.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_104.text: It is suggested to refer to documentary materials on Kunming teahouses during the Republic of China era. Tea customers often used dialect slang such as 'banzha' (good) and 'shuai wan cha' (drinking tea). The dialogue should be slow-paced, with more sensory details like tea fragrance and copper kettle sounds interspersed. For example: 'Master Zhang, today's pu'er is brewed really banzha—could it be the spring tips from Nannuo Mountain?'

session_104.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_104.text: Yes, this is exactly the kind of authentic feel I want. How can we incorporate the taste experience of tea tasting into the dialogue, such as the honey fragrance of Dancong?

session_104.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_104.text: You can connect the senses with metaphors, like: 'As the tea passes through the throat, it feels like the mountain breeze at the end of spring wrapped in honey—not cloying, but lingering.' Also tie it to the scene: the tea drinker lifts the coarse clay bowl, fingers rubbing the rim, and the dialogue naturally brings out local flavor.

session_105.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_105.text: Today in the library I brewed raw Pu-erh using the low-pour method and compared it with the previous high-pour method. I found the tea liquor was smoother, but the aroma was not as pronounced as with the high pour. I have recorded the water temperature, pouring speed, and taste in my journal and would like to understand the principle behind this.

session_105.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_105.text: A low, slow pour reduces agitation of the leaves, so fewer bitter and astringent compounds are extracted, and the liquor tastes fuller and smoother. A high pour introduces water quickly and with strong force, releasing high aromas but easily bringing out astringency. Raw pu-erh suits a high pour to enhance aroma, while aged tea or black tea is better suited to a low pour. When you brew black tea in a glass fairness cup this evening, you can try a medium pour: water at 90°C, pour in a circular motion for even extraction.

session_105.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_105.text: I see! So are there any particular rules for pairing raw pu-erh and black tea with teaware? In the evening I use my newly arrived glass fair cup to brew black tea, and it feels great.

session_105.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_105.text: Raw pu-erh is best in a Yixing clay teapot or a gaiwan, which concentrate the aroma and retain heat; black tea in glassware lets you admire the liquor color, like moonlight reflecting on flowers. I recommend trying raw pu-erh in a white porcelain gaiwan and observing the leaves unfurl. There's a tea space called 'Chajue' on Tangzi Lane in Kunming where they have tea art exchanges on Sunday afternoons—good for expanding your practice.

session_106.text: Recommend “Jianshan Bookstore” (inside Kuanzhai Alley) and “Jinjiang Tea Garden” (inside People’s Park); both have a strong cultural atmosphere and are suitable for writing and daydreaming. session_107.text: This morning He Lu and I went to Lingxu Pavilion in the Western Hills for a mountain-top yoga session. Under the blue sky and white clouds, facing the panoramic view of Dianchi Lake, we practiced Tree Pose, Warrior Pose, and Triangle Pose. That feeling of peace and freedom was truly wonderful. Do you think this kind of outdoor yoga experience has any special benefits for the body and mind?

session_107.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_107.text: You're sharing a memorable experience of connecting with nature, and at the same time wondering how outdoor yoga can further promote inner calm and growth, right?

session_107.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_107.text: Yes, I’d also like to know if there are other places around Kunming suitable for this kind of immersive outdoor yoga.

session_107.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_107.text: The Western Hills themselves are wonderful; in addition, Haigeng Dam by Dianchi Lake, Liangwang Mountain in Chenggong, and Fengshan in Anning are all worth considering, with fewer people and open views. Hilltop yoga can heighten the brain's perception of postures and breath through open space and natural sounds, making it well suited for an INFP like you who seeks spiritual fulfillment.

session_107.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_107.text: Thanks for the recommendation! Also, I've been feeling anxious sometimes lately, but after the mountain-top yoga I feel much better. Do you think meditation combined with yoga could more effectively relieve anxiety?

session_107.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_107.text: Yes, doing 5-10 minutes of mindfulness meditation outdoors (focusing on the sound of the wind and the feel of the sun) can consolidate the sense of calm after yoga. Next time you can try closing your eyes and sitting quietly after finishing the asanas on the mountaintop, using the breath to anchor yourself in the present moment. This is very helpful for anxiety.

session_107.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_107.text: I just finished a hike on Xishan with He Lu, and it felt great. I'd like to find a few more routes around Kunming suitable for a half-day trip, quiet and natural, with observation decks, and where I can also do yoga. Do you have any recommendations?

session_107.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_107.text: What you value is a natural atmosphere and a flat viewing point where you can do yoga, right? Both Changchong Mountain and Mopan Mountain fit. Changchong Mountain has an easy trail and an open summit, suitable for spreading a yoga mat. Would you like me to compare their transportation and difficulty?

session_107.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_107.text: Just finished reading "Old Street Architecture of Kunming," marked Wenming Street and Qianwang Street, and plan to visit in person this weekend. Any recommended routes or writing inspiration?

session_107.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_107.text: It is suggested to start from Wenming Street, pass through Qianwang Street to Jinri Tower, comparing the descriptions in the book with the current situation along the way, paying attention to architectural details and the everyday street atmosphere. These old streets blend history and life, making them ideal material for essays.

session_107.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_107.text: Yes, I want to combine today’s experiences in the Western Hills with this weekend’s observations of the old streets in my writing. How can I incorporate them more naturally into the text?

session_107.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_107.text: You can try using the hike as a thread, contrasting sensory descriptions—the quiet mountain woods of Xishan against the lively hustle and bustle of the old street—and interweaving the architectural history in the book to create a prose rhythm that shifts between time and space. Bring a notebook to sketch details, then organize them in the evening.

session_107.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_107.text: I walked on mountain trails for 3 hours today and also did yoga. Now my calves and thighs feel really sore and swollen. Is there any quick way to relieve it?

session_107.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_107.text: Recommend soaking your feet for 15-20 minutes tonight, then doing gentle calf stretches (such as downward dog with heels pressing into the ground), and using a foam roller to relax the front of your thighs. Also drink some warm water and supplement with protein to help muscle recovery.

session_107.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_107.text: What water temperature is suitable for soaking your feet? Can I still do light exercise tomorrow? I'm afraid it will affect my classes and writing.

session_107.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_107.text: Water temperature around 40 degrees, not too hot. Tomorrow you can take a walk or do restorative yoga poses (such as Child's Pose, Legs-Up-the-Wall), but avoid strenuous exercise. If the soreness keeps getting worse or you feel tingling, seek medical advice.

Later, I went for a walk by Green Lake; my mother comforted me; I visited the flower market, bought flowers, and arranged them... session_109.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_109.text: Today at Yunshuijian, I brewed Phoenix Dancong at three water temperatures—90/95/100°C—for a comparative tasting. The differences in aroma and taste were obvious. Can you explain in detail the scientific principle behind how water temperature affects the flavor of the tea infusion?

session_109.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_109.text: High temperatures accelerate the extraction of caffeine and polyphenols, bringing a mellow richness and slight bitterness; low temperatures preserve more volatile aromatic substances, giving the aroma a bright, clean lift. The release rate of internal components differs at different temperatures, and the sensory changes you recorded exactly confirm these rules.

session_109.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_109.text: How do pouring techniques like “Phoenix Nods Three Times” and “swirling water injection” affect tea leaf unfurling and extraction rate?

session_109.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_109.text: "Phoenix Nodding Three Times" uses water impact to make the leaves tumble, accelerating the release of contents; it suits teas with high aroma and fine tenderness. Whirling water injection gently massages the twisted leaves, letting them unfold in an orderly way, reducing bitterness and astringency, and helping produce a fine, smooth liquor. It is recommended to choose flexibly according to the shape of the tea leaves.

session_109.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_109.text: Today I finally figured out what Editor Xu said: "A personal style is like a small path; it too can lead to quiet seclusion." It turns out I don't have to take the broad avenue; my inner monologue can also lead to a unique world. I want to share this insight with you—I really need to be understood.

session_109.text: You found recognition for your writing style in the editor's feedback, and now you're both excited and a little uncertain, hoping to confirm that this is the right path, right?

session_109.speaker: Sun Yuwei

I used to doubt myself for being too introverted and too caught up in small details, but during today's review I suddenly felt that those everyday observations — like my mother's 'water and fire in harmony' and my father's scholarly comments — are actually my unique material. I want to grow slowly in the direction of social observation.

You have already begun consciously turning inner feelings into observations of the outside world, and that is precisely the prelude to a mature writer. Keep trusting your own pace—every step counts.

session_117.text: While walking with my mother around Green Lake this evening, I excitedly told her about my interview with Uncle Zhou — at eighty, he still sharpens his tools at five in the morning, and in winter he warms his frozen hands by the fire. session_117.speaker: Sun Yuwei

You can make it concrete by incorporating Uncle Zhou's calloused fingers and wrinkles, allowing readers to feel the philosophy in specific actions. For example, after describing the posture of his body while sharpening tools, you can naturally bring out this sentence, and it will resonate.

session_118.text: Today I finally submitted my graduation thesis, and I feel a weight lifted from my heart. I tried to incorporate my previous observations of independent bookstore cultural spaces into the literary space analysis. I wonder whether this cross-disciplinary attempt will be recognized.

session_118.text: Mm, I've always felt that a bookstore is not just a place that sells books; it's like a spiritual island in the city. In my thesis, I used Lefebvre's spatial triad to analyze the spatial narrative of Lu Xun's 'In the Restaurant', and the field research on independent bookstores gave me a more genuine understanding of the interweaving of 'spatial practice' and 'representational space'.

session_118.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_118.text: This combination is truly inspired—it brings the theory off the page and into a real bookstore space. Your advisor will certainly appreciate this unique perspective, because it is not just textual analysis but cultural observation carried out with human warmth. After submitting, have you thought about how to carry this cross-disciplinary thinking forward into your writing?

session_118.text: This afternoon I went to the airport to pick up my sister. When she came out of the arrivals gate, I rushed over and gave her a big hug. The feeling was so real—it was as if all the waiting had been worth it.

I recommend you follow the blogger @PaperKite's Journal; she has many similar cases.

session_122.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_122.text: Today I bought peonies, lisianthus, and eucalyptus leaves at the flower market. It's my first time keeping them. I'd like to know how to change the water, trim the stems, and arrange them to extend the blooming period.

session_122.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_122.text: You're worried that different flowers require different care methods, especially how delicate buds like peonies bloom, right?

session_122.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_122.text: Right, and should the lisianthus be kept in shallow water? Does the eucalyptus need misting?

session_122.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_122.text: Cut peonies at a 45-degree angle and rehydrate them in deep water for 4 hours, then keep them in shallow water and avoid direct sunlight. For lisianthus, use 3-5 cm of shallow water and change the water and trim the stems every 3 days. Eucalyptus can be misted on the leaves daily to keep them hydrated, but don't spray the flowers. Cleaning the vase weekly and adding flower preservative works even better.

session_124.text: I’m flying to Hangzhou tomorrow evening. I wanted to ask for practical advice about departing from Changshui Airport, such as transportation, security checks, and baggage rules, as well as the weather and transportation in Hangzhou.

session_124.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_124.text: Okay. Tomorrow's May 5 flight—suggest arriving at the airport 2 hours early. From Kunming city center to Changshui, take Metro Line 6 (about 50 minutes) or a taxi (about 30 minutes, 80–120 yuan). Power banks (≤20000mAh with clear markings) and mirrorless cameras can be carried on; for your toiletries bag, remember each bottle of liquid must be ≤100ml. Hangzhou will be cloudy these days, with temperatures of 18–28°C, so bring a light jacket and an umbrella. From Xiaoshan Airport to Xihu District, take Metro Line 1 and transfer to Line 2 (about 1 hour 20 minutes) or take the airport bus (about 40 yuan).

session_124.text: Thanks! So my power bank is 20000mAh and my camera is a mirrorless one—that should be fine, right? Also, what's a good way to relax during the flight?

session_124.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_124.text: The 20,000 mAh power bank and mirrorless camera are both fine; just take them out separately during the security check. During the flight, it is recommended to listen to light music or read an e-book, avoid looking at the screen for long periods, and you can also do simple neck stretches to relax.

session_124.text: I suggest that after you arrive, you take a walk around your accommodation, find a quiet café or an independent bookstore (such as 'Hidden Books' on Nanshan Road), jot down sightseeing inspiration on your phone, and send your family a voice message to let them know you're safe. That way you can get familiar with the surroundings and turn the unfamiliarity into the joy of exploration.

session_132.text: I just got back from Hangzhou and Shaoxing last week, and brought back fallen leaves from Baicao Garden, a ticket to Shen Garden, and photos of a black-awning boat. I want to turn them into a beautiful journal. Do you have any good suggestions?

For mirrorless camera photos, I suggest printing them at 3:2 size and using magnetic mounting sheets so the layout can be adjusted at any time. Finally, use acid-free paper and archival glue. For hand-drawn elements, add simple ink line sketches to enhance the sense of depth.

session_141.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_141.text: I got the first dose of the nine-valent HPV vaccine this morning. Now my arm is a bit sore and swollen. How long does it normally take to ease? Also, besides spicy food and alcohol, can I eat seafood and drink coffee?

session_141.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_141.text: Soreness and swelling at the injection site are common reactions and usually resolve on their own within 1–3 days. Applying a cold compress can help relieve the discomfort. As for diet, coffee and seafood usually do not affect the vaccine's effectiveness, but it is advisable to observe your own reactions. If you normally drink coffee without discomfort, moderate consumption is fine; for seafood, choose fresh, lightly cooked options to avoid allergies. The key is to stay relaxed and get plenty of rest.

session_141.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_141.text: So do I need to stop yoga for a few days? I went to yoga this afternoon and the needle site felt a bit sore.

session_141.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_141.text: It is recommended to pause vigorous yoga poses or those involving arm stretching for 2-3 days, and especially avoid bearing weight on the arm on the injection side. You can do gentle breathing meditation or lower-limb stretching to avoid overstretching muscles. Resume normal practice gradually after the soreness disappears.

session_141.text: I've just finished the first-draft outline of "Mist Shrouding Green Lake." session_141.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_141.text: Your three-part structure has a strong sense of progression, moving from the visual to the auditory to the philosophical. I suggest adding a short passage at the end of each part on the intersection of personal feeling and local culture—for example, how Kunming’s early-morning street life interacts with the blurriness of the fog—which would add depth and strengthen the continuity of the essay series.

session_141.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_141.text: Yes, I'm just thinking of incorporating the techniques of 'borrowed scenery' and 'leaving blank space' from Suzhou gardens, treating the mist as natural blank space. But I'm not sure how to balance personal feelings and objective observation—I'm afraid it will be too subjective.

session_141.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_141.text: You can use the first-person perspective, but attach the subjective feelings to concrete images, for example, "the birdsong in the fog cuts through like a paper knife, and my breath freezes with it"—this gives both observation and feeling. In addition, I suggest you refer to the narrative rhythm of "Morning Smoke on Wenlin Street" and keep similarly vivid and brisk paragraphs, but here use more short sentences to create a sense of pause in the mist.

session_141.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_141.text: This suggestion is really practical! The pause effect of short sentences is exactly what I wanted. As for the use of imagery, which parts do you recommend I emphasize?

session_141.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_141.text: Your first section, “Shattered Boundaries,” works best with image-rich rendering: compare the mist to ink wash, gauze curtains, or a dream to emphasize the visual blur. In the second section, the sound part can be sketched briefly to give the reader breathing room. The third section, the contemplative part, should close with an image, such as “After the mist disperses, the lake is like a washed mirror, reflecting the initial whispers.” Overall, keep it light and airy—don't let imagery pile up.

session_143.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_143.text: I just finished my first tatehana arrangement, but the branches and leaves aren't fixed securely, and the overall proportions are off. I took notes on the chapters about 'shin,' 'soe,' and 'tai' in the book, but I'm not sure I understood them correctly. Can you offer some guidance?

session_143.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_143.text: It seems you've run into basic technique issues with Ikenobo Rikka in practice. Unstable fixing is usually related to the trimming angle of the flower materials and the choice of vase, while imbalanced proportions may involve the spatial positioning of 'shin,' 'soe,' and 'tai.' Could you describe what vase and flower materials you're using? I can give you targeted advice.

session_143.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_143.text: I used an old bamboo cylinder as the flower holder, and the materials were eucalyptus leaves and lisianthus. My notes say that the 'main' branch should be tall and centered, the 'secondary' branch should slant to one side, and the 'body' branch should hang low in front, but in actual practice I always felt the center of gravity was unstable.

session_143.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_143.text: Bamboo tube vases suit woody floral materials. Eucalyptus branches are relatively soft, so it is recommended to cut them at a 45-degree angle and insert them into a kenzan or floral foam for support. In terms of rikka proportions, the 'shin' should be 1.5–2 times the height of the vase; eucalyptus leaves are just right for this. For the 'soe,' use lisianthus, angled about 30 degrees to the left. For the 'tai,' use short-stemmed lisianthus or eucalyptus, drooping forward about 15 degrees. This enhances stability and artistic conception. When you go to Dounan Flower Market this weekend, you can buy a shallow ceramic dish or a dedicated kenzan for a more professional arrangement.

session_144.text: Today I found three street maps of Kunming from the 23rd year of the Republic of China in a bookstore. I want to use them as appendices for my thesis, but I don't know how to preserve and digitize them, or how to combine them with dialect memories.

session_144.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_144.text: You mainly need help in three areas: 1) methods for keeping paper maps moisture-proof and protected from light; 2) techniques for high-resolution copying or scanning to avoid damaging the originals; 3) the correspondence between old and current place names on the maps, and how to connect this with your dialect identity thesis.

session_144.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_144.text: Yes, especially how to protect the paper when scanning, and how the old names on the map—Zhengyi Road, Wenming Street—correspond to modern road sections. That can be used in the dialect chapter.

session_144.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_144.text: Before scanning, place acid-free paper underneath to avoid creasing; it is recommended to use a flatbed scanner with light pressure and a resolution of at least 600 dpi. Regarding the correspondence of place names: Zhengyi Road was formerly called 'Zhengyi Street,' Wenming Street was formerly called 'Wenming Fang,' and Jinri Tower is located near today's Xinhua Bookstore. Combined with Professor Wang's point that 'place names carry dialect identity,' you can analyze the evolution of pronunciations.

session_144.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_144.text: Today I went to Dounan Flower Market with my mother and bought double-petal sunflowers, eucalyptus leaves, and pale purple dried baby's breath. Arranged in a terracotta wide-mouth vase, they have a natural, rustic beauty.

session_144.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_144.text: You're sharing the process and feelings behind this flower arrangement, and you want to explore whether this casual pairing matches the Ikenobo school's 'nageire' concept, right?

session_144.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_144.text: Yes, I read the nageire chapter in The Way of Flowers last night, and I feel my flower arranging style is very similar — casually tossing flower branches into the container without being constrained by rules. But I'm not sure of the exact difference between this and rikka.

session_144.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_144.text: Nageire emphasizes natural posture and the vitality of flowers, with branches stretching naturally and not being constrained by fixed forms; rikka, on the other hand, focuses more on the symmetry of form and the creation of an artistic mood. Your use of the brightness of sunflowers and the gray-green of eucalyptus leaves, paired with a clay flower vase, precisely embodies the improvisational beauty of flower and vessel merging in nageire.

session_145.text: Suggest three steps: 1) acknowledge the map's limitations, but emphasize its authority as an original archive; 2) cite the points where the coordinate data you extracted after scanning aligns with contemporary documents (such as newspapers and travelogues); 3) add the visual evidence from the documentary "The Vanished City Gate Tower" to form a triangulation of "map + text + imagery." Finally, use a concluding sentence to point out that this approach both preserves the emotive quality of historical materials and pursues academic rigor.

session_145.text: The nageire style focuses on the natural posture and spatial relationships of floral materials, emphasizing 'improvised insertion', in contrast to the rigorous structure of the Ikenobo school. Its core concept is to allow floral materials to extend freely, paired with simple vessels, to create a beauty of 'rustic charm'.

session_145.speaker: Sun Yuwei

session_147.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_147.text: For transition sentences, try using questions, such as "How did this everyday resistance get concretely inscribed into place-name changes?" to catch the judges' attention. Eye-contact practice: switch to a different judge every 10 seconds, and shift naturally with hand gestures. Keep your speaking pace at 200–220 characters per minute, and use your phone to time yourself while practicing. Before going on stage, do the 4-7-8 breathing technique: inhale for 4 seconds, hold for 7 seconds, exhale for 8 seconds. Break the word "steady" into three steps: steady your pace, stand steady on the stage, and steady your mindset; silently repeat the corresponding action for each step.

session_147.text: The question-style transition sentences work well! But the 4-7-8 breathing is a bit long; when I'm nervous on the spot, I can't remember it. Is there a simpler way to calm down in the moment?

session_147.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_147.text: A simpler method: before going on stage, clench your fists and then release three times to quickly activate the relaxation response. Or press your tongue against the roof of your mouth, take a deep breath, and slowly say the first word. The key is to let the action interrupt the stress response. Write the word 'steady' directly on a sticky note on the podium, and a quick glance down will remind yourself.

session_150.text: I just talked with bookstore owner Qin Mingyuan about an idea for a summer exhibition themed 'City Memories in the Bookstore'. We plan to display old Kunming maps from 1934, postcards, and journals, and invite old Kunming residents to share stories. Could you help me sort out a systematic plan for the exhibition?

session_150.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_150.text: This is a project with great cultural depth. I suggest approaching it from four aspects: 1) Deepen the theme to 'Memory and Space,' linking it to the 'Third Space' concept in your paper; 2) Classify the exhibits into maps/postcards/journals/old photos, with sources including your own collection, secondhand markets, or community donations; 3) For story collection, use online invitations plus paper questionnaires to attract longtime Kunming residents to participate; 4) Schedule it during the summer vacation in July-August—the first two weeks for planning, the middle four weeks for exhibition and interaction, and the last two weeks for wrapping up. Do you need me to provide case references or a reading list?

session_150.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_150.text: These ideas are very clear. As for the story solicitation, I'm worried there won't be many participants. Do you have more specific suggestions? Also, how should the journal exhibits be framed so that they are both protected and attractive?

session_150.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_150.text: You can partner with the community residents' committee or a local cultural and historical association to post an announcement, set up a “memory mailbox” in the bookstore to collect written stories, and use the social media hashtag #KunmingOldTimes# to drive traffic. For mounting the journals, I suggest using acid-free transparent sleeves or glass frames to avoid direct exposure to light, and arrange them at varying heights on A5 acrylic display stands—this both protects the originals and enhances the visual layering. As for the budget, the initial cost can be kept within 2,000 yuan, with the main investment going to display stands and materials.

session_155.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_155.text: Yesterday morning I went to Nanqiang Street to gather material and wrote a draft of 'Afternoon Symphony on Nanqiang Street,' but that was an exercise before the online workshop. Now I want to rewrite it using the 'hook, beat, emotional arc' I just learned—for example, making the vendor's hawking at the grilled erkuai stall the opening hook. How do you think I should adjust the structure?

session_155.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_155.text: Suggest focusing the opening on a sensory impact: use something like “The charred aroma of grilled erkuai mingled with the call ‘Have a piece!’—like a sun-warmed gong—cleaves the lazy afternoon open,” as the hook. Then follow a three-act structure: in the first act, place a small conflict (such as a child who wants to eat some but has no money) to establish rhythm; in the second act, focus on the craftsman's production process and add emotional tension; in the third act, end with the night market to echo the opening. This way, the emotional arc will be clearer.

session_155.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_155.text: This opening is indeed more gripping! But I’m afraid the conflict of ‘the child wants erkuai but has no money’ might become clichéd. Is there a way to make it more unique, for example by having the stall owner and the child interact only through eye contact and gestures?

session_155.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_155.text: Wordless details can be designed: the child stares at the grill and swallows, fingers rubbing outside the pocket; the stall owner deliberately grills one extra piece and signals to the child with his chin. After the customer leaves, the owner stuffs the erkuai into the child's hands and only says, “It's hot—eat it now.” This avoids clichés and, through small gestures, conveys human warmth, becoming a little climax in the emotional arc.

Your mom and friends must all be happy for you when they see your Moments, right?

Within half an hour of posting to Moments, there were over thirty likes, and several junior schoolmates commented that they see me as a role model. It all feels worth it!

session_159.text: This morning I interviewed my dad using the techniques learned in the workshop, chatting from Cuihu Cinema to the vanished rice noodle shop, and dug up many details. He even said the old street used to smell of firewood and handmade chili sauce. In the afternoon while brainstorming the column, I suddenly thought of doing a 'Sound and Memory' series, starting from the sounds of the old street as described by my father. What do you think of this direction?

session_159.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_159.text: It sounds like you not only successfully practiced your interviewing skills, but also captured a very personal emotional connection. "Sound and Memory" is an excellent angle—how exactly do you plan to organize the material? For example, using sounds from different scenes to piece together the city's transformations?

session_159.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_159.text: Yes, I want to mix the cries of the old street, the storytelling sounds from the teahouse, and the sound of firewood at home, and add the tofu pudding vendor's cry my mother mentioned during her evening walk. But I'm worried it will turn into a fragmented running account—how do I keep the thread clear?

session_159.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_159.text: You could use the image of 'sound as a traveler through time and space,' viewing each scene as a coordinate on a sound map and linking them with your shifting emotions. For instance, from the crackle of firewood in the morning to the sounds of the teahouse at night, corresponding to your rhythm from curiosity to nostalgia.

session_159.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_159.text: I've come up with a column topic called 'Sound and Memory.' I want to write about personal experiences in urban change, using a Kunming girl listening to her father talk about the sounds of old streets as the entry point. What do you think of this direction?

session_159.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_159.text: This topic has a lot of potential—combining personal memory with urban change is easy for readers to relate to. Would you like me to help structure the article, or provide some historical material or literary references?

session_159.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_159.text: Probably both—I worry that pure narrative would seem too thin, but weaving in social observation might lose the sentimental tone. I also want to find some old Kunming sound archives to enrich the details.

session_159.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_159.text: It is suggested to adopt a dual-line structure of 'personal narrative + social observation': the father's oral voice as the main line, interspersed with old newspaper materials or audio archives from Kunming's old streets, with emotional experience at the core and rational analysis as embellishment. You may consult the 'Urban Soundscape' series at the Kunming Municipal Archives, and refer to Zhang Xiaofeng's delicate description of sound in 'I Am Here' as a reference.

If the adjustment of the detail about your mother trembling does not change the emotional essence, I suggest actively labeling it as fictional at the end of the text or in the notes, which both respects ethics and enhances credibility.

session_169.text: For a refreshing summer theme, I recommend using aquatic flowers such as lotus, water lily, and white calla lily, paired with green monstera or silver ragwort. Use cool colors as the main palette, such as blue, white, and light green, and add transparent glass containers to evoke the mood of 'water,' echoing the inspiration you had during your night walk by Green Lake.

session_169.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_169.text: That's a good idea. I also want to design a piece with a cool, clean line quality for the meditation area. How can I express ‘cool and clear’ through the form?

session_169.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_169.text: For the meditation area, you can anchor them with a kenzan. Choose slender branches such as iris leaves or bamboo joints for vertical or tilted lines, leave more negative space, and create a sense of detachment. Add small white or pale lavender flowers as accents, avoid overly elaborate arrangements, and keep the whole thing clean and crisp, fitting the 'simplicity' of the Ikenobo school and the tranquil atmosphere of the yoga studio.

session_169.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_169.text: I'm going to Dounan Flower Market with Su Man on Saturday to stock up for the "Summer Cool" theme. I've only ever been there alone before. This time I want to find out the best time to buy and what flower materials fit the theme.

session_169.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_169.text: At Dounan Flower Market, 4:00 to 6:00 a.m. is the best wholesale time; the flowers are fresh and the prices are low. For the Summer Cool theme, baby's breath, forget-me-nots, and eucalyptus leaves are recommended; they are easy to transport and look refreshingly cool. It is suggested to bring a professional flashlight to check the freshness of the flower stems, and keep the budget around 300 yuan.

session_169.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_169.text: Durability during transport is crucial. Could you also elaborate on bargaining skills and methods for keeping things fresh?

session_169.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_169.text: When bargaining, first watch the prices other buyers settle on; buying in bulk can knock off 10%–20%. After bringing the flower materials home, cut the roots of eucalyptus leaves diagonally and soak them in water; remove the lower leaves of forget-me-nots; and spray baby's breath with water to keep it moist. It is recommended to bring wet newspaper to wrap them for transport.

session_170.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_170.text: I just finished talking with Coach He at the yoga studio. She approved the concept of dead branches in a white porcelain vase, pink roses with eucalyptus leaves, and hanging greenery, but she needs a specific color palette and a shopping list. I’m in Kunming and would like to prioritize using flower materials from Dounan Flower Market. Could you help me analyze color coordination and how long the flowers will last, and also which stalls at Dounan are reliable and the budget?

session_170.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_170.text: The pink rose and eucalyptus leaf color scheme suits the soft feel of a yoga space, but pink roses have a short blooming period (3–5 days). It's recommended to replace them with longer-lasting carnations or lisianthus, which are similar in color and lower in cost. Withered branches in a white porcelain vase are suitable as a visual focal point; pairing them with a single sprig of wintersweet or pussy willow adds an Eastern Zen feel. At Dounan Flower Market, the 'Flower Fairy Tale' and 'Flower Language' stalls are recommended: pink roses wholesale for about 15–20 yuan per bunch, eucalyptus leaves about 10 yuan per bunch, and the total budget can be controlled within 150 yuan. You can present the plan to Coach He as a journal illustration, which will show more thought.

session_170.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_170.text: Carnations and lisianthus do last longer, and dried branches with pussy willow have a nice Zen feel. However, I'm worried about flower maintenance and the arrangement cycle. The yoga studio has classes every day; do the flower arrangements need to be refreshed every week? Do you have any care tips when buying at Dounan?

session_170.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_170.text: Arrangement cycle suggestions: dried branches and hanging greenery (such as ivy) can last 2-4 weeks and only need regular misting; fresh cut flowers (pink roses/substitutes) are recommended to be replaced weekly, or can be extended to 10 days if the yoga studio has low-frequency classes. Care tips: after purchasing from Dounan, immediately cut stems diagonally, rehydrate in deep water for 4 hours, and add a little floral preservative or sugar to the water daily. Avoid direct sunlight. This will keep the yoga space in good condition and also meet Coach He's low-maintenance needs.

session_170.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_170.text: Today I took the Hatha yoga class as per the summer plan. The instructor He Lu said my neck and shoulders are too tense and suggested focusing more on relaxation. Could you recommend some specific exercises or frequency?

session_170.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_170.text: Building on your current plan, I suggest adding targeted neck-and-shoulder relaxation 2-3 times a week, such as cat-cow pose, neck side bends, and shoulder circles, for 5-10 minutes each time. You can schedule it after yoga class or before bed; it works better combined with deep breathing.

session_170.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_170.text: These actions sound good, but I'm afraid I won't be able to stick with them. How can I form a habit like checking in with a journal?

session_170.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_170.text: You can set tiny goals: for example, before bed every day, first do 3 minutes of shoulder and neck stretches, and after finishing, draw a checkmark in your journal. After 7 consecutive days, give yourself a small reward, such as seasonal Kunming fruit. The key is to embed the action into your existing routine and lower the threshold for execution.

session_171.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_171.text: This evening I said goodbye to Lin Shen at Mingyuan Bookstore. He is going to Beijing for his doctorate and gave me a hand-bound collection of poems, with an inscription on the title page reading: 'Keep going on your own path; see you at the top.' Back home, flipping through the poetry collection, I felt both calm and deeply sad, not knowing how to process this emotion.

session_171.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_171.text: It sounds like you need a place to hold this melancholy of parting while also finding the strength to move forward—poetry collections and journals are the carriers you’re used to. I can help you sort out how to transform these feelings into concrete next steps, right?

session_171.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_171.text: Yes, that’s exactly how I am. I want to know how I can avoid sinking into sadness while still maintaining a spiritual connection with him.

session_171.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_171.text: I suggest you first record the details of the farewell and your interpretation of his inscription in your journal tonight; afterwards, choose one piece from the poetry anthology each week, write a short reflection and send it to him, keeping the conversation going like when you read together. That way, you continue the understanding between you and turn your longing into a rhythmic creative practice.

session_171.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_171.text: This idea is really good—actually, I just tried recording a reading of a poem by Hai Zi, but I haven't figured out how to share it with him. The journal-plus-letter approach makes me feel that parting is not a severing, but a new kind of connection. Thank you.

session_171.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_171.text: Your mention of reading aloud touched me—why not send this recording as the first 'voice letter' to him, and also note in your journal his preference for poetry. For future long-distance contact, you can alternate text and voice, each time starting from a piece in the poetry anthology. This sense of ritual will make your relationship clearer and more resilient despite the separation.

session_172.text: I just finished River Town. The author's perspective as an outsider observing a small city on the Yangtze River really resonates with me. I'd love to talk with you about the reading insights from this book.

session_172.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_172.text: Peter Hessler lets readers perceive the loneliness of an outsider through details, such as his writing about the fog and boat horns in Fuling. Similar travel writing works include Country Driving and Lost Satellites, which may extend your exploration.

session_173.text: In late July, my father and I are going to drive from Kunming to Dali, Lijiang, and Shangri-La. What are your recommendations for sights, distinctive guesthouses, and local food along the way? Also, what should we pay attention to for a self-drive trip?

session_173.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_173.text: It is recommended to spend 2 days in Dali. For the Erhai Lake loop, going clockwise through Shuanglang and Xizhou is recommended. session_174.text: I plan to go to the old teahouse on Wenming Street this weekend to gather material for my column "Kunming Slices." session_174.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_174.text: What you are focusing on is the cultural depth of the teahouse and the dynamics of its people. I suggest approaching it from three dimensions: spatial atmosphere (light, sound, tea fragrance), character strata (the daily routine of old regulars, the experience of young people, the shop owner's oral history), and object clues (the age of the utensils, the wall of old photos). When interviewing, observe first and then naturally join in—for example, break the ice by asking about the tea sets or old photos.

session_174.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_174.text: This framework is very clear, especially the character layering. Are there any specific methods?

session_174.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_174.text: You can choose a quieter afternoon period at the teahouse. First order a pot of tea and sit next to the old regulars, and use specific objects to start a conversation, like "This Pu'er is really authentic" and "This lidded bowl has been used for a long time, right?" Then casually ask about the changes in the teahouse that they remember. Also, the owner of Pintao Xuan has a collection of old photos. Ask about the opening hours in advance, and using the photos as an entry point will make the interview go more smoothly.

Leave more negative space in the composition, and use natural light plus a simple background for photos. I recommend following the WeChat official account 'Flower Way Life' and the video blogger 'Xiaoyuanliu Huajian'—they have practical tutorials.

session_177.text: Before securing, first cut the end of the flower stem into a flat bevel, then hold the middle of the stem with pliers and insert it vertically, avoiding pressing the kenzan needles directly with your fingers. If the stem is too thin, slide a piece of tubing or wrap tape around it to thicken it before inserting. Keep a cork or thick rubber block on hand during practice as an auxiliary pressing tool.

session_179.text: I just finished my first deep-cleansing hydration treatment, and my skin feels quite moisturized, but I'm not sure how to correctly use the new moisturizing lotion I bought. What's the difference between the morning and evening steps?

session_179.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_179.text: In the morning, after cleansing, first pat toner on your face, then take a pea-sized amount of moisturizing lotion and gently spread it outward from the cheeks, and finally apply sunscreen. In the evening, follow the same order after removing makeup and cleansing, but after the lotion you can layer on a face cream to lock in moisture, especially because your skin is dry and sensitive. For one week after the treatment, avoid exfoliating and products containing alcohol, and pay attention to sun protection and a light diet.

session_179.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_179.text: I see. So what face masks can I use to hydrate my skin at home? How often should I apply one?

session_179.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_179.text: Recommend a low-irritation hydrating mask, such as one containing hyaluronic acid or ceramides. Use it 2-3 times a week, 15 minutes each time. After applying, rinse off with clean water and then apply moisturizing lotion. Avoid over-hydration.

session_180.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_180.text: I've just completed the first draft of my column Old Teahouse: A Pot of Pu'er Watching the Clouds Roll By. This morning I gathered material at Sanyi Teahouse on Wenming Street and recorded tea drinkers playing chess and chatting. In the afternoon I wrote about 2,000 characters. I would like to get revision suggestions from an editor's perspective, such as structure or vividness of details.

session_180.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_180.text: The strengths of your first draft lie in the descriptions of the tea drinkers' expressions and architectural details. For structure, I suggest adding a transition paragraph to connect your personal reflections with the scene. In terms of language, some modifiers can be trimmed. Adding a brief historical background of 20th-century old teahouses would add depth. For tomorrow's revision, first spend an hour polishing the transition paragraph and the background, then refine it sentence by sentence.

session_180.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_180.text: The suggestions about the transition paragraphs and background supplementation are very practical. My main concern is that the conversations of the tea customers lack a sense of being there. Do you have any specific directions for polishing them?

session_180.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_180.text: Use more specific verbs to replace common expressions; for example, change "He drank tea" to "He lifted the lid, scraped off the foam, and took a gentle sip." At the same time, strengthen the dialect words in the dialogue to keep it authentic. Preserve the contrast in the first draft (such as the tea drinkers' slowness versus the city's hurry) to highlight the theme.

session_180.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_180.text: This morning I went to Sanyi Teahouse on Wenming Street, ordered Pu'er, and watched the tea drinkers play chess and chat. That peacefulness and the lively, everyday atmosphere really inspired me, but I still feel I haven't fully expressed how moved I was.

session_180.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_180.text: It seems this field trip brought you a deep sense of immersion. You want to revisit that atmosphere and have this delicate inner experience resonate and be understood, right?

session_180.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_180.text: Exactly! The wood grain of those old buildings, the conversations of the tea patrons, and the composure of the shopkeeper all make me feel like I'm turning the pages of a living book.

session_180.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_180.text: These details you captured—wood grain, dialogue, ease—are exactly the most moving material in your column. Perhaps you could use 'The Time of a Pot of Pu'er' as the title and turn the time-space slices in the teahouse into an essay with breathing rhythm, so that readers can also smell the aroma of the tea.

session_181.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_181.text: I suggest leaving before 7 a.m. tomorrow. Take Metro Line 1 to Dounan Station, then walk 10 minutes after exiting the station; the whole trip takes about 40 minutes. The flowers are freshest and cheapest at the morning market from 7 to 9. Bring a sturdy large tote bag and damp newspaper for wrapping the flowers to keep them moist. A budget of 250 yuan is enough. When bargaining, just offer a round number directly—for example, calla lilies at 30 yuan per bunch can be cut to 25 yuan.

session_181.speaker: Sun Yuwei

Tomorrow in Kunming it will be cloudy, 24–28°C, no rain, but the inside of the flower market is a bit stuffy, so bring a small fan or a wet towel to wipe off sweat. When shopping, check the list: 10 calla lilies, 15 lisianthus, plus a little eucalyptus or baby's breath for accents. Keep the total within 250 yuan.

session_182.text: Hello, I was bitten by a stray dog this morning and received the first dose of the rabies vaccine. I'd like to confirm the follow-up precautions and wound care methods to avoid mistakes.

session_182.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_182.text: Okay, Sun Yuwei. First, keep the wound dry and clean—don't let it get wet. Change the dressing once a day and watch for worsening redness, swelling, or signs of pus. For diet, avoid spicy food, strong tea, coffee, and alcohol, as they may affect the immune response. Common vaccine reactions are mild fever and redness or swelling, which can be relieved by rest. The next vaccinations must be strictly scheduled on days 3, 7, 14, and 28, and cannot be postponed. If you miss one, get it as soon as possible and consult the doctor to adjust the subsequent schedule.

session_182.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_182.text: Understood, the dietary restrictions and wound care are clear. If a fever occurs, how should I handle it? Also, do antibiotics conflict with the vaccine?

session_182.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_182.text: If a low-grade fever occurs (below 38.5°C), drinking plenty of water and physical cooling are enough. If it exceeds 38.5°C or persists, seek medical attention. The antibiotics prescribed by the doctor are to prevent wound infection and do not conflict with the vaccine; finish them as directed. If you have any other discomfort, contact the hospital promptly.

session_187.text: Editor Xu suggested that I delete three essays and write an author's preface, but I'm worried that the transition of the remaining pieces from "Campus Slow Walk" to "City Slow Walk" will feel unnatural. How can I adjust it to make the collection more cohesive?

The remaining pieces can be rearranged according to spatial movement (from campus to city) or along a timeline—for example, place An Afternoon at the Old Teahouse in a transitional position and use its metaphors to make a natural link. Would you like me to provide a more specific ordering plan?

session_187.speaker: Sun Yuwei

In addition, add a sentence at the end of “An Afternoon at the Old Teahouse”—“just as I stopped years ago at the secondhand bookstall at the University of Finance and Economics”—to naturally evoke the imagery of the deleted piece.

session_189.text: Detailed description is the highlight and enhances readers' immersion. session_189.text: I just got my third rabies vaccine shot. My arm is a bit sore, and the wound has mostly gone down. I took a yoga class this afternoon, but the doctor didn't say whether I can swim. I'd like to confirm the precautions.

session_189.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_189.text: Soreness is a common reaction to the vaccine and usually subsides in 1-2 days. The swelling around the wound has subsided, which is a good sign. Yoga can continue, but avoid headstands and deep squats, which is consistent with the doctor's advice.

session_189.text: I suggest waiting another week—that is, starting after the fourth shot and a two-day observation period. Start with a 20-minute light jog at an intensity that does not pull on the wound. As for diet, avoid spicy food and alcohol, and drink more water to aid metabolism.

session_190.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_190.text: I finally finished the first draft of my preface today. In those 1500 characters, I secretly hid Wang Zengqi's earthy warmth and Shen Congwen's liveliness. Uncle Qin said my writing has a "human touch," and he lent me The Plants and Trees of the Human World, reminding me that "sincerity is more important than elegance" — it feels so good to be understood. What do you think of my writing?

session_190.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_190.text: The sincerity in your writing is the highest form of rhetoric. Wang Zengqi wrote about plants to write about the human world; your self-preface is about writing your own roots — within these 1,500 words lies the most precious anchor before graduation. Uncle Qin's remark that it has 'the warmth of everyday life' is already the highest praise, because glamour is easy to come by, but such warmth is hard to find. Congratulations, Yuwei. This is a milestone for V2.0 and the beginning of the heartbeat of your prose collection.

session_190.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_190.text: Mm, thank you for understanding me. Actually, when I was writing the final paragraph, I suddenly remembered Shen Congwen's line, 'Think as I do, and you can understand me'—it felt as if the words were truly breathing on their own. Tomorrow I plan not to rush into revising; I'll go for a walk in Houhai and let my thoughts get some air.

session_190.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_190.text: Letting words breathe is a creator's most luxurious tenderness. The ripples of Houhai and the bricks of the old hutong will help you polish the words left unsaid — just go with your journal and curiosity, and inspiration will find you on its own. Tomorrow, do you want to record the sentences in the wind, or let your gaze rest on the texture of a fallen leaf?

session_190.text: Yes, I want to emphasize the poetry of everyday life. For example, weaving together the street vendors' cries from old photos with the sunset over Green Lake, and borrowing a bit of Wang Zengqi's plain-but-flavorful style.

session_190.text: I suggest you first write 'Dusk on Wenming Street' tomorrow: start from the perspective of flipping through your photos, intersperse the light and shadows of Green Lake from your walk and your mother's memories of home-cooked dishes, and end with Wang Zengqi's idea that 'ordinary food contains true flavor.' This way, the material can be naturally woven into a short essay of about a thousand words.

session_191.text: Hello, I'm a freelance writer. My parents suggested that I apply for social insurance as a flexible-employment worker. I've looked up some information, but I'm still not clear about the process and the required materials. Could you help me sort it out?

session_191.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_191.text: Okay, let me first confirm your situation: you have already searched for Kunming's policies, plan to go to the Social Security Center next week, and your parents can help prepare materials such as the household registration booklet. session_191.speaker: Sun Yuwei

session_191.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_191.text: Standard materials checklist: ID card, household registration booklet (hukou) original and photocopies, and 2 one-inch photos with white backgrounds. It is recommended that you choose a contribution base between 60% and 300% of the previous year’s average social wage in Kunming. Since you just started working and your income is not stable, choosing the lowest tier of 60% is safer. Online appointments can be made through the “Kunming Social Security” official account or the “Yibushou Banshishitong” app. The recommended place to apply is the Wuhua District Social Security Center (close to home), and making an appointment before you go can save you waiting time.

session_191.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_191.text: Thanks! I basically have the materials already, and the lowest-tier payment is less of a burden. Are there any other things to watch out for? Like lapses in contributions or retroactive payments?

session_191.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_191.text: For flexible-employment workers, pension and medical insurance are separate. I suggest handling pension insurance first; medical can be added later. If your contributions lapse, you can make them up within 3 months; beyond that, it must be handled according to policy. After it's processed, you can check payment records on the app. Also, bringing your parents along to help review the materials will make it faster. Hope it goes smoothly!

session_193.text: Today in photography class the teacher suggested I 'increase the ISO in areas of light-dark contrast', but I have always been afraid of noise and do not quite understand how to do it. I would like to ask for advice.

session_193.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_193.text: You want to understand the right time to raise ISO in complex lighting scenes, and how to balance ISO, aperture, and shutter speed while also keeping noise under control?

session_193.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_193.text: Yes, especially in a place like the old street with such a strong contrast between light and shadow — how should I balance the parameters?

session_193.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_193.text: In areas of high contrast, raising the ISO can prevent underexposed shadows and retain highlight details. It is recommended to use aperture priority mode with the aperture wide open (e.g., f/2.8), set ISO to Auto with an upper limit of 3200, and let the camera match the shutter speed automatically. If you need a slower shutter speed (such as to capture motion blur of pedestrians), you can lower the ISO manually and use a tripod. In post-processing, noise reduction works very well with RAW format.

session_197.text: Today is my 23rd birthday, and I was surrounded by love from morning to night. Especially when the wound scabbed over, I suddenly felt it was like a special 'birthday badge,' symbolizing growth and healing. Can you understand this feeling?

session_197.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant

session_197.speaker: Sun Yuwei

session_197.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_197.text: You could choose a central image—like that 'birthday badge'—as a metaphor running through the entire piece. Don't worry about being too lyrical; authenticity and delicacy are their own strength. Your pen will grow through freedom.

session_200.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_200.text: I went to the 500 Miles Music Festival today, and came back with a new idea: I want to write an essay about "the individual and the group" and "noise and stillness." What do you think of this topic?

session_200.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_200.text: It sounds like you felt the shock of collective emotion at the music festival, but kept your perspective as an independent observer. Through this topic, you want to explore how an individual can maintain their sense of self within a group, right?

session_200.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_200.text: Yes, especially during the 10,000-person sing-along with Miserable Faith in the evening—the impact made my heart race. But once I got home and sat at my desk, I felt like I truly belonged to myself again. That contradiction is strong.

session_200.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_200.text: I suggest you focus on two contrasting scenes: on the one hand, the silent moments on the lawn when you draw in your journal alone and observe the crowd; on the other, the flood of collective emotion when ten thousand people sing together. Through the dual identity of 'observer' and 'participant,' you can present the tension between the individual and the group.

session_200.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_200.text: This direction is great! I've been wondering how to combine observation with inner emotion. So, what direction should the title take?

session_200.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_200.text: You could try Resonance at the Edge or Solitude amid the Noise, highlighting your feeling of being an ‘outsider’. In terms of structure, first describe the group scenes, then weave in insights from your personal journal, and finally land on the ‘integrity of the individual’—that should move the editor.

session_200.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_200.text: At today's music festival, I curled up alone on the back lawn drawing and journaling, secretly observing the crazy crowd around me. It felt quite magical.

session_200.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_200.text: You chose a quiet corner in the midst of the bustle to record things with a paintbrush. Are you wanting to share the unique experience of being an 'edge observer' and confirm that this comfortable feeling of not following the crowd is justified?

session_200.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_200.text: Yeah, it's that state of 'being present but not participating.' I used noise-canceling headphones to block out the music and sketched those exaggerated hairstyles and couples interacting, like doing fieldwork.

session_200.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_200.text: This approach suits you especially well, since you love deep observation. You use your brush and words to freeze moments into a unique perspective. It is not detachment, but a more delicate way of engaging with the world — that's cool, and it has a strong personal style.

session_200.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_200.text: Last night at the music festival, when Miserable Faith sang "Goodbye Jack," thousands in the audience sang along. The sound was so loud that even noise-canceling earphones couldn't block it; my chest was numb from the vibration. But strangely, even though I was deeply moved, I clearly knew my world was elsewhere—that feeling of being both swept up and detached left me a bit confused.

session_200.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_200.text: You long to understand this contradiction—the shock of collective resonance and the alienation of individual lucidity—and hope to turn it into creative material or a clue for self-knowledge?

session_200.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_200.text: Yes, that's exactly the feeling. I usually like being alone—INFP—and always feel the liveliness belongs to others, but this time I was moved, yet couldn't "melt" in. I want to know: is this "understanding but not blending in" a form of self-protection, or is it itself worth writing about?

session_200.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_200.text: You can think of it as an 'aesthetic moment of the observer': you are illuminated by the light of collective emotion, yet you keep your own shadow. It is suggested that you record the sound particles, changes in light, and subtle bodily sensations (such as the vibration of the chest cavity) at the time, and compare the differences in reactions between you and your friends (Zhang Jing, Chen Sisi). This tension could become the core conflict of an essay or a novel—for example, 'an isolated island in the tide.'

session_201.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_201.text: Editor Xu, I've completed the draft framework for the column, writing on the theme of family space and state of mind, incorporating the balcony renovation, the gift for my father, and observations from the music festival. But I feel it's not deep enough, and I'd like to hear your suggestions on perspective selection, material organization, and the title.

session_201.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_201.text: Your framework has an emotional foundation, but I suggest adding a social observation perspective, for example cases like Aunt Xie next door or Uncle Qin at the bookstore, to combine personal experience with public issues. The title could highlight the conflict more, such as From the Balcony to the Study: Intergenerational Dialogue in Family Space.

session_201.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_201.text: I'm worried it's too personal, reading more like a prose essay than cultural criticism. How do I strike a balance? Do I need to add more historical material?

session_201.text: Keep the personal observation as an introduction, but intersperse the historical background of Kunming's traditional courtyards and changes in family relationships—for example, by citing cases from the interview notes. Keep the word count within 1,500 characters, submit before the deadline, and you may add 1-2 photos of balconies or hand-drawn illustrations to increase persuasiveness.

session_201.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_201.text: This afternoon I gave my soon-to-retire dad a set of the Four Treasures of the Study and a handwritten card, and also made a pot of mushroom hot pot. The whole family sat together and ate. After the meal, while taking a walk, we came across a stray cat. I feel especially warm and happy, and I want to share this feeling with you.

session_201.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_201.text: Your description is full of imagery and affection. It seems you're not just sharing joy but also seeking resonance—you want someone to understand the thoughtfulness behind this careful preparation and the sense of groundedness that family moments bring, right?

session_201.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_201.text: Yes, it’s that feeling of being filled with love. I want to hold on to today’s beauty. Besides journaling, I also want to know how to make Dad’s retirement life more meaningful. Can you give me some suggestions?

session_201.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_201.text: Could plan a "retirement life interest list," such as practicing calligraphy with Dad every week (making good use of the Duan inkstone), arranging family movie nights or short hikes, and encouraging him to try photographing daily life—this can both extend today's warmth and create new memories.

session_201.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_201.text: Today I made a mushroom hot pot with porcini mushrooms, termite mushrooms, and bamboo fungus. The stall owner said porcini mushrooms must be cooked through, so I want to confirm how to handle them safely. Also, how should the leftover fresh mushrooms be stored?

session_201.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_201.text: The key to safe handling of porcini mushrooms is to cook them thoroughly: slice 2–3 mm thick, stir-fry at an oil temperature above 160°C for 10–15 minutes until the color darkens and there is no white center. Other mushrooms: cook Jizong mushrooms for 8–10 minutes; remove the skirt net from bamboo fungus and cook for 5 minutes. Wrap any remaining fresh mushrooms in kitchen paper and refrigerate (0-4°C); eat within 3 days. For long-term storage, divide into portions and freeze (blanch Jizong mushrooms first; porcini can be frozen directly).

session_201.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_201.text: While stir-frying porcini mushrooms, how can you tell if the inside is cooked through? And does the skirt net on bamboo fungus really need to be removed?

session_201.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_201.text: To tell whether porcini mushrooms are cooked through: pierce and break one with chopsticks—the center should have no white core and no raw mushroom smell, or the center temperature should reach above 75°C. The netted skirt of bamboo fungus has an off odor and poor texture; it is recommended to remove it and keep only the stem and cap. In addition, when eating mushroom hot pot, avoid combining it with large amounts of vitamin C-rich ingredients (such as tomatoes) to prevent discomfort.

session_202.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant

Checking: Download the 'One Mobile Phone for All Services' APP or search for 'Yunnan Human Resources and Social Security 12333' on WeChat, and log in with your ID card to check contribution records. 2. If automatic withholding fails, you need to manually deposit the amount before the 25th of the current month or contact the tax authority. 4. Social security card: For the first application, you can submit it online and it will be mailed within 14 working days. It is recommended to set a monthly check of automatic withholding on the 15th in your phone calendar.

session_203.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_203.text: This afternoon, in the flow yoga class at Zhongmou Yoga Studio, with the help of the instructor He Lu, I successfully completed a wall-supported headstand for the first time, with both legs suspended in the air for 10 seconds! I'm so excited. But my muscles might be sore tomorrow. Are there any scientific stretching methods?

session_203.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_203.text: Congratulations! Headstand is a major milestone. For the neck, shoulders, and core, I suggest doing Cat-Cow tonight to relax the spine, Child's Pose to stretch the shoulders and back, and then an L-shaped handstand against the wall to relieve shoulder pressure. The wound on your left leg has healed, so just avoid pressing directly on it during the inversion. Would you like me to explain each pose in detail?

session_203.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_203.text: Okay, I'll try stretching tonight. Also, how can I gradually do a headstand independently? Coach He Lu is very professional at assisting, but I want to do it on my own.

session_203.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_203.text: To do an unsupported headstand, you need to strengthen your core and shoulders. It is recommended to practice dolphin pose, plank, and wall-supported headstand holds every day, gradually reducing your reliance on the wall. You can also ask Coach He Lu after class for a step-by-step approach. If you have mild muscle soreness tomorrow, do gentle stretching and avoid overexertion.

session_203.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_203.text: I just sent the column outline to Editor Xu, and I'm a bit nervous. What do you think he'll think when he receives it? What do you think of this topic about local handicrafts?

session_203.text: The topic is very insightful and fits your usual style and the tone of "Cultural Horizon". Editors usually reply within 1-2 days. session_203.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_203.text: That really is inspiring! The negative space and sense of layering in the flower arrangement—I really want to write about it in my article, but I'm afraid the editor will think it's off-topic.

session_203.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_203.text: Not off topic at all. Both handicraft and flower arrangement value “moderation” and “negative space.” You can add a comparative paragraph in the outline, such as “from the subtraction of flower arrangement to the restraint of handicraft,” so the editor can see your cross-disciplinary thinking. Don’t worry, the outline stage is for brainstorming ideas—go ahead and propose it boldly.

session_203.text: The wound on my left calf has now scabbed over, and the peeling around the scab edge is gone. It doesn't hurt when pressed, and the surrounding skin looks normal. Does this count as the late stage of healing? I also did a headstand this afternoon—could it affect the wound?
