session_203.text: Based on your description, the wound has entered the late stage of healing, and a headstand poses no risk to the tough scabbed wound. The disappearance of flaking and the recovery of skin color are signs of improvement. Just continue with your current care.

session_203.text: Then I plan to go shopping for shorts tomorrow, and it might involve a lot of walking. What should I pay attention to? Is there a step limit?

session_203.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_203.text: Normal walking is fine; there is no need to deliberately limit the number of steps, but avoid standing for long periods or rubbing the wound. It is recommended to wear loose trousers and rest appropriately if you feel uncomfortable. Continue applying the ointment for protection, and you can stop after the scab falls off naturally.

session_203.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_203.text: Got it, so do I still need to keep the wound wrapped in gauze? About how long until I can completely stop the medication?

session_203.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_203.text: The wound has scabbed over with no oozing, so it can be left uncovered to allow it to breathe; if you go out and worry about friction, you can apply a band-aid. It is recommended to apply the ointment for another 3–5 days. Once the scab falls off naturally, no more medication is needed.

session_208.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_208.text: Tonight, while copying a summer lotus pond painting, the layers kept getting messy and the color transitions were stiff. Halfway through, I felt really frustrated. Am I simply not suited to become an illustrator?

session_208.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_208.text: It sounds like you've hit a common technical bottleneck in digital painting, and that frustration is normal. But I saw that you wrote in your journal, "A bottleneck is a signpost for a turn," and you tried a watercolor sticker style and found a comfortable feel — that adjustment was actually very wise, proving you're looking for a way of expression that suits you better. Want to talk about how to turn this sense of relief into a steady pace of progress?

session_208.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_208.text: Yes, temporarily setting aside my illustrator goal and switching to drawing simple plant stickers did make things much lighter, but deep down I still wonder if I'm running away. Do you think this direction is right?

session_208.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_208.text: This isn’t avoidance—it’s a smart roundabout way forward. I suggest you treat the new style as an exploration period: spend just 30 minutes a day drawing one sticker, deliberately practice color matching and layer simplification, and after accumulating 10-15 pieces, compare and evaluate them. You can also draw on your experience overcoming bottlenecks in writing, such as “finish first, perfect later.” That creative desire inside you is still there; the direction is just a change of path, and it’s worth continuing on.

session_208.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_208.text: Tonight I did my first night walk at Cuihu: 2.5 kilometers at a pace of 8 minutes 10 seconds per kilometer. I also took night photos and felt a great sense of achievement!

session_208.text: Awesome! Your first brisk walk had such a good rhythm, and the new gear and the night view of Green Lake are both worth recording. Have there been any noticeable changes in your body or mood after the walk?

session_208.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_208.text: The quick-dry clothes are really comfortable. After the walk, my whole body feels light, and I feel very fulfilled. I really want to keep it up now. Do you have any advice on maintaining a habit?

session_208.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_208.text: You can turn it into a fixed ritual 2-3 times a week, for example after dinner on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays. Checking in is itself a good motivator; with proper warm-up and stretching, it can help you persist long-term and maintain your rhythm amid a busy academic life.

session_208.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_208.text: I just bought a comprehensive accidental injury insurance policy with an annual premium of 496 yuan, but I'm not sure how the deductible is calculated. Also, since I usually do brisk walking and yoga, can I get compensation if I'm accidentally injured?

session_208.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_208.text: The deductible for accident insurance is usually an absolute deductible per accident, such as 100 yuan, with the excess reimbursed proportionally. Brisk walking and yoga are everyday non-high-risk activities and are generally covered, but pay attention to exclusions (such as high-risk sports not being covered). I suggest checking the "Accidental Medical" section of the policy terms. Does your insurance include accidental medical coverage?

session_208.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_208.text: The policy says “comprehensive accident insurance” — it should include accidental medical coverage, right? I would also like to know about the claims process, and whether I need to buy an additional medical insurance.

session_208.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_208.text: Comprehensive accident insurance usually includes accidental medical coverage. Claims process: promptly report the incident after it occurs, collect medical records, invoices, and other documents and submit them. As a student/freelancer, it is recommended to add a million-yuan medical insurance (annual premium of a few hundred yuan) to cover inpatient medical expenses, complementing the accident insurance. Student medical insurance can reimburse part of the costs, but the coverage is limited. With an annual income of 80,000 yuan, first get accident + medical insurance, and consider critical illness insurance in the future.

session_210.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_210.text: Today I finally did a headstand on my own! I held it away from the wall for 15 seconds. My legs were slightly shaking, but I could really feel my core engaging, and the instructor even led everyone in applause. It was so rewarding! Next, I want to safely extend the hold to 20 seconds or more, but I'm afraid of injuring my neck or shoulders. Do you have any specific training suggestions?

session_210.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_210.text: Congratulations! This breakthrough is wonderful! The slight trembling in your legs shows there is still room to improve shoulder and back strength and core stability. I suggest adding Dolphin Pose (3 sets of 30 seconds each) and dynamic planks 2–3 times a week to strengthen your shoulder blades and core. Next time you try, focus on distributing your weight evenly between your hands and head (with your palms supporting 60% of the weight), tuck your chin slightly to avoid neck strain, and try to hold for 5 more seconds each time. Also, inversions are very helpful for improving posture—they stretch the thoracic spine and strengthen the back, which is perfect for relieving shoulder and neck tension from sitting and writing for long periods.

session_210.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_210.text: I occasionally practice Dolphin Pose, but maybe my engagement is off—next time I’ll focus on activating my shoulder blades. By the way, I’ve been gaining weight recently (44.5 kg). How long should I wait after eating high-protein food before practicing handstands? Also, I want to move on to handstands next—what basic movements should I strengthen first?

session_210.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_210.text: During a weight-gain period, it is recommended to wait at least 1.5–2 hours after a high-protein meal before practicing inversions, to avoid stomach discomfort affecting your strength. If you feel hungry before practice, you can eat a small amount of banana or whole-wheat crackers. Basic preparation for the handstand: first strengthen the pushing force of the shoulder blades into the ground (practice Chaturanga variations and Dolphin pose with leg lifts), and the stability of one-legged handstands (practice lifting one leg up against the wall, holding for 5–10 seconds each time). In addition, continuous core engagement will help you control balance—treat every headstand as neural-pathway training of 'shoulder-girdle stability + core activation,' and you will progress faster.

session_210.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_210.text: I've just had the last shot of the rabies vaccine, and the doctor confirmed it's safe, but I still want to confirm: how long before the antibodies reach their peak? Do I still need to avoid strenuous exercise or specific foods afterward?

session_210.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_210.text: Antibodies usually reach their peak in 7-14 days, and you are safe now. Normal yoga, brisk walking, and coffee do not affect anything, so there is no need to avoid any foods. After the wound heals, you can consider using scar cream. If you are bitten again, within six months you generally only need a booster shot.

session_210.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_210.text: What if I get scratched by a cat or dog again? How should I deal with it specifically? Does the 10-day observation method still apply?

session_210.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_210.text: Immediately rinse with soap and water for 15 minutes and disinfect, then seek medical attention to assess the exposure level. For a household pet, the 10-day observation method can be started at the same time; if the animal shows no symptoms within 10 days, the remaining vaccine doses can be stopped. It is recommended to stay relaxed—you have already produced protective antibodies, so there is no need to be overly anxious.

session_210.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_210.text: I just finished the first draft of the preface to my essay collection, Confession of a Slow Walker, at Paper Cloth Stone Bookstore. It uses a balcony renovation as an entry point to discuss slow living. I'd like to hear your thoughts—is this angle strong enough?

session_210.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_210.text: You hope to balance personal experience with universal resonance, while also worrying that the philosophical reflection on “slowness” in the preface might lack literary depth. Do you need specific suggestions on structure, technique, or details?

session_210.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_210.text: Yes, especially whether to add a childhood memory anchor point to reinforce the sense of time depth, and whether more literary allusions are needed to support it.

session_210.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_210.text: Suggest keeping the life-oriented entrance of the balcony renovation—it naturally resonates. Consider inserting a snippet of slow childhood time at the end (such as the grandmother's courtyard), using details and contrasts to strengthen the theme. Literary allusions should be refined rather than abundant; one quote from Tao Yuanming or Thoreau is enough, to avoid diluting the texture of the personal narrative.

session_210.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_210.text: That makes sense. Childhood episodes do add layers. As for the structure of the preface, do you think the order needs adjusting? For instance, write first about the confusion of “slowness” and then return to the balcony?

session_210.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_210.text: Starting with the balcony scene is very direct and quickly draws the reader in. If you want to state the confusion first, you could try adding a line at the beginning of the first paragraph—'When did I begin to realize I was moving too fast?'—as an introduction, and then naturally transition into the balcony renovation. This keeps the scene anchor while giving it more reflective depth.

session_212.text: In today's yoga class, with my coach's assistance, I completed a headstand on my own for the first time and held it for 20 seconds. I feel a huge sense of accomplishment! But I signed up for the advanced class and am a bit worried that my core strength isn't enough. How should I continue training?

session_212.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_212.text: Great job! Your breakthrough at Zhongmou Yoga Studio on the afternoon of 2025-07-31 is something to be proud of. Behind that feeling of accomplishment is a longing for self-growth. For core strength, I suggest adding 2-3 sessions of plank and Boat Pose practice each week, starting with 30 seconds each time and gradually building up. Advanced poses like Scorpion Pose require a stable core, so don't rush; consolidate the basics first.

session_212.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_212.text: Yes, my main concern is not being able to keep up in the advanced class, because my fitness base is weak. Scorpion pose looks really hard. How can I get started safely?

session_212.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_212.text: Don't worry. session_222.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_222.text: I have a blister on my left heel. In the morning I cleaned it with warm water and put on a band-aid; in the evening I disinfected it with povidone-iodine and changed to a larger band-aid. Is this the right way to handle it? Should I pop it?

session_222.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_222.text: Your treatment steps are generally correct, but it's not recommended to deliberately pop the blister, to avoid increasing the risk of infection. Keep the wound clean and dry, and just continue disinfecting and protecting it with an adhesive bandage.

session_222.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_222.text: Got it, so how should I take care of it afterward? How can I tell if it's infected?

session_222.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_222.text: Before changing the dressing every day, observe: redness, swelling, heat, pain, and pus are signs of infection. It is recommended to switch to a hydrocolloid dressing, which absorbs fluid and prevents friction. Do not puncture; it usually absorbs on its own within 3 to 7 days.

session_222.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_222.text: Okay, I'll buy more hydrocolloid dressings. Also, how can I prevent blisters in the future? This time it might be because I wore new shoes for too long.

session_222.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_222.text: Wear new shoes for short periods at first and break them in gradually. Wear thick cotton socks or toe socks to reduce friction. If you walk a lot, use anti-friction patches or silicone insoles. The iodophor and large band-aids you bought are good for emergencies, but daily prevention matters more.

session_223.text: I've just become interested in watercolor painting and want to buy a starter set, but I'm worried about buying the wrong thing or overpaying. Can you help me analyze the cost-effectiveness of Sakura solid watercolors, Baohong watercolor paper, and nylon brushes? I'd like to keep the budget between 300-500 yuan.

session_223.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_223.text: You want to clarify a beginner's essential list and avoid common novice pitfalls, right? Specifically, are you more concerned with brand comparisons, paper texture choices, or differences in pen materials?

session_223.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_223.text: Yes, especially the value for money of Sakura, Winsor & Newton, and Schmincke, and also whether to choose Baohong paper in hot-pressed or cold-pressed, and the difference between nylon brushes and animal-hair brushes.

session_223.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_223.text: I suggest choosing the Sakura 24-color solid watercolor set (about 120 yuan) as an entry-level choice—great value for money; Baohong medium-texture 300g watercolor paper (about 80 yuan for 20 sheets) is good for beginners and easy to control water; pair it with a set of nylon brushes (two flat and two pointed, about 60 yuan), plus a palette (15 yuan) and masking fluid (10 yuan), for a total budget of about 285 yuan, leaving some room. Avoid animal-hair brushes—they're hard to maintain and expensive.

session_223.text: I am writing "The Cultural Texture of Kunming's Independent Bookstores." I have the new bookstores I observed myself, the old-bookstore anecdotes Uncle Qin gave me, and some material from "Yunnan Anecdotes," but I don't know how to organically integrate these materials into an article, and I feel confused about the structure.

session_223.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_223.text: You want to find a structural logic that balances personal experience, historical material, and academic observation, right? You could consider taking spatial change as the explicit thread and character stories as the implicit thread, or using a contrastive structure—juxtaposing old and new bookstores—to highlight shifts in the cultural fabric.

session_223.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_223.text: Yes, I've had that idea of intertwining spatial changes with character stories too, but I'm worried the transitions between paragraphs will feel stiff. And how can the language be both professional and literary? For example, how should the opening be written to be both captivating and substantive?

session_223.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_223.text: Suggest opening with the scene of the moment when Uncle Qin hands over the notebook to create a vivid picture, then naturally introduce the old bookstore that disappeared on Dongfeng Road, and layer in historical fragments from 'Yunnan Anecdotes'. In the middle paragraphs, use a three-layer progression of 'bookstore—street—era', alternating sensory descriptions (such as the smell of books, the touch of handwritten notes) with rational analysis (such as the carrying of local culture), and leave a transitional sentence at the end of each paragraph.

session_225.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_225.text: I'm just starting to learn flat washes in watercolor. As soon as I made the first stroke, the paint spread, and the color was uneven. Are there any tips for controlling water and making the color more uniform?

session_225.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_225.text: You've run into a common beginner problem. Ink bleeding is usually related to too much water or the paper's absorbency. Would you like me to explain specifically how to judge the water content in the brush, the holding posture, and ways to fix it?

session_225.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_225.text: Yes, especially how to control the amount of water on the brush and avoid uneven coloring.

session_225.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_225.text: Before flat painting, use a tissue to absorb excess water from the brush tip, so the strokes are full but not dripping; when applying, keep a 45-degree angle and pull at a steady speed, avoiding repeated overlaying; choose 300g cotton pulp paper to reduce bleeding; for the parts that went wrong, while still wet, use a clean damp brush to absorb the paint. It is recommended to practice monochrome flat painting for 15 minutes every day.

session_225.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_225.text: I'm writing an essay about memories of Old Street, blending historical materials about the old medicine shop on Guanghua Street, the seal-engraving stall on Yongdao Street, and the street scenes my grandmother described. But I feel the rhythm of the prose and the integration of details are not natural enough. What suggestions do you have?

session_225.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_225.text: You could try starting with sensory details, such as the sounds of the street and the fragrance of herbs, before naturally bringing in the historical background. Refer to Wang Zengqi's "Five Tastes" or Jian Zhen's "Water Questions", use imagery to connect the real and the abstract, and alternate long and short sentences for rhythm.

session_225.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_225.text: Yes, I thought of using the herbal scent of an old medicine shop as a starting point. But how should we handle the boundary between historical materials and fiction, to avoid being too factual or too fictional?

session_225.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_225.text: Historical materials serve as the background framework, while fiction fills in specific characters and activities, keeping the emotions true. You can refer to Chen Danyan's Shanghai's Golden Branches and Jade Leaves — a limited literary imagination based on facts, without straying too far.

session_225.text: It sounds like you're completely immersed in the joy of learning something new; that clumsy yet focused process is truly precious. Did you mark the amount of water added? That sense of ritual must make the color chart even more special!

session_225.speaker: Sun Yuwei

Although my brushstrokes were not steady, the unexpected beauty of the ink bleeding through the paper surprised me instead. The feel of the Qiuhongzhai brush is also very comfortable, as if I had opened a new world.

session_225.text: From your description, I can feel that pure joy—the sense of exploration and satisfaction unique to a beginner. Painting doesn't need to be perfect; those "accidents" are exactly the charm of watercolor. Looking forward to hearing more little joys from your classes!

session_231.text: What you're after is a deep fusion of paper media and literary emotion — you hope the characteristics of the paper (such as mulberry paper's rough texture and light purple tone) can reinforce the imagery of the prose (the mistiness of morning fog, the dampness of the rainy season), thereby raising the artistic level. session_231.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_231.text: Suggestions: 1) For the color scheme, choose gray-white or off-white mulberry bark paper for the morning mist, and dark blue or light green floral paper for the rainy season, so as not to let the romantic feel of light purple dilute the quiet calm of nostalgia; 2) For the layout, increase the blank space on the upper half of the page (to one-third), set line spacing to 1.5 times the character height, write with a fine weasel-hair calligraphy brush, and use slightly light gray ink to simulate mist; 3) Use dried flower stickers only to decorate the beginnings of paragraphs (for example, use a single ginkgo leaf to match the rainy season), and do not spread them all over. session_232.text: Today I tried watercolor wet-on-wet technique for the first time, painting a gradient sky and clouds. The color bleeding felt very healing, but the result wasn't ideal—I could never control the water well. Could you help me see where the problem lies?

session_232.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_232.text: When you’re first learning the wet-on-wet technique, controlling the water can certainly make you flustered—that’s perfectly normal! Your gradient attempt has already taken an important step. I suggest checking how damp the paper is first: wet the surface evenly with a large brush, and when the sheen disappears and the paper is semi-matte, apply the color. Make the pigment somewhat thicker than usual; this will make the blending easier to control. Next time, try practicing simple color-block transitions and slowly get a feel for it.

session_232.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_232.text: Mm, I do feel the paper is too wet, and the paint is running everywhere. So how exactly can you tell when the paper reaches a semi-matte state? And what is the rough ratio of paint to water?

session_232.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_232.text: How to judge: lightly touch the paper surface with the back of your hand; it should feel slightly cool but not damp, and there should be no obvious water pooling. As for the paint ratio, after dipping the brush tip in paint, gently scrape it against the edge of the palette, then dip it in water and mix; the consistency should be like thin yogurt. If the color spreads too fast, immediately use a clean tissue to absorb the excess water as a remedy. Practice these techniques a few more times and you will get the feel for it. You are doing great!

session_237.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_237.text: I just submitted my short story 'Alleyway' to Qingcheng Magazine. I'm excited but also a bit nervous. What do you think I should pay attention to?

session_237.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_237.text: Do you want to share this sense of accomplishment while also needing some psychological adjustment after submitting and creative feedback suggestions? For example, review cycles, how to handle rejections, or whether the description of "the Kunming atmosphere" in the novel is on point?

session_237.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_237.text: Yes, I especially want to know the review cycle for 'Qingcheng,' and whether the environmental descriptions and the understated ending in my novel are appropriate. The inspiration came from the morning's analysis of Shen Congwen and the subway podcast.

session_237.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_237.text: Qingcheng's review period is usually 1-3 months. Your 'Kunming Flavor' piece, which blends classroom and podcast material, is quite distinctive—the detailed environmental descriptions immerse readers, and the understated ending is a common technique in short fiction. While waiting, I suggest collecting feedback. If you're rejected, don't be discouraged; after adjusting your mindset, you can submit to other magazines. The next step could be to balance prose and fiction, for example, by writing a series. Would you like to discuss specific writing techniques?

session_237.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_237.text: I just took my parents for a walk and we talked a lot about stories from the 1980s. I recorded and transcribed them. Now I have a pile of fragmented material—how can I organize it into themed chapters?

session_237.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_237.text: You want to extract the highlights from the oral recordings and build an essay collection framework based on the memories of the era, right?

session_237.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_237.text: Yes, especially how to avoid making it a mere chronicle, and I also want to find a balance between literariness and truthfulness.

session_237.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_237.text: You can start by clustering by keywords—for example, prices, transportation, and forms of entertainment—and group similar passages into different sections. Use your parents' original words as the opening for each section, then interweave your observations and the historical background. That way it has both warmth and structure.

session_238.text: It's been nearly two months since I submitted "The Alley Entrance" to Qingcheng, and I haven't heard back. I'm a bit anxious. Uncle Qin suggested submitting it to Dianchi instead. Do you think that's reliable?

session_238.text: I understand your anxiety; it’s common for submissions to disappear without a trace. Uncle Qin’s advice is very practical. The young writers section of “Dianchi” welcomes newcomers more, and its style leans toward regional narrative and delicate emotion, which suits your prose collection perfectly. Need me to analyze the direction for adjusting “The Alley Entrance”?

session_238.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_238.text: Yes, and how should I write the self-recommendation letter to impress the editor? Uncle Qin is willing to write a recommendation letter—should I discuss the details with him first?

session_238.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_238.text: In your self-recommendation letter, highlight your literary background and the themes of "The Alleyway" (such as urban memory and personal growth). Including Uncle Qin's recommendation letter will significantly increase your chances of success. I suggest confirming the contents of the recommendation letter with Uncle Qin first, and compressing the manuscript to within 6,000 words to match the regular requirements of the "Dianchi" section. Would you like me to give you a template for a self-recommendation letter?

session_238.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_238.text: I have a podcast interview this afternoon, and I need to read aloud the essay “The Alleyway” and talk about the creative process. session_238.text: Would you like me to give you specific feedback on your pronunciation, speaking pace, and emotional expression from the perspective of a host or a reading coach? Also, regarding questions like 'Family and Vigil,' would you like me to help you organize a logical framework?

session_238.text: When reading, pay attention to key words such as 'alley entrance' and 'vigil' — slow down and add more emotional weight. session_238.text: She cares so much about your writing, which shows she has been quietly supporting your dream. The distance actually makes this concern more precious—she trusts your persistence, and her expectations give you more motivation. Writing this longing into your words might allow it to become nourishment for your inspiration.

session_238.speaker: Sun Yuwei

session_248.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_248.text: I've just made an outline for 'Day and Night at Green Lake,' but I'm not sure how to balance description and narrative between day and night. Do you have any suggestions?

session_248.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_248.text: It seems you want the essay to have both vivid imagery and narrative appeal. Your outline is divided into four sections in chronological order. I suggest weaving a specific person or event into each section as a narrative thread, such as the elderly person doing morning exercise or the bookstore owner in the afternoon, so the descriptions can connect naturally.

session_248.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_248.text: I've accumulated some light, shadow, and sound material during my morning runs, and also sentences from magazines about independent bookstores. How can I incorporate them without making it feel cluttered?

session_248.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_248.text: Sensory description should serve the emotional tone. For example, in the dusk passage, you can echo the sunset with the warm light of the bookstore, and when quoting the magazine sentence, rewrite it appropriately so that it becomes part of your observation. Remember: 'the scene is set for the emotion, and the emotion grows out of the scene.'

session_248.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_248.text: I'm really happy tonight! My column draft was accepted by Xu Mingyuan, editor of Cultural Vision, and I scored 95 on the Subject 1 mock exam. My family is very supportive, but I'm still torn: should I become a full-time writer after graduation, or go to graduate school first? Can you help me analyze it?

session_248.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_248.text: Congratulations, Sun Yuwei! These two accomplishments are truly well deserved. You mentioned the choice between full-time writing and further study; the core is balancing creative passion with career stability — do you lean toward first building up a body of work and income, or deepening your writing theory through systematic study?

session_248.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_248.text: I want both, but I'm afraid I don't have enough time and energy. My mom encourages me to keep working hard, and my dad worries about my health. I'm actually an INFP, and I'm especially afraid of losing creative freedom, and also afraid that further study might be too academic and constrain me.

session_248.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_248.text: I understand your ambivalence. I suggest planning in stages: after graduation, first spend six months to a year writing full-time, complete the first draft of a collection of essays and try submitting it, while building up your portfolio and industry connections. At the same time, pay attention to more practice-oriented graduate programs such as an MFA in Creative Writing, and use your spare time to prepare for the exams. This way you keep your freedom and broaden your horizons through academia. Your family's financial situation can support this transition period, and for your father, a concrete plan will put his mind at ease.

session_248.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_248.text: This approach makes so much sense! Writing for a while before deciding on further study makes me feel much less pressure. Thank you for affirming my sense of accomplishment and for giving such a concrete path.

session_248.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_248.text: You're welcome. Your writing talent and self-discipline have already proven your ability. Remember, after Subject 1 there are more parts of the driving test; you can fit them in between writing sessions to adjust your rhythm. Keep your creative passion alive—you are well on your way to becoming a cultural observer.

session_249.text: I compared Haoyibao and Lanyibao, but I can't figure out how exactly the guaranteed renewal for 20 years protects me, and what the risk is if the products are discontinued. Can you help me sort out the core differences?

session_249.text: Both plans guarantee renewal for 20 years, meaning that within 20 years you can renew regardless of discontinuation or claims. session_249.text: Are details like the deductible and green-channel medical services practical for young people?

session_249.text: Practical. Young and healthy people have a low probability of hospitalization, so a 10,000 yuan deductible makes little difference. Given your conservative approach to managing finances, choosing Blue Medical Insurance has a slightly higher annual premium, but its value-added services are more comprehensive, making it suitable for long-term holding.

session_249.text: This afternoon at Douji Café, my best friend Zhou Lin taught me to use a drawing tablet. For the first time, I drew the outline of a leaf, and it felt so novel! But in the evening, while organizing my journal, I couldn't help pasting in the little ticket stub from the group photo at Maitian Bookstore. Comparing the two, I think I prefer the tactile feel of paper.

session_249.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_249.text: It sounds like you enjoy the novelty of digital tools but can't let go of the texture of paper journals. Are you torn about how to combine the two to make your creative work more interesting?

session_249.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_249.text: Right! Digital drawing is convenient, but paper has more warmth. For example, the photos I take and my own sketches inspired by osmanthus and maple leaves—how can I incorporate them into my journal in a more interesting way?

session_249.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_249.text: You can try the "mixing approach": draw simple sketches or materials on a graphics tablet, print them out, and cut and paste them into a paper journal; or use your phone to photograph the digital creation process, then print them as small photos and stick them into the journal. This way, you keep the convenience of digital tools without losing the ritual feel of paper.

session_249.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_249.text: That's a good idea! I also want to jot down today's insurance insights in my journal. I used to find it boring, but adding a few little illustrations makes it much more interesting.

session_249.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_249.text: You could draw some cute icons with a drawing tablet (like a safe, leaves), print them, and stick them on the relevant journal pages. With short text labels, that makes the study records more visual and gives a greater sense of achievement.

session_251.text: I just passed Subject 1, the written driving test, and booked a Subject 2 practice session for the afternoon of September 11. I’m a bit nervous about getting behind the wheel for the first time. Can you tell me what I need to prepare for the first lesson?

session_251.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_251.text: It is recommended to wear flat-soled soft shoes that day to feel the clutch more easily, and to bring your ID card and student card. Focus on adjusting the seat and rearview mirrors before shifting gears. Use your left foot to try pressing the clutch to find the biting point (the car body vibrates slightly and the engine sound becomes deeper). Hold the steering wheel at the 3 and 9 o'clock positions, and turn slowly and return gently. First-day goals: get familiar with clutch control and driving straight; don't be afraid of stalling.

session_251.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_251.text: Today at Zhibushi Bookstore, I talked with my book friend Lin Yue about the three-branch concept of Ikenobo's 'Seika' — shin, gyo, so — and it felt very philosophical. Can you help me explain in more depth the specific meanings of these three branches?

session_251.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_251.text: Of course. "Shin, gyo, so" originates from Japanese calligraphy. In the Ikenobo school, they represent heaven, earth, and human — "shin" is the upright main branch, symbolizing heaven; "gyo" is the middle branch, representing human; "so" is the low-hanging secondary branch, signifying earth. The angles and spatial relationships of the three branches embody the balance of yin and yang and the beauty of negative space. This is the core philosophy of seika.

session_251.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_251.text: I see. Space and negative space are exactly the artistic mood I felt today while admiring the osmanthus flowers in Green Lake Park. I also want to write this autumnal mood and the osmanthus fragrance into my essays. Do you have recommended books on Japanese flower arrangement, or techniques for turning the observation of flower arrangements into literary imagery?

session_251.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_251.text: I recommend “Kado: The Traditional Japanese Art of Flower Arranging” and “Introduction to Ikenobo” for beginners. Pay special attention to the passages about ‘waiting’ and ‘balance.’ When writing, you can treat shin, gyo, and sō as three narrative layers: ‘shin’ is the direct narration of the osmanthus branch, ‘gyo’ is the pause when you catch the fragrance, and ‘sō’ is the melancholy of falling leaves—use the tilt angles of the three branches to express emotional ups and downs.

session_251.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_251.text: This metaphor is wonderful! I happen to have a sketch of osmanthus in my journal, so I can use the structure of three branches to organize the paragraphs. Thank you for the suggestion—I'll try writing a passage tonight.

session_251.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_251.text: Looking forward to your work. If you need inspiration, you might recall the book about 'waiting' that Boss Qin Mingyuan showed us today at Jiuguan Fangtang—in flower arranging, 'waiting' is the silence before a branch enters the vase; in writing, 'waiting' is the gap in which words settle. The two share the same rhythm.

session_255.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_255.text: I just had a deep debate with my mom about the subject matter of my writing. At first she was very insistent that I write about grand history, but I insisted on writing about the everyday life of the city. In the end, she understood me and even said, 'Your pen, your decision.' I was really moved.

session_255.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_255.text: I can tell you experienced a precious emotional shift, from the tension of the debate to the warmth of eventual understanding. You want to sort through this experience and confirm the creative values you hold on to, right?

session_255.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_255.text: Yes, I really feel that the breath of everyday city life is also precious, but I used to worry that my mom wouldn't understand. Her final words of support made me feel relieved and also more determined in my writing direction.

session_255.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_255.text: This kind of mutual understanding is rare nourishment for growth. You can turn this emotion into creative motivation—for example, by writing a prose piece about a mother-daughter conversation, recording the specific arguments in the debate and the moment she changed her mind. In the future, you can also proactively share the stories you write with her to continue this spiritual resonance.

session_255.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_255.text: I'm writing an essay about the old streets of Kunming. I got stuck when describing the changes and the memories of the elderly, and I can't express the theme of "heritage and change"—my writing feels thin. Are there any techniques to make abstract themes more vivid?

session_255.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_255.text: Do you want to use details and contrasts to present the passage of time, such as comparing people and scenes past and present? Or do you need to sort out the emotional threads in the oral history materials?

session_255.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_255.text: Both are needed, especially how to carry abstract themes with concrete details—for instance, a conversation between an old man in his youth and his present self under the same tree on the old street.

session_255.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_255.text: You could try the 'object anchoring method': choose a core object (such as the signboard of an old teahouse) and use its fading, mending, and repainting to connect three generations of memories. At the same time, use contrasts in the oral accounts—for example, an old man saying 'the road has widened, but the heart has narrowed'—to directly highlight the changes. For reference, I recommend Wang Zengqi's 'Hutong Culture' and its structure of interweaving movement and stillness.

This will make the curves smoother. For the gradient, I suggest a radial gradient with two overlapping layers—add a little light yellow to the pink base to enhance the layering. Also, when exporting, choose PNG at 300 dpi to ensure clear printing.

session_259.speaker: Sun Yuwei

session_259.text: First draw a petal outline. Select it, double-click the Mirror Tool, choose Vertical, and copy. Then merge the paths of the two copied petals, and rotate and arrange them as a whole. The key is to make sure the start and end anchor points of each petal are perfectly aligned; you can use the Align Panel to set this.

session_262.text: Steering timing: For a left turn, when the outside of the left rearview mirror aligns with the left line, immediately turn the wheel one full turn to the left, then make small adjustments to keep the mirror corner close to the line. session_266.speaker: Sun Yuwei

session_266.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_266.text: In late September in Kunming, consider cosmos, sage, reeds, and eucalyptus leaves, with blue-purple, white, and green as the dominant colors to echo the lake and sky. It is suggested that the floral arrangements be concentrated at the entrance and the meditation area, with low garlands around the yoga mats to avoid blocking sight lines. The Ikenobo style can be simplified into free-standing flower arrangements, using branches to express a sense of flow.

session_266.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_266.text: Free-form ikebana with the flowing quality of branches is a great idea! But how exactly should the zoning be designed in the homestay courtyard so that participants can both appreciate the flowers and focus on yoga?

session_266.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_266.text: It can be divided into three zones: at the entrance, use a floral arch to guide the eye; in the meditation area, enclose it with a circular flower wreath; in the yoga practice area, place low flower borders along the edge. The circulation path should be S-shaped, letting the flower arrangements unfold with each step and match the breathing rhythm of yoga. For the budget, I suggest first choosing five main flower varieties and pairing them with local wildflowers to reduce costs.

session_266.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_266.text: I attended the second day of the writing workshop this morning. As the instructor required, I rewrote the opening of “Landscapes in a Bowl of Rice Noodles” in a colloquial style. session_266.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_266.text: Of course. Your revised version captures the rhythm of everyday conversation. For example, using 'When that bowl of rice noodles was set down, the hot steam rushed straight at my face' instead of the original's bookish description creates a strong visual. Its strength is that the chosen details are close to everyday life and quickly close the distance with the reader. My suggestion for improvement: add one or two more personal sensory details, such as the change in temperature when your fingers touch the rim of the bowl, or the color of the scallions floating on the soup under the light—this will enhance emotional resonance on top of the colloquial tone. Also, you mentioned wanting to apply the technique of 'details triggering resonance' to your next column. The morning scene at Green Lake or neighborhood stories are both good topics. I suggest starting with a small moment that touches you the most, such as the interaction between an elderly morning exerciser and the pigeons, and using one or two close-up shots to set the tone for the whole piece.

session_266.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_266.text: Thank you for the comments. The suggestion to add sensory details is very specific! I am indeed considering writing about the morning scene at Cuihu, wanting to highlight the warmth of that slow-paced life. If I were to distill a reusable method from the workshop notes, how would you suggest systematically training one's ability to observe details and write?

session_266.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_266.text: You could try the “Three-Senses, One-Day Journal” exercise: every day, choose one life scene (such as a morning market or a bus stop), use three senses (sight, hearing, smell) to write down the three most striking details, then add one layer of personal emotion or memory to form a 50- to 100-character passage. After a week, you'll find your eye for details becomes sharper, and you'll naturally incorporate “details that resonate” into your column. Also, when writing about the morning scene at Green Lake, you can first list five potential details, then choose the one most likely to touch shared emotion as the anchor of the article.

session_267.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_267.text: My advisor said that the “skeleton” of my nonfiction story outline is “not solid enough”—what exactly does that mean? How should I strengthen the structure?

session_267.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_267.text: You're looking for a way to organize the old teahouse material into a stronger narrative framework, right? 'A solid skeleton' usually means a clear main line, reasonable pacing, and coherent causal logic.

session_267.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_267.text: Yes, I'm writing a story about old teahouses. I have a lot of material but don't know how to choose the core plot.

session_267.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_267.text: It is recommended to adopt a 'character ensemble + thematic progression' structure: first determine the core theme (such as persistence amid change), slice by character perspective, let each segment advance the theme, and connect them with a timeline. List all characters and events, and select 3-5 scenes that best embody the theme as the backbone.

session_267.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_267.text: Aunt Xie, my neighbor, just told me a story about the weekend open-air movies at Green Lake in the 1980s. I want to work it into my essay about the old teahouse, but I don't know how to bring it in without feeling out of place.

session_267.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_267.text: Use the old teahouse as the narrative anchor, treat the open-air film as a memory fragment of the old tea regulars, and naturally connect the changes of the era by contrasting the 1980s with the present. Keep the emotions authentic and appropriately literarize the scene details.

session_267.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_267.text: Comparing the changes of the times is a good direction, but inserting memories directly might interrupt the main thread of the teahouse. Is there a more clever way to connect them?

session_267.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_267.text: Try using ‘Aunt Xie's reading notes’ as the narrative framework. Each Wednesday, her story becomes the insertion point for ‘I remember what my neighbor said...’ in the essay, forming a dual-line structure of reality and memory, making the material a natural part of the teahouse character portraits.

session_267.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_267.text: The dual-line structure is wonderful—it preserves the authenticity of the oral account without disrupting the rhythm. So how do you draw the boundary between emotional truth and literary embellishment?

session_267.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_267.text: Emotional truth is the skeleton, and literary craft is the flesh and blood. Retain the core details and emotional tone; you may embellish scene descriptions moderately, but do not fabricate key facts. It is recommended to first organize the oral recording, mark which parts can be polished, and then start writing.

session_268.speaker: Sun Yuwei

For example, invent an action she never said out loud (a pause while mending clothes), but keep it believable. You can also use her exact words as an opening, and then expand.

session_269.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_269.text: Tomorrow is the flower arrangement exam. I've prepared withered branches, purple gentians, and smoke tree leaves, and I want to make a slanting-style arrangement. What's the best way to combine and secure them?

session_269.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_269.text: The slanting style emphasizes asymmetrical balance: use the dried branch as the main branch, insert it at a 45° angle into the kenzan, and cut the base into a wedge to secure it; use gentian as the guest branch, extending it at a low angle from the front of the main branch; use smoke tree leaves as the filler branch, filling space at the rear. Keep the flower materials facing the same direction and leave room for a sense of flow.

session_269.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_269.text: Got it. What should I keep in mind during the exam? For example, time limits and mindset adjustment.

session_269.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_269.text: The exam usually involves on-site creation with a one-hour time limit. The evaluation focuses on proportion, color harmony, and expression of artistic conception. It's recommended to arrive early and take deep breaths to calm your nerves; while arranging flowers, focus on every movement and trust the practice you've accumulated. Rest well tonight and take it in stride tomorrow.

session_270.text: I just added a passage to my essay "Dusk at the Alley Entrance" describing "Three Generations' Grocery Store" and "Light and Shadow of the Old Street", but I feel the imagery isn't vivid enough and the pacing drags. Can you help me see how to revise it?

session_270.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_270.text: You want to improve the narrative depth? I suggest using different action details from three generations to show the passage of time — for example, the old man counting coins, the middle-aged person stocking shelves, and the child standing on tiptoe to reach for candy — together with the natural transition of light and shadow from the shopfront to the street corner.

session_270.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_270.text: Yes, the writing group also suggested something similar. But I always feel the light-and-shadow description is too straightforward—for example, 'the setting sun dyed the shelves gold'—how can it be made more subtle?

session_270.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_270.text: You could try using the shadows of objects to suggest light: for example, 'the soy sauce bottle's shadow stretches long and climbs onto the old calendar in the corner,' or 'the trail of dust on the glass cabinet is lit up by the slanting light.' This creates both a visual image and a sense of the passage of time.

session_270.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_270.text: It sounds like you've taken an important step and gained a specific writing direction. The two perspectives of old shops and neighborhood relationships are very suitable for enhancing the sense of place in the essay. I suggest you first sort out the relevant clues in your memory before next week, and then further verify them against the materials in the WeChat group.

session_270.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_270.text: Actively participating in the simple sharing before each activity can gradually build connections. Next time you can bring a short piece you are satisfied with and ask the group leader or auntie for feedback; sharing your work can reduce social pressure. Stick with it for three months, and you will find a more comfortable place in the circle.

session_272.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_272.text: I just ran 4 kilometers with my coach, and she suggested starting interval running and strength training next week to prepare for the half marathon. I want to learn the basic training framework and injury prevention tips in advance to cooperate with her.

session_272.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_272.text: Understood. You need a scientific, progressive half-marathon training plan, including interval run pace calculations, strength training exercise recommendations, and recovery methods such as knee protection.

session_272.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_272.text: Right, especially how to calculate the interval running pace based on today's pace (7 minutes 15 seconds), and how to divide the training cycle.

session_272.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_272.text: It is recommended to divide the plan into base phase, build phase, peak phase, and taper phase. For interval pace, use the formula: take your current best 1 km pace and subtract 15-20 seconds. For example, if your easy run pace is 7:15/km, try intervals at 4:40-50 per kilometer, starting with 400-meter repeats. For strength training, prioritize squats, lunges, and planks, along with wall sits to protect the knees.

session_272.speaker: Sun Yuwei

session_272.text: Completely suitable. Yoga can be scheduled after strength training or on rest days from running, focusing on hip and leg stretches and the core; meditation helps relax the nervous system and improve focus. Be sure to take in protein and carbohydrates after training to avoid excessive fatigue.

session_272.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_272.text: Today at Mingyuan Bookstore I came across "Jiangnan Sketches". The passage about the sense of place made me instantly find the feeling for revising "Dusk at the Lane Entrance". Later I also called my advisor, and everything felt right.

session_272.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_272.text: It seems you had a very fulfilling intellectual journey today, and you gained insights in both reading and writing. Can you tell me specifically how the techniques in the book inspired you?

session_272.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_272.text: For example, the book uses taste and touch to convey the dampness of Jiangnan alleys, so I tried to write in the childhood hawking cries of the sugar-figure vendor at the alley entrance and the swaying of locust tree shadows. My advisor said this established the identity of a local young observer.

session_272.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_272.text: This transformation is great, combining external sensory details with internalized memory and emotion—that's exactly the beauty of “locality” in nonfiction writing. Doesn't the ritual feeling of painting a little running figure in watercolor in your journal also echo that rhythm and breath?

session_272.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_272.text: This morning I ran into my literary friend Zhang Xin at Mingyuan Bookstore. We chatted briefly about 'Jiangnan Sketches', and I felt the book's treatment of 'sense of place' was very distinctive, but we didn't have time to go deeper. Could you analyze with me in detail how this kind of nonfiction writing presents regional culture?

session_272.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_272.text: “Jiangnan Sketches” elevates personal experience into cultural observation through delicate sensory descriptions (such as smell and sound) and the capturing of everyday scenes—this is exactly the essence of a “sense of place.” A similar approach appears in Yunnan writer Yu Jian’s “This Side of Yunnan”: he excels at using plain, unadorned description to capture the temperament of a region.

session_272.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_272.text: Yes, Yu Jian really does pay close attention to detail. Also, the store owner Qin Mingyuan recommended several local essay collections; I flipped through them but didn’t buy them. Could you introduce more essays from Yunnan or in the Yunnan style? For example, the works of Lei Pingyang and Hai Nan, or your evaluations of those essay collections.

session_272.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_272.text: I suggest paying special attention to Lei Pingyang's “Notes on Pu'er Tea” — he connects tea culture through personal experience, with plain but profound writing. Hai Nan's “Biography of Dianchi Lake” approaches it from history and mythology, offering a unique perspective. Among the books recommended by the bookstore, “Kunming Memories” is a popular one, worth buying and reading closely, especially suitable for accumulating material for “Dusk at the Alley Entrance.”

The restraint of Japanese prose can be incorporated into observations of the city's rhythm. Mention the National Day atmosphere briefly in the background, write the marathon experience as its own paragraph, and use the rhythm of footsteps to echo the rustling sounds from the opening.

session_277.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant

Also, Chen Chen's suggestion is key: let the image become "living stitches" rather than decoration.

session_278.text: Today I finally printed and bound the manuscript of my essay collection “Slow Travel Notes” and sent it to three publishers! I had been preparing for months, and now I feel both relieved and a bit nervous.

session_278.speaker: Sun Yuwei

session_278.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_278.text: My friend and I are planning a 7-day cultural trip in Yunnan, passing through Dali, Weishan, and Shaxi. Could you help me look up what distinctive guesthouses there are in Weishan Ancient Town? How can I contact the jiama paper workshops in Shaxi? And what are the transportation options from Dali to Weishan and from Weishan to Shaxi?

session_278.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_278.text: Okay. Recommendations for Weishan Ancient City: the guesthouses "Bailuyuan" and "Mufu Bieyuan" cost 150-300 yuan per person and preserve the Bai ethnic architectural style. For the Shaxi Jiama paper workshop, you can contact "Tea Horse Road Jiama Workshop" at 0872-*** (to be verified). From Dali to Weishan, you can take a bus (about 2 hours); from Weishan to Shaxi, you need to return to Dali first and then transfer (about 4 hours in total). It is recommended to rent a car or carpool for more flexibility.

session_278.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_278.text: Thanks! Are there any guesthouses in Weishan near the Jiama paper workshop? Also, how do we apply for the Bai tie-dye experience shop and volunteer positions? We want to do field notes combined with Jiama paper research. What suggestions do you have?

session_278.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_278.text: In Weishan County, most guesthouses are within walking distance of the Jiama Paper Workshop; the recommended Old Town Lodge is only 200 meters from the workshop. For tie-dye experiences, Zhoucheng Puzhen Tie-dye Workshop is recommended; reservations can be made by phone (0872-***). Volunteer spots require a recommendation from Uncle Qin at Paper, Cloth and Stone Bookstore, and it is advised to contact him a week in advance. For field records, it is recommended to use daily phone recordings and handwritten journal sketches, focusing on the symbolic meanings of Jiama paper patterns and the tie-dye process.

session_278.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_278.text: Hello! I am preparing for a cultural trip to Weishan and Shaxi, and I am particularly interested in Bai ethnic jiama paper. Could you tell me about its specific uses in sacrificial rituals and warding off evil spirits? Also, what are the differences in patterns between different regions?

session_278.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_278.text: Bai jiama paper is commonly used in rituals such as worshiping Benzhu (village patron deities), funerals, and exorcising ghosts. The patterns vary greatly from village to village—for example, those in the Dali basin area tend to be fine and detailed, while those in mountainous areas are bold and simple. When you travel, you can look at actual pieces in old houses around Sideng Street in Shaxi or at markets. During fieldwork, ask elders especially about the specific talismans such as 'Zhao Gongming' and 'Mountain God' and the occasions on which they are used.

session_278.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_278.text: I understand. So during fieldwork, how should I communicate with local artisans or elders? Are there any ethical concerns or recording methods I should pay attention to?

session_278.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_278.text: It is recommended to bring a journal and a voice recorder, but be sure to get the other person’s consent first. You can start with “Grandpa/Grandma, what is this jiama paper pasted on your wall for?” and avoid directly asking “Do you have any cultural relics?”. When recording, note the complete time, place, and form of address, and also be mindful of ritual taboos (for example, some jiama paper cannot be touched casually). It is recommended to carry “Research on Yunnan Folk Prints and Folk Beliefs” for reference.

session_278.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_278.text: This morning I went to Wenlin Street to photograph the ginkgo trees. I used a tripod and slow shutter speed and successfully captured the trajectory of falling leaves and the translucent leaves in backlight. What do you think of the color tone and composition of these photos?

session_278.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_278.text: Great work! The backlit leaves have strong layering, and the slow shutter speed gives the falling leaves a sense of flow. For post-processing, I suggest focusing on warm golden tones—slightly increasing the saturation of orange and yellow, lowering the blue hue, and highlighting the warmth of autumn. You could also compile these photos into a journal or essay collection; they have a very artistic atmosphere.

session_278.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_278.text: A warm golden tone sounds right. Can you recommend some reference values for the specific parameters? For example, how should color temperature and tone curve be adjusted?

session_278.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_278.text: Set the color temperature between 5500 and 6000K, with the tint slightly toward yellow at +5. Use an S-curve to enhance contrast, lower the highlights a bit to preserve leaf detail, and brighten the shadows slightly. In HSL, shift orange hue to -10, saturation to +15, and lightness to +5; treat yellow similarly. Finally, add a soft warm light filter to make the effect gentler.

When choosing meals in the cafeteria, pick more steamed or boiled dishes such as chicken breast, tofu, and leafy greens. Halve the staple food but keep whole grains. session_280.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_280.text: Yes, please give me a one-week meal plan template. And what should I do if I get hungry after fasting past 8 p.m.? How can I coordinate less oil and less salt when eating with family?

session_280.text: Okay. Communication with family: suggest your parents replace red-braising and deep-frying with steaming, blanching, and cold tossing; you should take charge of one light dish (such as blanched okra). Long-term adherence can improve metabolism and give you more energy, but you need to monitor your weight and complete blood count monthly to ensure adequate nutrition.

session_285.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_285.text: For the essay collection, I suggest grouping pieces by theme or emotional thread, such as “Urban Monologue” and “Hometown Memories,” so that the table of contents has a narrative feel. For the sample chapters, choose 3–5 pieces that best represent your style and are relatively complete, and the first piece should be compelling. In terms of timing, the topic selection meeting is usually held in March at the beginning of the year, so you need to send him the table of contents and sample chapters before the end of December so he has time for internal discussion. In the email, briefly thank him for the meeting, attach the materials, and ask for his revision suggestions — this can also indirectly show how much he values you.

Tomorrow you can follow these steps: open Alipay → search for 'Simulated Auto-Invest' → select 'CSI 300' → customize the amount and frequency (weekly investment is recommended).

session_285.text: The long-term return difference between weekly and monthly investing is very small; beginners are advised to invest monthly for less hassle. When losing, stick with regular investing, and consider “buy more as it falls” — appropriately increase the regular investment amount during market drops (for example, invest 20% more), but don’t exceed your total budget. The key is to hold for more than 3 years.

session_291.text: The ideal place to insert it is before the protagonist leaves the town: a flashback to a similar farewell scene from childhood, using sensory details (such as the smell of the wind and the sound of footsteps) to transition naturally, which can soften the pacing and strengthen emotional resonance. At the chapter transition, a short inner monologue is recommended as a bridge to replace the current blunt scene change.

session_292.text: I've been drawing a set of 'Four Seasons at Cuihu Lake' bookmarks. I just finished the sketches of spring willows, summer lotus, autumn leaves, and winter gulls, but I'm struggling to capture the mood with the color palette and lines. Could you give me some advice?

session_292.text: You want the bookmark to be simple, elegant, and in keeping with the mood of the four seasons. You may want to consider the integration of watercolor and line, seasonally representative symbols (for example, besides plants and animals, whether to include poetry or water ripples), and the texture of the printing paper. I suggest starting by choosing a dominant color palette: spring with green, summer with azure blue, autumn with orange-yellow, and winter with gray-white, keeping lines minimalist and watercolor washes light. How do you feel about this direction?

session_292.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_292.text: Yes, the main palette of green, blue, orange, yellow, grey, and white fits the feeling of the four seasons in my mind. But I'm worried that lines that are too simple will seem monotonous. How can I add detail without destroying the overall mood? Also, I'd like to give it to a friend as a gift, or turn it into a series. Do you have any concrete suggestions?

session_292.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_292.text: You can add one or two detailed accents to the minimalist line drawings: for example, add an early swallow on a spring willow branch, draw a swimming fish under a summer lotus leaf, let a light drizzle fall beside autumn leaves, and fold snowflakes along the wing edges of winter gulls. Use a light gray pencil for the outlines, with partial watercolor washes to create a contrast between the concrete and the ethereal. As a gift, you can handwrite a poem matching the season on the back. To make it a series, it is recommended to use a uniform size (e.g., 6×15cm), print on 300g cotton paper, and pair it with a journal as a set.

session_294.text: At 5 a.m. this morning, I braved the rain and took a taxi to Xishan. I waited nearly half an hour at the observation deck at Nie Er's Tomb and finally captured the moment when the morning light pierced through the rain and fell on Sleeping Beauty and Dianchi Lake. My outdoor jacket was soaked through, but I felt incredibly fulfilled!

session_294.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_294.text: Wow, I can feel your persistent joy! The light in the rain and mist is truly dreamlike—especially the moment captured after waiting, it's full of poetry. You captured not just the scenery, but also the mood of that moment, right?

session_294.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_294.text: Yes, after I got home I transferred the photos to my iPad, and also printed a sample print in my journal and wrote down my thoughts. The gold of the morning light after rain interwoven with the blue of Dianchi Lake was especially healing—just as after wind and rain, beauty can always be seen.

session_294.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_294.text: This metaphor is fantastic. The color palette and composition you describe make me feel like I can see the scene. session_294.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_294.text: Today the editor approved my column topic 'The Aesthetics of Life in Kunming's Wet Markets.' I'm so happy! But I'm wondering how to naturally weave the details of the market — such as the elderly people queuing, the white steam from steamers, and the damp stone paths — into the theme of 'life aesthetics'?

session_294.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_294.text: It seems you want to find a way to connect everyday details with deeper aesthetics. Have you considered using a perspective of spatial movement, for example walking from Zhuanxin to Donghua, using the rhythm of a stroll to bring out different scenes? Just like the linking technique you used in today's Xishan essay.

session_294.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_294.text: Yes! I was just thinking of borrowing that 'movements as clues' writing style, but I'm afraid it might be too loose. Also, I've collected photos of the morning crowd at Zhuanxin Vegetable Market and notes from the Donghua cooked-food stall, but I don't know how to balance personal feelings with objective observation.

session_294.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_294.text: You could try the structure of ‘observation + association + leaving blank space’: each paragraph first depicts a scene (such as an elderly person slowly picking green beans), then blends in your feelings (like time becoming thicker in the waiting), and finally leaves an open-ended question or a poetic summary, letting readers experience the ‘life aesthetics’ for themselves. In this way, it preserves the authenticity of human observation without losing personal warmth.

session_294.text: Today, from the rainy, misty Western Hills in the early morning to the family dinner, I felt I experienced a dreamlike, complete day. I kind of want to integrate these feelings of happiness and make them footnotes to the meaning of life. Can you talk with me?

session_295.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_295.text: I'm writing a lesson plan on First Encounter with Autumn Home Flower Arrangement, using daisies, solidago, and eucalyptus leaves. The parts about flower material handling and kenzan use in the lesson plan aren't detailed enough. Could you provide professional advice?

session_295.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_295.text: Okay. Daisies should be cut at a 45-degree angle and cut underwater to help water absorption; when removing thorns, wear gloves to prevent sap residue. For goldenrod, remove the lower leaves and cut them into short sections to prevent rot. For eucalyptus leaves, make a slanted cut and crush the end of the stem to promote water absorption, and remove the bottom 4–5 leaves to avoid spoilage in water. Kenzan usage note: keep the kenzan moist before inserting, insert vertically downward, use a support or water flow to help fix the stems, and remind students to keep fingers away from the insertion point.

session_295.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_295.text: Thank you! The kenzan safety tip is very important. In class demonstrations, how can I control the pace to prevent students from cutting or damaging the flower materials?

session_295.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_295.text: Suggest demonstrating in three steps: first demonstrate angled cutting and thorn removal in slow motion, then let the trainees observe your technique; emphasize "measure the length before cutting, better too long than too short" to allow room for correction; when a cut goes wrong, show how to fix it with extra flower materials or by adjusting the angle, to reduce frustration.

session_296.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_296.text: This afternoon I attended Teacher Chen's lecture The Poetics of Everyday Life, and was especially moved by the aesthetics of the Mosuo people's hearth. I want to try to bring that kind of poetry into my own prose writing, but I always feel that what I write is just a record of phenomena, lacking that moving quality. Are there any specific methods you can suggest?

session_296.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_296.text: What you are concerned with is how to shift from “recording phenomena” to “expressing feelings”—this is precisely the core of anthropology’s “thick description.” You could try sensory writing: for example, when describing a fire pit, first close your eyes and recall the crackling of firewood, the smell of pine resin, and the sensation of heat waves hitting your face; then connect these sensations with metaphors rather than listing smoke, fire, and wood.

session_296.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_296.text: Yes, this morning on Xishan I saw mist wrapping around the mountainside, and during yoga class, at the moment blood rushed to my head during a handstand, I had that same urge. But when I write it out, it's just a pile of adjectives. Can you give me an actionable exercise?

session_296.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_296.text: Try the 'Five Senses Diary': each day pick a moment that moves you (like the mist over the Western Hills), and write just one sentence for each of touch, smell, and hearing. Strictly avoid nouns like 'mist', 'mountain', 'handstand'. For example, 'My fingertips pass through cold, wet cotton' instead of 'mist'. After a week, add blank space and metaphor, letting readers feel the poetry through the gaps.

session_296.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_296.text: This method is very specific! I'll try it right away. Also, could you recommend a few books on sensory writing or transforming field notes?

session_296.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant

session_297.text: Hi Yuwei, tomorrow I'll be teaching my first flower arrangement class, with the theme of autumn home arranging. I've already written the basic flow in the lesson plan, but I'm not sure whether I should add flower care instructions, and whether there are any variations on the upright style in autumn. Could you help me take a look?

session_297.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_297.text: I understand your nervousness. You're worried about the completeness and professionalism of the lesson plan, especially how to incorporate the autumn theme into the upright style. I suggest you add two points: first, when fixing on the kenzan, make sure to cut flower stems at a 45-degree angle to improve water absorption; second, for the autumn upright style, emphasize a sense of clean, sparse lines—for example, use the slanting branches of nandina to express elegance, and use pompon chrysanthemums as the focal point. This way, it stays true to the theme and guides students to observe line and color.

session_297.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_297.text: Yes, I’ve been trying to figure out how to help my students understand how lines and colors work together. When it comes specifically to securing spray gerberas and eucalyptus leaves with a kenzan, are there any details that are easy to get wrong that I should remind them about?

session_297.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_297.text: The stems of gerberas are relatively soft, so wrap them with wire to reinforce before inserting them into the kenzan. Eucalyptus leaves can be cut at an angle and then gently pushed in to avoid breaking. In addition, bring a pair of pruning shears for backup and demonstrate the cutting angles on site. If students ask about substituting flowers tomorrow, recommend similar autumn-colored foliage (such as red maple) to replace nandina and keep the style consistent. Finally, spend 5 minutes before class sharing the flower language: gerbera symbolizes mystery, and pompon chrysanthemum represents fulfillment; this can make the class more interesting.

session_297.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_297.text: Today my advisor reposted my article on Moments and commented that I am 'the student who breathes best with words.' I'm really happy. Right now I really want to talk with you about how to turn the fleeting poetry of life—like this morning's mist over the Western Hills—into warm, living words.

session_297.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_297.text: It seems this professional recognition has given you great encouragement. Can the morning mist over the Western Hills you mentioned be regarded as a concrete case of transformation? Combined with the idea of “the poetry of everyday life” from your teacher Chen’s lecture, you might try to establish a metaphorical connection between the misty landscape and inner feelings through detailed sensory descriptions, similar to Thoreau’s approach in Walden.

session_297.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_297.text: Yes, I want to connect the lightness of the mist with “breathing,” echoing my advisor’s comments. In the lecture, there was a line: “Poetry is the crystallization of everyday life.” I plan to use the misty scenery of Xishan as the starting point for an essay.

session_297.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_297.text: Great concept! I suggest first capturing the visual layers and tactile temperature of the morning mist, then bringing in your personal moment of contemplation. You could try opening with something like, 'When the mist spreads over the Western Hills, words begin to breathe,' directly engaging with your advisor's comments and giving the field poetry an aesthetic language.

session_297.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_297.text: Today was very fulfilling—from reading Walden in the morning to getting vaccinated, then decorating the classroom and taking a meditative walk. I feel especially peaceful inside. Would you like to hear about it?

It sounds like you truly experienced what Thoreau called 'simple and abundant' living today — morning light on the pages, the scent of the flower market, your mother's tomato scrambled eggs; these details made you feel your soul was nourished.

session_297.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_297.text: Yes, exactly. Especially during the meditation before bed, I felt that my commitment to my body and my anticipation for the flower arrangement class merged together, like a new seed.

Your heart has already found its rhythm; just keep it up.
