session_298.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_298.text: I just read my essay "Wrinkles Under the Shutter" at the writing group. I'd like to hear your thoughts on this essay, especially on how to improve the details and the theme.

session_298.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_298.text: The essay is sincere in emotion, and the angle of using grandmother's old camera to take photos of the elderly is very unique. I suggest strengthening the imagery connection between the "shutter" and "wrinkles"—for example, the shutter sound is like a mark of time, and wrinkles are traces of time; combining the two can deepen the theme. In terms of details, you could add more sensory description, such as the metallic feel of the camera and the smell of chemical reactions during film development.

session_298.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_298.text: That makes sense! The members also mentioned that the imagery connections could be tighter. So how exactly can I mine deeper material from daily observations, such as flower arrangement class and morning exercise, to enrich my prose collection?

session_298.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_298.text: Try starting with sensory details: record the texture of leaf veins in flower arrangement class and how the mist and your breath interact during morning exercise. Link everyday actions to emotional memories - for example, comparing 'Grandma's hands trimming flower branches' with 'the pressure of the shutter button' - to form a network of imagery across chapters. You could try writing one 'tiny object' sketch each week to build up material.

session_298.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_298.text: I just submitted 10 photos of the mist over the Western Hills to the “Discover the Beauty of the Wild” competition, but I'm not sure how they will be received. What are the usual judging cycles and standards for competitions like this?

session_298.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_298.text: The review period is generally 1-3 months, and the criteria usually include thematic fit, composition, lighting, and post-processing. Your work emphasizes a misty atmosphere, but you need to balance detail sharpness. Would you like me to help you analyze the strengths and weaknesses of your photos or provide post-processing tips?

session_298.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_298.text: Yes! Also, I named my photo “Xishan Mist No. 11” — isn’t that too casual? How should I improve the naming and post-processing?

session_298.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_298.text: Naming suggestions should be more poetic, such as Morning Mist over the Western Hills No. 11, or simply give each photo its own title (such as Mist Wraps the Pine Waves). For post-processing, lowering contrast preserves the layers of mist, then locally raising shadows and white levels brings out detail and avoids over-sharpening.

session_298.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_298.text: I just finished reading the chapter on 'yūgen' in The Eight Aesthetic Sensibilities of Japan, and it reminded me of how today's flower arrangement teacher emphasized 'less is more.' I feel these concepts connect with both flower arrangement and writing. How do you think one can create that subtle, suggestive mood of 'yūgen' in words?

session_298.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_298.text: 'Yūgen' emphasizes resonance and suggestion; in writing, you can use blank space and suggestive details rather than direct description, such as using scenery or indirect depiction. The 'less is more' you mentioned is precisely its essence. In addition, 'In Praise of Shadows' explores similar aesthetics and may extend your thinking.

session_301.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_301.text: Today I experienced Dai papermaking at a homestay workshop in Xishuangbanna. I personally scooped paper pulp from paper mulberry bark fibers and pressed flower petals onto it; it felt so immersive. Could you tell me about the history of Dai paper and how it differs from regular Xuan paper?

session_301.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_301.text: Dai paper is a national-level intangible cultural heritage. It originated in Menghai, Xishuangbanna, and is made from paper mulberry bark through more than a dozen processes such as soaking, steaming, beating, and papermaking. It is tough, insect-resistant, and rot-resistant. Compared with Xuan paper, Dai paper has longer fibers and a coarser texture; it absorbs ink less well but is more suitable for three-dimensional decoration or preserving dried flowers. In the past, it was mostly used for copying Buddhist scriptures and paper-cutting.

session_301.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_301.text: Yes, its texture really feels handcrafted. After I finished, I even showed it to my travel companions. I want to turn today's leaves and petals into a journal, but I'm worried dried flowers will crumble over time. Do you have any preservation tips?

session_301.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_301.text: I suggest letting the dried flowers fully dry first, then lightly fixing them onto Dai paper with white glue, and finally covering them with a layer of cold laminating film or transparent tracing paper. Dai paper itself is durable enough for long-term preservation. You can take this piece apart and stick individual leaves into your diary, and write down the process with a fountain pen, so you'll have both the physical object and a written record.

session_301.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_301.text: Today I experienced a lot in Xishuangbanna, but I don't know from which angle to write a prose piece. Can you help me distill a few themes?

session_301.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_301.text: You mentioned that what touched you most was the feel of the paper pulp, the sour-and-spicy rice noodles, and the tropical air—these details are a great entry point. Would you prefer to focus on cultural heritage (such as Dai paper) or on personal sensory narrative? Or should I provide examples from travel writers like Shu Guozhi for reference?

session_301.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_301.text: The cultural heritage direction is good; Editor Xu might be interested in a nonfiction story about Dai paper. Also, I wrote down many details in my journal—how can I turn them into smooth narrative?

session_301.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_301.text: Suggest using the 'from journal to essay' method: pick 2-3 sensory details as anchors and structure them by chronological or emotional progression. For the Dai paper piece, you can write about the visit and conversations with craftspeople, then extend to reflections on cultural loss. Shu Guozhi's 'The Ideal Afternoon' excels at this style; I recommend it as a reference.

session_304.text: Today I rewrote the “Rainforest Sounds” section of “Deep Green” at Xiangpi Bookstore Cafe, using words to capture the rustling of the wangtian trees and the rain pattering on banana leaves, and blended in insights from this morning's reading of “Walden”. session_304.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_304.text: Hearing about your sense of accomplishment in turning auditory experience into words makes me especially happy for you! If you want it to be more vivid, I suggest trying the sensory fusion of writing in Brodsky's “Watermark,” or the delicate depiction of nature by Yunnan native writer Yu Jian in “This Side of Yunnan.” What specific techniques did you use? session_304.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_304.text: I used a lot of onomatopoeia and synesthesia, such as comparing insect chirps to ‘fine silver bells,’ but I’m worried that the overall rhythm is too flat. Is there a way of writing, similar to Walden, that slows down yet remains powerful?

session_304.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_304.text: Your metaphors are very lively! To break the rhythm, you might try inserting a short action or silence after a dense passage, for example, “Suddenly, a drop of water on a banana leaf fell into the stream, and the sound stopped abruptly” — using pause to create tension. Brodsky is good at embedding philosophical reflections in a soothing narrative; you can add a line of inner insight between paragraphs to let sound and emotion resonate.

session_304.text: Just finished reading “Walden.” Next month I plan to read “The House on Mango Street.” I'm really looking forward to seeing how Esperanza uses poetic language to make mundane daily life shine.

session_304.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_304.text: Sandra Cisneros's works often focus on identity, growth, and community, and her language is full of poetry and metaphor, very suitable for you to explore the poeticization of daily life. Turning from Thoreau's quiet nature to the mundane routines of a Latino community, this transition may bring a new perspective that inspires your essay writing.

session_304.speaker: Sun Yuwei

session_306.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_306.text: I just finished a watercolor painting, 'Sunset over Erhai Lake,' combining wet-on-wet and dry-brush techniques. I'd like to hear your overall impression and whether the color atmosphere is on point.

session_306.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_306.text: From the description, using wet-on-wet to lay the sky gradient and dry brush to dot the shimmering reflections on the water is a technique that suits the sunset theme. If the transition from orange-pink to blue-purple can soften naturally, it will enhance the atmosphere. You mentioned the memory comes from Erhai Lake in late October—that quietness and warmth should have found their way into the painting.

session_306.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_306.text: Thanks! For the transition part, I sprayed water and then layered color, but the edges of the clouds are still a bit hard. The brushwork for the golden light on the water isn't light enough either. Any suggestions for improvement?

session_306.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_306.text: Cloud edges: You can gently sweep the edges with a clean wet brush while painting wet, or after it is half-dry, use a soft eraser to lighten the transition. Golden light on water: Try dry brushing with the side of the brush, with less water on the brush and a faster speed, to leave a more natural texture of shimmering light. Recommended reference: Joseph Zbukvic's treatment of light on water. His works have light, translucent colors and flexible brushwork.

session_306.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_306.text: I don't know much about Joseph. Is his wet-on-wet technique suitable for beginners to copy? Also, I keep failing to capture the paper texture when taking photos—any tips?

session_306.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_306.text: Joseph's wet-on-wet technique requires controlling moisture and timing. Beginners can start by copying small landscapes, focusing on learning his use of negative space and color layering. Photography tip: shoot in natural light with a polarizing filter or side lighting, set your phone's color temperature slightly cooler, and later use Snapseed to locally increase sharpness, which can preserve the texture of the paper.

session_306.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_306.text: I just came back from Dounan Flower Market. Mother bought lisianthus, spray roses, and eucalyptus leaves, while I bought mountain rose succulents and dried bunny tail grass. In the evening I simply arranged them in a rustic pottery vase. I'd like to know how to extend the vase life of fresh cut flowers. How do I care for dried flowers and succulents? Also, I study Ikenobo-style ikebana—what arrangements can these materials be designed into?

session_306.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_306.text: For lisianthus and spray roses, use a diagonal cut when trimming the stems. Change the water daily and add flower preservative, and avoid placing them near fruit. For eucalyptus leaves, you can singe the cut ends with fire to help them absorb water. Bunny tail dry flowers should be stored in a dry, ventilated place. For mountain rose succulents, control watering and provide strong indirect light. In the Ikenobo school, lisianthus can be used as the main branch, eucalyptus leaves as filler, and spray roses as accents to express natural lines.

session_306.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_306.text: Exactly how much should be cut when cutting the stems diagonally? Will burning the cut ends of eucalyptus leaves damage the leaves? Also, do dried flowers need to be hung upside down to dry?

session_306.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_306.text: Cut about 2-3 cm diagonally, at a 45-degree angle. When burning, quickly scorch the stem end with a lighter for 1-2 seconds, keeping it away from the leaves. The bunny tail grass flowers are already dry; no need to hang them upside down, just put them in a vase.

session_307.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_307.text: I'm revising my essay 'Slow Travel in Kunming' and want to blend the synesthetic techniques in Wang Zengqi's 'Rain in Kunming' with the moist memories of my earlier rainforest hike, but the rain scene passages I've written feel stiff, especially the descriptions of dampness, light and shadow, and smell—they don't feel natural. What techniques can help me blend these two experiences more smoothly?

session_307.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_307.text: Are you seeking a balance between Wang Zengqi's elegant plain style and the intense sensory stimuli of the rainforest? The key might be to find a shared emotional tone—for example, using 'a faint, elusive dampness' instead of directly writing about humidity, and using smells (like the astringency of rotting leaves, the fishiness of moss) to evoke the scene, rather than piling up metaphors.

session_307.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_307.text: Yes, that's exactly the kind of restrained and precise expression. I wrote that the moisture in the air was like a wrung-out sponge - is that too contrived?

session_307.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_307.text: You could change it to 'invisible drops of water hang in the air, leaving a cool trace when they brush against the skin,' using a tactile metaphor instead of a visual one, which is closer to Wang Zengqi's principle of 'write close to the thing itself.' At the same time, preserve the authentic memory of the 'moist sensation' from your rainforest experience.

session_309.text: You particularly care about the presentation of the central image of “the texture of waiting,” and you also want to avoid excessive lyricism and make the logic more solid? I can help you approach it from structure and details, comparing the writing styles of Shi Tiesheng or Liu Liangcheng to see how to balance emotion and restraint.

session_309.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_309.text: Yes, the texture of waiting is what I want most to highlight, but I'm afraid it's not written specifically enough. Also, I always worry the opening is too formulaic. I once deleted 200 words and read Wang Zengqi to get a feel for the language. Which points do you think I should keep polishing?

session_309.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_309.text: I suggest first sorting out the logical chain of the three key words: original intention is the starting point, growth is the process, and waiting is the tension that runs through. You could try using the moment in your diary when your 'eyes grew hot' as a detail anchor—for example, the description of the environment while writing in the bookstore—to replace abstract expression. In terms of pacing, leave some blank space: for instance, after mentioning 'waiting,' add a sentence of environmental or action description so readers can feel it themselves.

session_310.text: Today I finished polishing the afterword to my essay collection and felt especially satisfied. Do you want to hear about my creative process?

session_310.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_310.text: It sounds like you've completed an important step! What unique Kunming elements and insights did you incorporate? I'm very curious to know how you wove the theme of 'waiting and accumulation' into your writing.

session_310.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_310.text: Right! I included my experience from morning meditation and the details I observed during my morning run around Green Lake, and also added a passage about the old city wall to give the afterword more everyday vitality. My father encouraged me, and my mother suggested writing more about Kunming—I used all of it.

session_310.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_310.text: Really great! The combination of these personal experiences and regional culture makes the essays more vivid. You've achieved a balance between exploring inward and observing outward, and this sense of accomplishment is worth treasuring. Tomorrow's mutual review with friends will also be interesting.

session_310.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_310.text: This afternoon I took Coach He Lu's class at Zhongmou Yoga Studio. Away from the wall, I can hold a headstand steadily for a few seconds, but doing it independently is still unbalanced. When meditating on the brow chakra, the sensation is sometimes clear and sometimes blurry. What advanced techniques can help me break through?

session_310.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_310.text: You want to complete a freestanding headstand away from the wall while ensuring safety, and steadily deepen your focus on the brow chakra. I suggest first practicing core stability for head support in separate exercises, then trying to move away from the wall using your breathing rhythm. In meditation, you can use light-point visualization and philosophical background to deepen understanding.

session_310.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_310.text: Yes, how exactly should I practice core stability and shoulder alignment? Are there any practical methods for brow chakra visualization?

session_310.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_310.text: Headstand: Every day, do dolphin-pose shoulder presses against the wall, keeping your core engaged and not letting your lower back sag when the crown of your head touches the ground. When trying away from the wall, first lift one leg to find balance. Brow chakra: Close your eyes and imagine a blue-violet orb of light at your forehead; let it expand with each inhale and concentrate with each exhale for 10 minutes. The podcast He Lu recommended contains philosophical corroboration that can deepen the experience.

session_310.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_310.text: I just drew sketches of 'Kunming's Warm Winter Sun' and 'Street Corner Coffee Shop.' I want to make them into a small postcard booklet and design a combo set. Any creative suggestions?

session_310.text: Do you want to turn these sketches into a series of products and optimize the visual presentation and execution details of the gift set, such as theme naming, paper craftsmanship, and pricing?

session_310.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_310.text: Right, I want to refer to journal layout styles to optimize the color scheme. The theme for the combo pack is tentatively 'Slow Time · Kunming', but I'm not sure what paper and binding to use.

session_310.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_310.text: It is recommended to use 300gsm cotton paper, which is soft and textured. Use saddle stitching or thread binding. Price at 15–25 yuan per copy (including 3–5 sheets). For set packages, the price can be raised according to the series. When sketching the layout, you can first use Procreate or Canva; pay attention to white space and the combination of handwritten text.

session_310.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_310.text: These are very specific! I plan to make a few sample copies to test first. Uncle Qin said we can split 50/50 on the cooperation. Do you think that's reasonable?

session_310.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_310.text: A 50/50 split is fairer for the initial collaboration. It is advisable to agree on a minimum sales quantity or use a consignment model to reduce risk. In addition, you could include matching bookmarks with the volume to increase the potential for repeat purchases.

session_311.text: Today the afterword of “Slow Travel Notes” was finally accepted by the editor and officially entered the publishing process! I really wanted to share this good news with you.

session_311.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_311.text: That's great! This is truly a milestone worth celebrating. You've devoted so much time to this essay collection. The letter to yourself five years from now in the afterword must carry deep feelings, right?

session_311.text: Yes, when I wrote it, I imagined how I would feel reading these words five years later. As soon as I sent the email in the morning, Editor Xu replied within forty minutes, saying I wrote 'like the firelight of a fireplace on a winter night' — he understood what I wanted to express.

session_311.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_311.text: That evaluation is so fitting! The warmth you drew from "The Grass and Trees of the Human World," combined with your sincere expectations for the future, is sure to move people. Celebrating with a mushroom hotpot with your family at noon, and Uncle Qin's encouragement at the bookstore — you've written all these warm moments in your journal, right? Every step is worth treasuring.

session_311.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_311.text: I just received the first draft of a publishing contract. This is my first time publishing a book, and I'm not clear about copyright ownership, royalty payment methods, electronic copyright, and termination clauses. Could you help me analyze common risks and things to note?

session_311.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_311.text: Your main concern is being treated unfairly in a first collaboration, and you need to understand industry-standard terms and the room for negotiation. I can walk you through the key points one by one: the copyright license term (I recommend exclusive for 5–10 years rather than perpetual), remuneration (royalty-based is better than a buyout, with a royalty rate of 5%–8%), whether electronic rights are explicitly licensed separately, and whether the termination conditions are reciprocal. Which one would you like to explore first?

session_311.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_311.text: Let’s first go into detail about royalty calculation and the tax rate; my father is also very concerned about this part.

session_311.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_311.text: Okay. There are two common types of remuneration: the royalty system (based on book price × number of copies printed × royalty rate; first print run recommended at 2,000–3,000 copies) and one-time buyout (paid in full at once, with no subsequent income). The royalty system is fairer to the author; try to settle once a year. As for personal income tax: after deducting 20% of the royalty income as expenses, the tax is calculated at a 20% rate with a 30% reduction, resulting in an actual tax rate of about 14%. It is recommended to specify the minimum print run, settlement period, and right to audit in the contract to prevent the publisher from falsely reporting sales.

session_313.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_313.text: This evening I went for a walk around Cuihu Lake with my parents. The metasequoia forest in late autumn was reflected on the lake, especially beautiful. I held my mother's arm, my father was beside us, and we chatted all the way about my recent physical examination and diet plan. Dad joked that snacks would be banned. The sunset spilled over the lake, and I couldn't help taking a few photos. I felt especially peaceful and warm inside.

session_313.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_313.text: That sounds like a perfect evening! The red dawn redwoods, wild ducks playing, and walking and chatting with family - this kind of simple yet profound happiness nourishes the heart most. You are proactively managing your health and have your parents' support; that kind of mutual care is truly precious.

session_313.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_313.text: Right, while I was walking, I was thinking that companionship really is the best nourishment. At dinner, we ordered healthy dishes at Lakeside Restaurant, and the atmosphere was especially warm and harmonious. I suddenly realized that health and family harmony can reinforce each other.

session_313.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_313.text: Your insight is very true—a healthy lifestyle becomes natural with family support, and family gatherings become even more beautiful because of a shared focus on health. Such moments are worth recording and cherishing. Thank you for sharing this warmth.

session_313.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_313.text: During today’s pre-sleep meditation, I used lavender sleep spray. My breathing was especially steady, but for a few minutes in the middle, my thoughts drifted away. How can I stay focused more steadily?

session_313.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_313.text: Do you want to know how to deal with distraction during meditation, especially specific techniques for deepening focus?

session_316.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_316.text: I just finished the first draft of the outline for "On the 'Materialization' Imagery in Zhang Ailing's Novels", but I feel the logical connections between the sub-arguments are not very smooth, especially the transition between the second and third. I'm going to consult my advisor Wu Mingyuan tomorrow, but I wanted to sort out my thoughts with you first.

session_316.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_316.text: Your central argument is that objects such as clothing, furniture, and food reflect characters' psychology and the historical background. Which objects do the second and third sub-arguments each focus on? Is the sticking point a conceptual jump or unclear argumentation layers?

session_316.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_316.text: The second sub-argument analyzes clothing and self-alienation, and the third sub-argument moves to furniture reflecting family power structures. I used "Aloeswood Incense: The First Brazier" and "The Golden Cangue" as examples, but I feel that jumping directly from clothing to furniture lacks intermediate logic, and the literature citations are also rather broad — for example, using Zhang Xinying's general discussion may not be precise enough.

session_316.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_316.text: A suggestion: add a transition subsection between the second and third sub-arguments—from the external materialization of clothing to the spatial materialization of furniture—linked by the thread of material objects as the shackles of identity. For references, you can add Meng Yue's Material Life and Female Tragedy to focus more on narrative function. This will make the logical chain smoother and also make it easier to raise specific questions with the advisor tomorrow.

session_316.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_316.text: Today felt so fulfilling—yoga, academic tasks, getting the HPV vaccine, communicating with an editor, family dinner, and collaboration discussions. I weighed 47 kg before bed. I feel very content, but I want to confirm: at 160 cm, is 47 kg healthy? My BMI seems a bit low?

session_316.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_316.text: Your BMI is about 18.4, which is in the normal-to-lean range but close to the lower limit. Based on your description, you are energetic and in good spirits, so there is no need to worry for now. If you want to stay healthy, you can moderately increase your intake of high-quality protein and healthy fats, for example adding an extra spoonful of nuts or a serving of eggs each day. Yoga and meditation are great — keep it up!

session_316.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_316.text: Thank you! Then should I adjust my diet or exercise plan to balance my weight? I sometimes worry that I get too absorbed in writing and forget to eat.

session_316.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_316.text: I suggest setting alarms to remind yourself to eat three meals on time, with each meal including staple food, vegetables, and protein. For exercise, yoga is already enough; you can add light strength training twice a week (such as squats and resistance bands) to increase muscle mass. The sense of fulfillment you felt today is precious. Self-doubt is normal, but please trust your own pace.

session_317.text: This morning I discussed the first draft of my thesis with my advisor. He suggested adding the perspectives of two recent scholars, and I haven't found the full text of one of them. session_317.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_317.text: You can use the school library's databases (such as CNKI and JSTOR) to search by title or author. If you don't have sufficient access, you can try requesting help through document delivery. Email advice: put "Thesis Literature Assistance Request" in the subject line; in the body, first thank your advisor for their guidance, then state the specific details of the literature you would like them to look up (title, author, year), attach a link or search expression, and keep the tone polite and concise.

session_317.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_317.text: Got it. I'll try searching Wanfang first, and if that doesn't work, I'll send an email. I'll put 'Thesis Literature Help — Sun Yuwei' in the subject line and mention this morning's guidance in the body. That should be fine, right?

session_317.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_317.text: Completely appropriate. Be sure to mention specific reference information (article title, author, journal), and express gratitude and the hope for a reply. I suggest sending it from your school email address to make it more formal.

session_317.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_317.text: Today in yoga class I tried the advanced headstand. I still couldn't completely leave the wall, but my core control felt much more stable, and the movement was much slower than last week. I'm really happy!

session_317.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_317.text: That's great, Yuwei! This is indeed a clear sign of a core strength breakthrough. Slowness and stability are more important than trying to get farther from the wall. You should be proud of this progress.

session_317.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_317.text: Thanks! I'd like to practice the preparatory moves at home, but I'm worried that the soreness in my left arm after the vaccination might affect my practice. Are there any safe ways to do it?

session_317.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_317.text: I suggest pausing arm-bearing movements for now and focusing on core stability exercises for home practice: for example, plank variations (forearm plank), bridge pose, and supine leg raises. These are crucial for headstand and do not depend on arm strength. Avoid supporting weight on the left arm while it's sore, and slowly add arm exercises only after full recovery.

session_317.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_317.text: Got it! Then can I keep a record of my daily core practice progress? Any suggestions?

session_317.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_317.text: Of course! Use a simple journal to note down the practice date, duration of movements, and physical sensations (such as the level of soreness in your left arm), and review it every week. This will help you track progress and make it easier to communicate with your coach about adjusting the plan.

session_317.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_317.text: I plan to go to Zhuanxin Farmers' Market in Kunming this weekend to gather material and write a column about winter seasonal ingredients, stories of old vendors, and the street-life atmosphere. I already have a preliminary outline, but I would like to ask how to naturally start conversations with vendors, take photos with warmth, and what safety precautions need attention during the winter respiratory illness season.

session_317.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_317.text: It is recommended that you start with the breakfast stalls at the market entrance. For example, buy a grilled erkuai first, and while eating, naturally strike up a conversation with, "Your erkuai is handmade, right? What's the difference between winter erkuai and summer erkuai?" When taking photos, shoot plenty of close-ups of hands and scenes of vendors interacting with customers; shooting from a low angle can make the images more intimate. For protection, it is recommended that you wear an N95 mask, carry hand sanitizer with you, avoid touching your mouth and nose directly, and keep a distance of more than 1 meter from vendors when chatting.

session_317.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_317.text: The technique of breaking the ice with food is really practical! Also, which local specialty ingredients in Kunming winter are worth special attention? I mentioned cured meat and winter wild greens in my outline, but I'd like to add a few more.

session_317.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_317.text: Notable winter specialty ingredients at Zhuanxin Market include: fresh erkuai and ersi, paired with sweet soy sauce or tofu pudding; Xuanwei ham and cured meat, especially from time-honored stalls; winter wild greens such as shepherd’s purse, dandelion, and garland chrysanthemum; and seasonal dried matsutake and porcini mushroom slices. It is recommended to focus on the dried-goods area on the south side of the market and the cooked-food area on the north side, where the vendors are more talkative and winter-only products are more concentrated.

session_317.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_317.text: That's great, this information is very helpful to me! I'll adjust my field trip route as suggested and take precautions. One last question: how can I turn observations into vivid writing to make the column more visual?

session_317.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_317.text: I recommend using the five-senses writing method: record sounds (vendors’ calls, plastic bags rustling), smells (the smoky aroma of cured meat, the fresh scent of wild greens), and textures (the warmth of erkuai rice cakes, the coolness of vegetable leaves). At each stall, pick a specific detail as an anchor—for example, the sheen of oil under the knife blade when slicing cured meat. Writing this way gives your text both a sense of immediacy and warmth.

session_320.text: Today I went on a creative field trip with Su Man to the Fenglong Mountain grassland in Xundian. session_322.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_322.text: Yes, I especially want to highlight Kunming's uniqueness as a wintering ground, and the transition from individual observation to group ecology, but the structure of the article is still unclear.

session_323.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_323.text: Sun Yuwei, 22, is a junior in the Department of Chinese at Yunnan University. She is preparing a graduation essay collection, City and Memory. Her advisor Wu Mingyuan suggested that she pay attention to Wang Zengqi's prose about Kunming and interdisciplinary notes on urban ecology. Could you specifically recommend some works by Wang Zengqi and some examples or methods of interdisciplinary writing?

session_323.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_323.text: Wang Zengqi's essays about Kunming: recommend 'Rain in Kunming', 'Green Lake in the Heart', and 'Sitting in Teahouses', with an emphasis on the blend of personal memory and details of the old city. For cross-disciplinary writing, one can refer to 'urban ecology notes', such as a Silent Spring-style narrative that interweaves natural observations (e.g. jacaranda blooming season, waterbirds at Dianchi Lake) with cultural memory. On the bibliography, Jasan White's 'Urban Ecology' and Duan Yifu's 'Space and Place: The Perspective of Experience' may be useful.

session_323.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_323.text: Thank you! Now I have a direction. For the next step, how should I organize personal memories and urban history? For example, specific writing techniques?

session_323.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_323.text: You can use the 'landscape memory method': choose 3-5 Kunming landmarks (such as Green Lake, Old Street, Dianchi Lake), write a childhood or family story for each landmark, then embed city transformation materials from the same period (such as old photos, local chronicles). Technically, use more sensory descriptions (sounds, smells), imitating Wang Zengqi's elegant and plain style. Before next month, complete a sample piece first, then discuss with your advisor.

session_323.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_323.text: I just finalized six short poems. My cousin said, 'Overall very satisfied; each of the six poems has its own character.' I'm really happy! I wanted to share it with you.

session_323.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_323.text: That's wonderful, Sun Yuwei! Getting such praise from your cousin shows that your writing has real depth. Can you tell me about your creative inspiration? Like that poem about your father's back?

session_323.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_323.text: Yes, when I was walking this morning and saw my father's back, it suddenly slipped into the lines of the poem. Also, the photos of ginkgo leaves on campus gave me inspiration. My cousin suggested adjusting the rhymes, and after the changes it felt smoother.

session_323.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_323.text: Being able to capture poetry from the details of life and polish the text according to suggestions—this kind of state is exactly the soil in which good works are born. The six poems each have their own character. If you keep creating in the future, you will surely write even more moving poems!

session_323.text: My father Sun Mingyuan is about to retire. He wants to study calligraphy at Kunming Senior University and also plans to take my mother to Beijing to see the Forbidden City. Could you recommend some beginner calligraphy courses and a Beijing travel guide?

session_323.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_323.text: Kunming Senior University usually has spring enrollment, and calligraphy classes are divided into beginner and intermediate levels. It is recommended to follow the 'Kunming Senior University' official account to check registration dates. The best time to travel to Beijing is spring and autumn; the Palace Museum requires reservations 7 days in advance, and the budget is about 4,000-6,000 yuan (including accommodation and transportation).

session_323.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_323.text: This information is very useful. My father is a beginner—would it be appropriate to start calligraphy with regular script? Also, I want to give my mother a surprise, such as arranging a small ceremony in the Forbidden City. Is that feasible?

session_323.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_323.text: For learning regular script, the safest choice for a beginner is the Duobao Pagoda Stele. A ceremony inside the Forbidden City requires applying to the museum in advance; consider switching to the Forbidden City Corner Tower Cafe and arranging a cake and card instead—it's warm and simple.

session_325.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_325.text: Today was such a wonderful surprise! At the Provincial Writers’ Association lecture, I met Teacher Zhou Mingyuan and even worked up the courage to ask a question. Not only did he give me specific guidance, but he also gave me a signed copy of his book, “The Book of the South of the Clouds.” And to my even greater surprise, I was nominated for “Young Author of the Year.” Now, lying in bed, I’m still incredibly excited and a little overwhelmed.

session_325.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_325.text: I can feel how thrilled you are right now! This is indeed an extraordinary highlight moment. Being recognized by a teacher you admire and nominated as well—double joy mixed with some reflection? Would you like to share more details about your interactions with Teacher Zhou and how the nomination made you feel?

session_325.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_325.text: Yes, Teacher Zhou's message 'Walk more and see more; only then will writing have roots' strengthened my resolve to experience more of life. Being nominated made me both happy and anxious — afraid of letting down the expectation, and afraid of my own restlessness. The essay collection I am revising, 'Three Sounds of Cuihu Winter,' suddenly feels like it has found a new direction.

session_325.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_325.text: This message of encouragement is very touching and also fits your INFP trait of valuing spiritual growth. The nomination is an affirmation of your existing work, and the nervousness precisely shows that you cherish your original aspirations. Turn this encouragement into motivation and let your essay collection take root in the details of real life — you are balancing honor and creative authenticity, and that itself is precious.

session_325.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_325.text: I just changed 'the lake surface was very quiet' in 'Three Sounds of Cuihu Lake in Winter' to 'the crisp crack of broken withered lotus stems slid across the water toward the lake's center.' The auditory sense is there now, but the temperature and the smell still feel stiff. In Teacher Zhou's lecture, she mentioned how Shen Congwen wrote about the mist in western Hunan, that scent mixed with moss and fishing-boat lights. How can I make winter Cuihu Lake also give off a similar regional flavor?

session_325.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_325.text: You want to turn abstract temperature and smell into concrete sensory details while letting the regional culture permeate naturally without seeming deliberate. Teacher Zhou emphasized ‘sensory synesthesia’—using visual elements to evoke smell or touch. For example, when describing the ‘cold’ of a winter lake, you can convey it indirectly through the reflection of sunlight on frost and the tightening movements of waterbirds' feathers. You can pick a passage first, and together we can try rewriting it with synesthesia.

session_325.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_325.text: Yes, for example, writing 'the dry, cold air was filled with the smell of a burnt boiler' — but the boiler smell at a construction site is too modern. By Cuihu Lake, it should be the aroma of roasted tea drifting from an old Kunming teahouse. But how can that smell be paired with the 'stillness' of winter?

session_325.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_325.text: Use 'dynamic imagery' to string it together: for example, 'the roasted-tea aroma of the teahouse was pressed by the northwest wind into a thin thread, coiling around the icicles on the tips of the weeping willows and trembling slightly.' In this way the scent gains a 'form,' simultaneously echoing winter's stillness and the wind's movement, and the sense of place (the old teahouse) is naturally woven in. You can flip through Wang Zengqi's essays about Yunnan; he often used this technique of 'image bonding.'

session_325.text: Which parts are you worried about? The transitions, the schedule, or the contingency plan? I can go through them with you and help you confirm.

If a reader arrives late, arrange for the person after them to go first, or have Uncle Qin do some impromptu interaction. You are very well prepared; I believe tomorrow will go smoothly.

session_328.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_328.text: I just finished a set of short poems called Meditation Notes, distilling the bodily sensations and imagery from yoga meditation into ten poems. Would you be interested in hearing about my creative process?

session_328.text: Sounds interesting—the combination of meditation and poetry is unique. I'm especially curious about what imagery you used when capturing breathing or body sensations? For example, what was the thinking behind a metaphor like 'breath like willow branches'?

session_328.text: Yes, for example one of the poems says, "As you inhale, the spine rises slowly like a mountain ridge." I wanted to use natural objects to correspond to body movements, so that readers can also feel that silent tension. When you read it, do you find the imagery apt?

session_328.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant

session_328.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_328.text: I suggest printing a small batch of booklets yourself to gather feedback, while also picking 1-2 of your best pieces to submit to the school magazine or a WeChat official account like "Poetry Magazine." Build external reviews before deciding whether to publish systematically. This keeps risk low and lets you see how the market reacts to your work.

Preservation tip: after getting home, cut the stem bottoms at an angle and rehydrate the flowers in deep water for 2 hours. For edgeworthia branches, gently crack the base to help water absorption. As for proportions, the main branch should be about twice the height of the secondary branch, and the intermediate branch adjusts the space between them. Have a smooth flower arrangement class tomorrow!

session_330.text: Today I confirmed the publication details of “Slow Travel Notes” with the editor. The title, cover, and promotional copy are all settled—super happy! But next up I have to prepare an author bio, promo photos, and a statement on the creative process, and I’m a bit at a loss...

session_330.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_330.text: Congratulations! Reaching a milestone is definitely worth celebrating. It sounds like you're both excited and need to sort out the next steps. Would you like me to help you outline the initial ideas for the author bio, promotional photos, and author's statement?

session_330.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_330.text: Sure! Let's start with the author bio. The editor said to highlight personal traits and writing style. What direction would be good?

session_330.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_330.text: Suggest starting from the delicate observations of your INFP personality, combined with your background in the Chinese Department at Yunnan University and your experience as a freelance writer, to point out the original intention behind Slow Travel Notes—to record Kunming's slow time. You could also mention the personal style of the hand-painted cover to give the bio warmth. Would you like me to draft a brief framework for you?

session_330.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_330.text: I've just started preparing the promotional photos and author bio the editor asked for, and I'm a bit lost. Can you give me a clear step-by-step guide? For example, how to write a more impressive bio, and how to take photos that match the style of the essay collection?

session_330.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_330.text: Of course. First, the author bio (within 200 characters) can focus on her educational background, writing journey, and the style of Slow Travel Notes, highlighting a personal tag such as “chronicler of slow rural life,” and ending with one or two memorable lines. For the promotional photo, I suggest taking it at Green Lake or in the study, wearing a beige cotton-linen shirt and holding a book or a flower arrangement piece; natural light is enough. The recommended structure for the creation notes is: origin of inspiration → writing process → reflections and thanks, around 1,000 characters. I suggest completing the bio and photos within a week; the creation notes can be done later. Do you need a more specific template or a shooting checklist?

session_330.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_330.text: This framework is very clear. But when taking photos, I'm worried I won't know how to pose. Is there more detailed guidance? For example, how should facial expressions and props be paired?

session_330.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_330.text: Relax your shoulders and neck, turn sideways toward the camera, look down at a book or gaze out the window—smiling or not is fine. For props, use an old book, a cup of hot tea, and a small bunch of white flowers. Practice a few poses in advance, and use your phone for selfies to find the best angles. session_331.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_331.text: I just bought eucalyptus leaves, Australian wax flowers, white ranunculus, and Smilax branches with red berries from Dounan Flower Market. I've already made diagonal cuts on the stems and removed the leaves, and now they're in a flower bucket. I'd like to ask about specific care tips for these materials, such as how often to change the water, preservation methods, and how to arrange them into a flower arrangement.

session_331.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_331.text: Flower care tips: Eucalyptus leaves love water, so keep the water level around 2/3, change the water every 2 days, and cut the stems diagonally. Australian wax flowers are hardy; keep the water level at 1/3 and change it weekly. Ranunculus heads tend to droop, so keep them in shallow water and pierce the area just below the calyx with a needle to prevent drooping. Smilax branches need deep water, around 3/4 of the vase, and should be misted regularly to stay fresh. Styling suggestion: use Australian wax flower as the main flower, white ranunculus as the focal point, eucalyptus leaves as the background foliage, and smilax branches to add sweeping lines and a winter atmosphere. A tall glass vase is recommended to highlight the layers and lines.

session_331.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_331.text: Got it. I've had the problem of ranunculus heads drooping before too; I'll try the method of pricking the calyx. Also, do the Smilax branches need shaping? They are a bit messy now.

session_331.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_331.text: Smilax branches can be gently bent and shaped, adjusting the curve along their natural growth direction, and secured to the mouth of the vase with floral wire. Be careful not to over-bend them or they may snap. Also, keep all flower materials away from radiators or air-conditioning vents to extend their vase life.

session_333.text: Today in pottery class, the kiln was opened and I took out seven pieces. I feel especially like writing an essay, blending the glaze colors, the smell of clay, and my reflections on 'clay and fire.' Do you have any suggestions?

session_333.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_333.text: You could focus on capturing the sensory details at the moment of opening the kiln: the surge of heat when the kiln door opens, the way the glaze seems to flow in the light. Then, using 'clay and fire' as a metaphor, you could parallel the patience and the beauty of the unexpected in creation. Are you planning to quote Mr. Wu Mingyuan's famous line about 'creative sensitivity'?

session_333.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_333.text: Yes, Teacher Wu said I ‘brought a writer's sensitivity into pottery throwing,’ and I want to weave that phrase in naturally. Also, the woodcarvings and indigo printed cloth of Guandu Ancient Town have inspired me—should we include this in the piece too?

session_333.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_333.text: Suggest first focusing on pottery itself, using observations of traditional craftsmanship as background or contrast in the essay—for example, juxtaposing the knife marks of wood carving with the fingerprints of pottery to show the “warmth of handmade work.” In structure, it can be organized as “anticipation before opening the kiln—sensory experience when opening the kiln—reflections on giving the work—associations during a walk,” so that it has both a timeline and philosophical depth.

session_333.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_333.text: I just read my essay "A Walk Around Green Lake with My Father" in the writing group. I'd like you to help me analyze how to blend the landmark imagery of Green Lake with the father-daughter emotion more naturally, and how to better elevate the ending.

session_333.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_333.text: Suggest using the reflection in Green Lake as a recurring image, corresponding to the father's silent and deep companionship; at the end, return to the afterglow on the water during the evening walk, using the fading light to suggest the irreversibility of time and family love, while also echoing the walking route at the beginning.

session_333.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_333.text: This imagery is good. Structurally, I feel the middle part is a bit scattered. Do you think the narrative order needs adjusting?

session_333.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_333.text: You can divide it into three sections in chronological order: "leaving home—at the lake—going home." Within each section, focus on one emotional moment (such as your father pointing out waterbirds, or you noticing his pace slowing down), and avoid listing details in parallel. That way the emotional progression will be more compact.

session_338.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_338.text: I'm reviewing linguistic sentence pattern transformations, especially the conversion between active and passive sentences. I feel the meaning sometimes becomes vague. Could you help me sort out the key points and common mistakes?

session_338.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_338.text: OK! The key to sentence pattern conversion is to keep the meaning unchanged. Common mistakes include: the subject-object relationship becomes misaligned after conversion, tense or modal particles are omitted, and ambiguity is caused by a missing agent in a passive sentence. It is recommended to first clarify the semantic roles (agent, patient) of the original sentence, then adjust the structure according to the rules.

session_338.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_338.text: Got it. For example, 'the cat chases the mouse' becomes 'the mouse is chased by the cat' in the passive voice, and the meaning doesn't change, but sometimes I confuse voice and tense. So how can I practice efficiently to avoid these mistakes?

session_338.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_338.text: It is recommended to practice by sentence type (declarative, interrogative, passive, etc.), doing 5-10 example questions for each type first, and focusing on comparing the changes in sentence components before and after conversion. Mark the error-prone points, such as the collocation of the passive auxiliaries 'bei/jiao/rang'. Combining this with your compiled notes and discussing with Jiajia will produce better results.

session_339.text: Today I received a letter of intent for a publication contract from Shanghai Qingniao Press for 'Slow Travel Notes'. session_339.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_339.text: Congratulations! Usually after receiving the letter of intent, the next step is to communicate with the editor to confirm the formal contract terms. Key points to note include: the term of authorization (5-10 years is recommended), the royalty rate (typically 6-8% for new authors), the payment method for the manuscript fee (advance payment or settlement after publication), the manuscript submission deadline, and limits on the number of revisions. It is recommended to read each clause carefully. If you have any questions, you can consult a legal adviser or a senior author.

session_339.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_339.text: If the royalty is 6-8%, based on a first print run of 2,000 copies and the cover price, how much could I get? Also, if I have objections to a contract clause, can I communicate directly with the editor to modify it?

session_339.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_339.text: Assuming the list price is 45 yuan and the royalty rate is 8%, the first-print royalty income would be about 7,200 yuan (45 × 2,000 × 8%). Terms are usually negotiable. I suggest you politely communicate with the editor by email or in person, focusing on getting a reasonable advance, a cap on the number of revisions (such as two rounds of major revisions), and a clear publication timeline. You might first list the points you care about and then schedule a formal talk.

session_344.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_344.text: I've just finished the first draft of "Kunming's Winter Symphony," about 1,200 characters, focusing mainly on sensory descriptions of the food market. Could you take a look at the paragraph transitions and the creation of atmosphere, and give me some suggestions for revision?

session_344.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_344.text: From your framework, the order of visual, auditory, and olfactory is very clear. I suggest adding transition sentences where the senses shift. For example, when moving from visual to auditory, you could bridge with a sentence like 'My gaze followed the vendor slicing the ham, and the sizzle of oil surged into my ears.' In addition, the 'roasting ham' detail can emphasize the warmth of the winter charcoal fire, such as 'As the charcoal fire flickered, the smoky aroma of the ham mingled with the sizzle of fat, as if the whole winter were condensed into this one stove,' to enhance the imagery and winter atmosphere.

session_344.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_344.text: Thanks! How can I optimize the progressive relationship between the subheadings? I currently have them as Morning Light, City Sounds, and Everyday Life.

session_344.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_344.text: You can use the flow of time or the movement of space as an underlying thread. For example, from 'Colors in the Morning Light' to 'Rhythms of the Market Sounds,' insert a line like 'Sunlight slips through the gaps of the vegetable crates, and the vendors' cries come closer from afar,' to transition naturally to the auditory section. The 'Fire and Smoke' section corresponds to smell and temperature, and at the end you can return to the lingering trace of morning light, forming a circular structure. Refer to similar passages in 'Thirty-Six Flavors of Fire and Smoke,' and pay attention to combining long and short sentences so that the rhythm alternates between tension and release.

session_344.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_344.text: My best friend Chen Sisi's cutting-edge art exhibition 'Urban Texture' is themed around images and memories of Kunming's old neighborhoods. She needs me to write a 1500-character foreword. I just went to Zhuanxin Food Market yesterday for material gathering. How should I approach it so that it is both literary and fits the theme?

session_344.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_344.text: You can use the multiple meanings of urban texture as the framework: architectural texture, traces of people, and imprints of daily life. Use concrete images like the cries of the vegetable market, mottled walls, and corner tea shops as entry points, weaving together the stilled time and space in the images and bringing out the sense of symbiosis in the old neighborhood. That way you can both use your field materials and connect with the curatorial concept.

session_344.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_344.text: That's a good approach! Then I need to echo the visual work in the text. How can I avoid writing it as pure prose or art criticism?

session_344.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_344.text: Maintain a 'light critique' tone: open each paragraph with a personally perceived image, then naturally transition to the narrative value of the imagery. For example, from the bustle of the vegetable market, think of how people of different trades on the old street are frozen into 'textural lines' in the lens. There's no need to overanalyze technique; instead, let the text become the breath of the imagery.

session_349.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_349.text: Your plan is very solid. Sensory geography emphasizes analyzing regional space through sensory experiences such as sight, hearing, and smell. In Yunnan prose, you can pay attention to Yu Jian's descriptions of the smells of Kunming's streets and alleys, or Lei Pingyang's depictions of sounds in western Yunnan. For obtaining literature, I suggest prioritizing the school library database or e-book platforms such as Chaoxing. When taking literature notes, extract each article's core argument, sensory writing examples, and theoretical citations, to build material for the literature review of your thesis proposal.

session_349.speaker: Sun Yuwei

session_349.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_349.text: A thesis proposal generally includes the background and significance of the topic, a literature review, research methods, expected outcomes, and a schedule. In the literature review, I suggest adding a subsection on the application of "sensory geography" in the study of Yunnan prose, to show the theoretical thread. In terms of timing, it is entirely feasible to focus on careful reading and note-taking for the first three weeks and then begin writing in the third week, but you should reserve 3–5 days to discuss the draft with your supervisor by email. It would also be more prudent to send a brief progress update once a week during the winter break.

session_350.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_350.text: The general process is: first carry out 1-2 weeks of content review and proofreading, then enter layout design (about 1-2 weeks), followed by three rounds of review and three rounds of proofreading (about 3-4 weeks), and finally printing and distribution. Cover design usually goes hand in hand with layout design. The topic selection meeting mainly discusses market positioning and marketing plans. It will be very helpful if you prepare a 5-minute explanation of your creative concept and a portrait of your core readers. session_350.text: I see. I'll organize the reference images and creative description as soon as possible. However, I'm still a bit nervous about the topic selection meeting, afraid of being asked questions I don't understand, such as circulation and pricing. What key points should I prepare in advance?

session_350.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_350.text: Focus on three points: 1) The thematic innovation of the essay collection (for example, the resonance of "slow travel" with contemporary young people); 2) The potential readership (young literature lovers, travel-healing readers); 3) Your existing creative channels (your identity as a freelance writer and social media followers) that can support promotion. session_352.text: I'm reviewing Introduction to Linguistics. While doing practice problems, I found that I keep confusing the concepts of phoneme variants, free variants, and conditioned variants, and I also tend to make mistakes in morpheme segmentation exercises. Could you explain the differences and the steps for analysis?

session_352.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_352.text: Of course. Allophones are concrete manifestations of phonemes, divided into free variants and conditioned variants: free variants can be interchanged in the same environment (e.g., [n] and [l] in some Chinese dialects), while conditioned variants are constrained by the phonetic environment (e.g., English /pʰ/ and /p/). The key to distinguishing them is whether the environments of occurrence are complementary. Morpheme segmentation uses immediate constituent analysis: first find the largest component, then cut layer by layer down to the smallest meaningful unit.

session_352.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_352.text: I see. Complementary distribution corresponds to conditioned variants, and the opposition principle distinguishes phonemes, right? Then what about erhua like 'huar' in phonemic analysis — is it considered a variant? Also, how can I review more efficiently in the last few days before the exam?

session_352.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_352.text: Yes, that understanding is correct. Erhua is often treated as a sandhi phenomenon in phonological analysis, not a typical allophone, but it needs to be handled according to the specific language. Pre-exam suggestion: spend 1 hour a day redoing wrong questions and drawing concept relationship diagrams, focus on the typical mistakes in past exam papers, and keep up the rhythm of reviewing mind maps.

session_355.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_355.text: Tomorrow is the Introduction to Linguistics exam. In the case analysis using immediate constituent analysis, I always have trouble finding the way to break down the sentences. Could you help me sort out the steps for solving typical example problems?

session_355.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_355.text: Sure. The core of immediate constituent analysis is to divide from top to bottom, level by level; first find the main clause — subject, predicate, object — and then determine the modifying relationships. For example, for 'He bought an interesting book yesterday', first split 'he' and 'yesterday bought an interesting book', then split 'yesterday' and 'bought an interesting book', and so on. Note that each level can only be split into two immediate constituents. I suggest using vertical lines to mark the levels when practicing, and marking the structural type (subject-predicate, verb-object, modifier-head, etc.) of each node.

session_365.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_365.text: This morning I meditated by Erhai Lake, then went cycling and chatted with an old painter. I plan to write an essay titled 'Breath of the Lake,' blending the scenery of Cangshan Mountain, Erhai Lake, the wind, and the reeds with my reflections, but I'm worried it may be loosely structured. Do you suggest writing it chronologically or organizing it by theme?

session_365.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_365.text: Suggestion: use "the breath of the lake" as a metaphor and connect it through themes: morning meditation corresponds to the lake's "awakening," cycling and the sound of wind to "breathing," and the conversation with the old painter to "ripples." Each segment focuses on a sensory image (light and shadow, reeds, seagulls), and finally elevates to the flow of time and self-awareness. You can refer to the chapter transitions in Thoreau's "Walden" and use natural details to trigger philosophical reflection.

session_365.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_365.text: This idea is great! Using ‘breath’ to connect the three passages makes the transition feel natural. But I’m worried the descriptions are too trivial. How do you elevate from concrete details to philosophical reflection? For example, at the moment the seagull takes off, how do you write it with depth?

session_365.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_365.text: You can use the seagull’s sudden takeoff as a symbol of an instant awakening, starting from the reflection of white feathers and connecting it to the undercurrents beneath the lake and the fragility of life. Similar to Liu Liangcheng’s writing on dust and earth in One Man’s Village, you can magnify small details into a metaphor for the passage of time. Try using the contrast: the lightness of the seagull versus the heaviness of Cangshan Mountain, implying freedom and restraint.

session_365.speaker: Sun Yuwei
session_365.text: Just on New Year's Eve I wrote down the goal '2026, deepen my nature writing in Yunnan' and also posted a photo of Erhai Lake. I feel both excited and uneasy, afraid I won't be able to stick with it — after all, I've had too little outdoor practice before. Can you give me some encouragement and advice?

session_365.speaker: Sun Yuwei's Assistant
session_365.text: This goal is very insightful! Your INFP traits will bring delicate observation of nature. I suggest breaking it down into a quarterly plan: Q1 — write one nature-themed essay each month, set aside 30 minutes of writing every day (such as early in the morning), and arrange a short nature walk on the weekend. session_6.speaker: Song Yajing
session_6.text: I'm using CapCut for picture-in-picture, but the video blending never looks natural enough. How should I adjust the opacity to make the transition between the background and foreground smoother?

session_6.speaker: Song Yajing's Assistant
session_6.text: It is recommended to select the picture-in-picture track, lower the opacity to 40%-60% in the adjustment panel, and combine it with 'Multiply' or 'Screen' in 'Blend Mode' to make the two images overlay naturally. In addition, keyframes can control the opacity gradient, for example, gradually rising from 0% to 60% at entry, for a smoother effect.

session_6.speaker: Song Yajing
session_6.text: I tried Multiply mode and it is indeed better than before, but the two clips are always slightly off when aligned on the timeline. Manually dragging them is hard to make precise. Is there a quick way to align them?

session_6.speaker: Song Yajing's Assistant
session_6.text: In CapCut, you can enable the 'Magnet' feature (top toolbar); when you drag a picture-in-picture clip, it will automatically snap to the edit points on the main track. If you need frame-level precision, first zoom in on the timeline, then use the 'Split' tool to cut both clips to the same length, and then align their starting frames.

session_6.speaker: Song Yajing
session_6.text: I declined the short-term fixed-term wealth management product recommended by ICBC, but I'm still a bit curious about the risk-return profile of such products. My small shop has cyclical cash-flow pressure—is there a more flexible low-risk wealth management option suitable for me?

session_6.speaker: Song Yajing's Assistant
session_6.text: Short-term fixed-term wealth management usually has a low minimum investment (such as 10,000 yuan), a lock-in period of 1-6 months, and an annualized interest rate of about 2%-3%. Early redemption will result in lost returns. Since you mentioned that the store has periodic cash flow pressure, money market funds (redeemable at any time, annualized 1.5%-2%) or structured deposits (principal protected, flexible terms) are more recommended. For family emergency funds, it is advisable to set aside 3-6 months of basic expenses.

session_6.speaker: Song Yajing
session_6.text: Money market funds are indeed more flexible, so what's the approximate return? If I want to park some money during the gap before paying for goods, say for about a month, what do you recommend?

session_6.speaker: Song Yajing's Assistant
session_6.text: Money market funds currently have a seven-day annualized yield of about 1.8%, with daily interest accrual and T+0 or T+1 redemption. For a one-month gap period, you may also consider notice deposits (7-day notice, interest rate about 1.35%) or short-term treasury bond reverse repos (flexible terms, low threshold). I suggest you first keep 50,000 yuan as an emergency reserve, and allocate the remaining idle funds to these products.

session_7.speaker: Song Yajing
session_7.text: Tomorrow afternoon I'm going to have a heart-to-heart talk with Aunt Lin, a fellow churchgoer, at a café. I plan to talk about the decline in store revenue, the short-video transformation, and my anxiety about my daughter's transition from kindergarten to elementary school. But I'm very nervous, afraid that I'll sound like I'm complaining, and also afraid that showing up empty-handed (the cookies got burnt) will seem rude. session_7.speaker: Song Yajing's Assistant
session_7.text: It is suggested to break the ice with church activities or recent Bible reading reflections, for example, 'Auntie, since last week's Mass I have been thinking about Proverbs 3:5-6, about entrusting worries to God...' and then naturally transition to the current situation. When expressing vulnerability, use 'I've recently been learning to entrust things to God, but my heart is still uneasy; I'd like to hear your experience' instead of simply complaining. No need to mind arriving empty-handed; sincerity matters more than gifts. In addition, you can ask Aunt Lin, as a retired teacher, for advice on the kindergarten-to-primary-school transition, which both focuses on the core and shows respect.

session_7.speaker: Song Yajing
session_7.text: Starting with a faith topic did put me at ease and also avoided directly pouring out my grievances. But I'm worried the conversation might drift off-topic, or that Aunt Lin might think I'm complaining. Is there a way to stay focused and make it seem like I'm asking for help rather than complaining?

session_7.speaker: Song Yajing's Assistant
session_7.text: You can prepare 2-3 key points in advance: the specific figures or signs of the decline in revenue, the frustration of trying short videos, and the specific concerns about Xuanxuan's transition from kindergarten to primary school. After each point, take the initiative to ask, 'What do you think?' or 'Did you encounter a similar situation back when you were a homeroom teacher?' Turn the conversation into seeking advice. Asking for help is a sign of trust. As an ISFJ-type retired teacher, Aunt Lin will feel needed by helping others. And don't forget to silently pray to God to prepare her heart.

session_7.speaker: Song Yajing's Assistant
session_7.text: It sounds like you put a lot of effort into this baking, especially using the new matcha powder you bought. Burning it is indeed frustrating, but don't be discouraged. session_7.speaker: Song Yajing

session_7.speaker: Song Yajing's Assistant
session_7.text: Distraction is the biggest enemy of baking, and everyone is prone to it. Don't blame yourself too much! Matcha powder can't withstand high temperatures; next time try baking at 160°C for 8-10 minutes, and keep an eye on the color during the last two minutes. It's not too late to make up for it: you can use the remaining ingredients to make no-bake oat balls, ready in 15 minutes tomorrow morning; or just bring a token of your affection—Auntie cares more about your company. One mistake doesn't mean anything; your passion for baking is the most beautiful gift.

session_13.text: I reviewed my Hangzhou notes this morning and circled two strategies: 'start with communities of regular and familiar customers' and 'build trust through real outfit photos.' I want to confirm whether they're suitable for my current VIP group operations.

session_13.speaker: Song Yajing
session_13.text: Today I almost had a meltdown learning CapCut. The beat-sync was off and the transitions were stiff, and I got so angry that I threw down my stylus. Later I tried a cross-dissolve transition with a page-flip video and actually succeeded, which made me feel a bit better.

session_13.speaker: Song Yajing's Assistant
session_13.text: I understand your frustration — hitting a wall at the beginning as a beginner is normal. The way you went from feeling irritated to persisting until you completed the cross-dissolve transition is especially worthy of recognition. Do you want to talk about how to break through the specific sticking point, or do you need some mental preparation?

session_13.speaker: Song Yajing
session_13.text: You want all of them, right? Why is vlog stitching so hard? Is there a quick shortcut for complete beginners?

session_13.speaker: Song Yajing's Assistant
session_13.text: Editing is like putting together a puzzle. First practice with fixed templates: find 3-5 second clips and connect them with "cross dissolve" (transition duration 0.5 seconds), and put together one simple video a day (such as unboxing or outfit). Mentally accept that the first 10 hours are the "clumsy period"; small victories will gradually build confidence.

session_13.speaker: Song Yajing
session_13.text: I wrote the warm-up copy for tomorrow's VIP group: “Brother Zheng's designer friend — I picked these out myself, sisters, have a look.” But it feels a bit stiff. How can I polish it so it sounds sincere and sparks everyone's interest?

session_13.speaker: Song Yajing's Assistant
session_13.text: I understand your concern. You want to keep the intimate atmosphere of the 'Yajing Wardrobe VIP Bestie Group' while making the sample preview more natural and attractive. The key is to balance approachability with commercial guidance. Have you considered using story-based or interactive scripts? For example, adding your real try-on experience, or using a limited quantity sign-up chain to create a little urgency.

session_13.speaker: Song Yajing
session_13.text: Yes, I do want to add real try-on impressions, like "I've tried these wide-leg pants, the fabric is amazing." But I'm not sure whether to put the price directly, afraid it'll look too much like an ad.

session_13.speaker: Song Yajing's Assistant
session_13.text: It's best to start with an engaging preview: describe the fabric and cut in everyday language, for example, 'I actually tried these sample pants today—the drape is amazing, and they don't wrinkle even when you sit down.' You can leave the price in the comments, or let an active regular customer like Vivian take the lead in asking, and then you reply naturally—that feels more organic. Also, post a photo of yourself wearing them; it's more authentic than a flat-lay.

session_14.speaker: Song Yajing
session_14.text: I am the owner of a boutique clothing store and stand while working for 8 hours a day. Recently, my lower back soreness has worsened, especially today (January 14, 2025), when it felt uncomfortable from morning to night. I can only relieve it by rinsing my lower back with hot water. session_14.speaker: Song Yajing's Assistant
session_14.text: It sounds like it could be lumbar muscle strain from prolonged standing. I suggest trying heat compresses and adjusting your standing posture (for example, alternating placing each foot on a small stool). In the long term, you can wear a lumbar support belt to share the pressure, and do 5 minutes of cat-cow stretch every day. Have you been to the hospital for a check-up recently?

session_14.speaker: Song Yajing
session_14.text: I haven't gone to the hospital yet. I usually exercise little and have average health awareness. I tried hot compresses and they helped a bit, but it still aches when I stand. Do I need to wear the lumbar support belt all the time? Are there any simple exercises I can do in the shop?

session_14.speaker: Song Yajing's Assistant
session_14.text: Wear the lumbar support belt only when standing for long periods or carrying heavy items; don't rely on it all day. Two exercises are recommended: 1) Standing rear leg raise (hold the counter, extend your right leg backward 10 times, then switch sides); 2) Wall sit (hold for 30 seconds each time). If soreness persists for more than a week or you develop leg numbness, seek medical attention as soon as possible to rule out lumbar spine problems.

session_15.text: I stand in the store eight or nine hours a day. By the afternoon my lower back is unbearably sore. At night I use a massager to rub it, and it feels a bit better, but it recurs the next day. Are there any practical ways to relieve or prevent this?

session_15.text: It sounds like lower back muscle fatigue caused by prolonged standing. Would you like to get some stretching exercises for work breaks or massage techniques to help relieve soreness and prevent recurrence?

session_15.text: Yes, ideally stretches that can be done simply in the store, not the kind where you have to lie on the floor. And should we change the way we use the massager?

session_15.speaker: Song Yajing's Assistant
session_15.text: It is recommended that for every 1 hour of standing, do 5 "cat stretches" against the wall or single-leg back extensions while holding the wall. session_15.speaker: Song Yajing
session_15.text: Got it, I'll try that stretching tomorrow. I used the massager directly; next time I'll apply a hot compress first. Also, is lower back soreness related to calcium deficiency? I rarely drink milk.

session_15.text: It is somewhat related. Standing for long periods can accelerate calcium loss. I suggest drinking 300 ml of milk or eating soy products and dark green vegetables every day, and supplementing with calcium-magnesium tablets if necessary. But first adjust the stretching and massage, and observe for a week before seeing the effect.

session_16.text: Understood your needs. When you consult with an agent, you can ask them to provide a rate list for comparison.

session_24.text: Your hard work and dedication have really paid off! A sales breakthrough earned with such professionalism and passion is definitely worth treating yourself. Tomorrow you can carry this confidence and keep reaching new heights—and don’t forget to say a thank-you to God before bed~
