session_309.text: At noon today, I discussed with my colleague the influence of the three cutting parameters on surface roughness. He shared his practical experience, but when I reviewed the theory, I still had doubts about the specific mechanisms of depth of cut, feed rate, and cutting speed. Could you explain them systematically?

session_309.speaker: Yin Hao's Assistant
session_309.text: Cutting speed affects surface roughness by influencing built-up edge and vibration: at high cutting speeds, the built-up edge decreases and the surface becomes smoother. Feed rate directly determines the height of the residual area; the larger the feed, the greater the roughness value. Depth of cut mainly affects cutting force fluctuations and vibration, and has a relatively small effect on roughness, but in plastic materials it acts indirectly through deformation effects.

session_309.speaker: Yin Hao
session_309.text: Then under different materials—such as brittle cast iron and ductile steel—how would the weights of these three factors change? I'd like to understand this in the context of today's shaft part (45 steel) machining.

session_309.speaker: Yin Hao's Assistant
session_309.text: When machining ductile materials such as 45 steel, feed rate has the greatest influence on surface roughness, so a small feed (0.05-0.15 mm/r) is recommended. Cutting speed should avoid the built-up edge zone (about 20-60 m/min); use a high or low speed. In finishing, take a depth of cut of 0.2-0.5 mm and avoid vibration. For brittle materials, cutting speed has a more noticeable effect, so chip fragmentation needs to be controlled.

session_310.text: Today I solved the roundness deviation issue on the five-axis machining center. My master said it was caused by spindle thermal elongation. Could you explain in detail the physical principles of thermal elongation and common compensation methods? I want to build up knowledge for the skills competition.

session_310.speaker: Yin Hao's Assistant
session_310.text: Spindle thermal elongation is caused by temperature rise from high-speed operation, which causes linear expansion of the material (such as steel), and the axial length change affects the tool position. Typical compensation methods include: 1) coordinate offset compensation, which corrects the Z-axis zero point in real time based on the temperature rise curve; 2) coolant system control to maintain a constant spindle temperature; 3) using materials with low thermal expansion coefficients. In skills competitions, building thermal error models and adjusting compensation parameters are often tested; it is recommended to combine simulation for optimization.

session_310.speaker: Yin Hao
session_310.text: Got it. Regarding today's parameter adjustments specifically, I solved the problem by reducing tool overhang and optimizing coolant flow. But in the compensation model, how is the real-time calculation of coordinate offsets implemented? Is there a general calculation formula?

session_310.speaker: Yin Hao's Assistant
session_310.text: A common method is to embed temperature sensors and establish a linear relationship between thermal displacement and temperature (e.g., ΔL = α·L0·ΔT). For real-time calculation, you can read the temperature values via the PLC, plug them into the calibration formula, and generate the offset. You can look up the machine tool's built-in 'thermal compensation' parameter groups in the manual, such as Fanuc system parameter No. 1300 and others. I suggest you compile the temperature rise curve from this commissioning session and compare the effects of different cooling strategies after the competition.

session_310.speaker: Yin Hao
session_310.text: Good idea! I'll organize today's recorded temperature data and compensation parameters into a case study. Also, if I encounter a similar problem in the skills competition, is there a quick troubleshooting approach to determine whether it's thermal elongation or another error?

session_310.speaker: Yin Hao's Assistant
session_310.text: Quick troubleshooting in three steps: 1) After idling and preheating, check the precision to see whether the error increases with temperature; 2) Use a dial indicator against the spindle face and record the axial runout at different speeds; 3) Compare the dimensional changes with the coolant on and off. If it matches the thermal expansion trend, prioritize adjusting the cooling and compensation parameters. I suggest you prepare an "error diagnosis flowchart" — it's very practical for the competition.

session_312.speaker: Yin Hao's Assistant
session_312.text: G10 is used to dynamically modify tool compensation or coordinate system offsets, with a format such as 'G10 L2 P1 X0 Y0 Z0', avoiding manual modification. WHILE loops are often used in five-axis machining for repeated paths, such as layered cutting; pay attention to condition checks and nesting levels. Example: use a WHILE loop to implement Z-axis layered milling, with the loop variable incrementing and the exit condition being the depth reaching the target value.

session_312.speaker: Yin Hao
session_312.text: Can you give another specific example of five-axis linkage? Also, what mistakes are likely when embedding macro programs into G-code? Are there any debugging tips?

session_312.speaker: Yin Hao's Assistant
session_312.text: In five-axis linkage, WHILE can control the gradual change of the tool axis angle. For example, “WHILE #1 LT 90 DO1” combined with a rotation command achieves continuous sweeping. Common errors: the loop variable is not updated, causing an infinite loop; incorrect G10 parameters affect subsequent tool compensation. When debugging, it is recommended to add #1=#1+1 printing at the beginning of the program; you can also run it in segments for verification. Recommended learning resources: the book “FANUC Macro Programming Guide” or search for “Five-Axis Macro Program Examples” on Bilibili.

session_317.speaker: Yin Hao
session_317.text: In the evening, I used AutoCAD to practice five-axis programming. I'm still unclear about how RTCP keeps the tool tip point precisely following the complex surface when the tool axis vector changes. Could you explain the compensation mechanism in detail?

session_317.speaker: Yin Hao's Assistant
session_317.text: The core of RTCP is to compensate in real time for the tool tip position offset caused by the rotation of the tool axis, ensuring that the tool center point always moves along the programmed trajectory. Compensation is based on the machine tool kinematic model and involves coordinate system transformation: transform the tool tip point from the workpiece coordinate system to the machine coordinate system, and then back-calculate the movement of each axis. In simple terms, no matter how the tool axis swings, the controller automatically adjusts the linear axes to compensate for the offset caused by rotation.

session_317.speaker: Yin Hao
session_317.text: Does the compensation have a threshold for taking effect? For example, how much tool axis change is needed before compensation starts? I'm worried that compensation may be imprecise for small angle changes.

session_317.speaker: Yin Hao's Assistant
session_317.text: Compensation is continuous; there is no threshold. Any angle change triggers compensation. Accuracy depends on the machine tool’s RTCP calibration and post-processor configuration. I recommend setting the output format in the post-processor to linear interpolation (G01/G02) and enabling CYCLE800 or an equivalent command. When verifying, use software simulation to check whether the tool tip path is smooth. Common alarms such as “rotary axis over travel” or “coordinate offset error” are usually caused by the compensation calculation exceeding the machine travel or the coordinate system not being correctly activated.

session_321.text: Do you want to transform the intelligent compensation principles learned in the lecture into actionable parameter adjustment methods for SK-433 machining, such as set values for thermal compensation and force compensation, as well as optimization of cutting fluid flow and tool paths?

session_321.speaker: Yin Hao
session_321.text: Right, especially how to match cutting depth and spindle speed to both reduce thermal deformation and prevent tool deflection. Also, which indicator should we measure first during trial cutting?

session_321.speaker: Yin Hao's Assistant

If thermal deformation is obvious, enable the thermal compensation function and set the tool thermal elongation compensation coefficient to 0.02 mm/°C. At the same time, optimize the tool path: use trochoidal milling to reduce radial cutting force.

session_322.speaker: Yin Hao
session_322.text: On the simulation software, I increased the position loop gain from 3500 to 4000, and resonance and overshoot occurred. What is the matching principle between gain and following error?

session_322.speaker: Yin Hao's Assistant
session_322.text: If the position loop gain is too high, the system becomes too rigid, and resonance and overshoot are typical symptoms. Following error = command speed / position loop gain. It is recommended to first reduce the gain to the original value and simultaneously adjust the speed loop damping ratio (e.g., 0.7-0.8) to eliminate oscillation. Refer to the gain and speed loop matching table in the Manual.

session_322.speaker: Yin Hao
session_322.text: How is the transmission ratio calculated in five-axis post-processing? And which point on an oscilloscope can quickly distinguish whether it is a motor fault or a drive fault?

session_322.speaker: Yin Hao's Assistant
session_322.text: Transmission ratio = actual angle of the rotary axis / commanded angle; it needs to be combined with the mechanical reduction ratio and the electronic gear ratio. Use an oscilloscope to measure the current waveform: normally it is a sine wave; if the waveform is distorted or abruptly changes, it is mostly a drive fault; if the waveform is normal but becomes abnormal as the load increases, it is mostly a motor or mechanical problem. It is recommended to draw a decision tree to sort this out.

session_328.text: Today, while machining a precision valve body, I encountered slight drilling chatter. After consulting CNC Advanced Operator Practice and adjusting the cutting angle and coolant, it was solved. However, I want to deeply understand the cause of chatter from a physical mechanism perspective, and would like to know how to systematically prevent it in high-precision machining, as well as the scoring criteria and response strategies for similar problems in the finals of the skills competition.

session_328.speaker: Yin Hao's Assistant
session_328.text: The physical mechanism of drilling chatter mainly originates from the coupling of cutting force fluctuations with resonance of the tool-workpiece system. The core factors are excessive tool overhang, insufficient workpiece rigidity, or improper cutting parameters. In competitions, this type of problem often tests 'fault diagnosis and rapid problem-solving ability.' Key scoring points include: accurately judging the chatter type, the logicality of the adjustment plan (such as checking tool rigidity first, then optimizing depth of cut and spindle speed), and whether the machined surface quality meets the standard. I suggest you build a preventive plan from these three levels: 1. Use heat-shrink or hydraulic tool holders to improve clamping rigidity; 2. Use contour programming to reduce sudden radial force changes; 3. Choose a low-vibration drill point geometry for the valve body material (presumably aluminum alloy or stainless steel).

session_328.speaker: Yin Hao
session_328.text: Understood. I especially want to know, for multi-axis machining of complex surfaces, if chatter occurs, which steps do judges value most in on-the-spot handling? Also, are there any recommended authoritative resources (books or online courses) to systematically learn these?

session_328.speaker: Yin Hao's Assistant
session_328.text: Evaluators typically score using a three-step 'observe-analyze-verify' approach: first, they check whether the operator immediately pauses and observes the vibration pattern (e.g., spiral marks or transverse chatter marks), then listens to the cutting sound to judge the frequency; they evaluate whether the adjustment sequence is reasonable (first checking tool overhang and spindle dynamic balance, then fine-tuning the speed to avoid the resonance zone, and finally adjusting the cooling direction); and finally, they verify whether the improved surface roughness reaches Ra≤1.6μm. Recommended resources: 'Metal Cutting Principles and Cutting Tools' (4th edition) focuses on mechanisms, and the Udemy course 'CNC Milling Troubleshooting' includes chatter case exercises. It is also recommended that you practice simulating different stiffness conditions in simulation software.

session_334.speaker: Yin Hao
session_334.text: I just read a forum post about bathroom waterproofing, but the information is all over the place. The wire channels in the bathroom of my new house in Yulan Bay were cut a bit shallow. I'm about to do waterproofing and lay tiles. Which do you think is more suitable, Oriental Yuhong or Davco? What should I pay attention to during construction?

session_334.speaker: Yin Hao's Assistant
session_334.text: Oriental Yuhong and Davco are both mainstream brands. I recommend polymer cement waterproof coating (JS-II type), which is cost-effective and suitable for bathrooms. The conduit grooves need to be patched and smoothed first, then apply the waterproof coating; additional reinforcement coats should be applied at internal corners. For the floor, it is recommended to apply the waterproof coating 2-3 times, with a thickness above 1.5mm, followed by a 48-hour ponding test. For tiles, choose anti-slip antique tiles or full-body tiles for the floor; the glaze should show no marks when scratched with a key. Prices vary greatly between online and physical stores, so it is recommended to compare prices by model in physical stores. Do you have a specific budget or preference?

session_334.speaker: Yin Hao
session_334.text: Is ordinary cement enough for the repair at the wire trough? I looked at tiles from Gold Medal Asia and Dongpeng at the market yesterday. I want antique-style tiles for the floor, but I'm worried the slip resistance won't be enough. Also, how exactly is the waterproofing test done?

session_334.speaker: Yin Hao's Assistant
session_334.text: For the wire groove, it is recommended to repair it in layers with Leak Stopping King or cement mortar; after it dries completely, apply waterproof coating, and you can add a layer of fiberglass mesh to prevent cracking. Antique tiles usually have sufficient slip resistance; you can feel the back with your hand — lower water absorption means more slip resistance. Water-retention test steps: plug the floor drain, add water to a height of 2–3 cm, let the water stand for 48 hours, then go downstairs to check that there is no leakage. Do you need me to list a detailed construction step checklist?

session_334.speaker: Yin Hao
session_334.text: This is much clearer; the checklist is better. Also, my father said to pay attention to floor leveling. Before waterproofing, does the leveling layer have to be completely dry?

session_334.speaker: Yin Hao's Assistant
session_334.text: Yes, the leveling layer must be completely dry (moisture content below 9%), otherwise the waterproof layer will blister. I recommend leveling with cement mortar and making a drainage slope (1% gradient) for faster water runoff. Send me the bathroom dimensions and I can help you estimate the amount of materials needed.

session_335.speaker: Yin Hao
session_335.text: I just reviewed complex surface programming. I'm unsure about the details of coordinate calculation for I, J, K in G02/G03, and I often make mistakes with the timing of establishing and canceling tool radius compensation. Can you summarize the key techniques and common pitfalls?

session_335.speaker: Yin Hao's Assistant
session_335.text: I, J, and K are the incremental coordinates of the arc center relative to the starting point. When calculating, pay attention to their vector relationship with the endpoint coordinates. Tool radius compensation should be established before entering the machined surface and canceled after exiting; avoid enabling it in non-cutting segments, otherwise it may easily cause a tool collision. In addition, when subprograms M98/M99 are used for repeated profile machining, note that the coordinate system must be returned to zero and offsets reset. It is recommended to focus on checking these steps.

session_335.speaker: Yin Hao
session_335.text: Understood. So what's on the safety checklist to prevent tool collision? For instance, how do you avoid interference in multi-axis simultaneous motion?

session_335.speaker: Yin Hao's Assistant
session_335.text: Basic checklist: 1. Run a simulation to verify the program; 2. Check tool length compensation and workpiece coordinate system settings; 3. Confirm a safe retract height; 4. During multi-axis simultaneous machining, pay attention to spatial interference between the tool, fixture, and workpiece. You can run in single-step mode first or reduce the feed rate for a trial cut. In addition, it is recommended to use dynamic simulation software to predict collisions for complex surfaces.

session_341.speaker: Yin Hao
session_341.text: Today I bought a scraper, a sandpaper holder, and floor protection film, and I also asked Master Chen for tips on scraping walls. But I'm still not sure how to tell in practice whether the putty is water-resistant, how much scraping is enough to be acceptable, and how exactly to deal with cracks. Could you explain it to me systematically?

session_341.speaker: Yin Hao's Assistant
session_341.text: Okay. To distinguish water-resistant putty: after splashing water on the surface, it does not absorb water, and the scraped marks are smooth and hard; non-water-resistant putty bubbles when it comes into contact with water, and the scraped marks turn powdery. Removal criteria: water-resistant putty only needs the loose layer removed until the firm base layer is exposed; non-water-resistant putty must be completely scraped down to the cement layer. For cracks: cut a V-shaped groove, fill it with joint compound, apply mesh tape, and then apply putty. When laying protective film, cover the baseboards and leave an edge margin; wear gloves and a mask for dust protection.

session_341.speaker: Yin Hao
session_341.text: So is the medium-coarse sandpaper holder I bought suitable? After scraping the wall, what should I pay attention to when sanding?

session_341.speaker: Yin Hao's Assistant
session_341.text: Medium-coarse sandpaper is suitable for initial sanding and leveling; use fine sandpaper afterward for a smooth finish. When sanding, be sure to wear a dust mask and sand in even circles from one side to the other, avoiding overdoing any one spot. Clean the dust off the sandpaper holder before each sandpaper change. After using the tools, promptly clean the scraper and apply oil to prevent rust.

session_342.text: I'm learning PLC analog input signal processing. How do I convert the 4-20mA signal to the corresponding numeric range?

session_342.speaker: Yin Hao's Assistant
session_342.text: Usually 4-20mA corresponds to 0-27648 (Siemens S7-1200) or 0-4095 (12-bit module). Use SCL instructions to linearly map the raw value to the actual engineering value. Formula: Actual value = (raw value - offset) * (range upper limit - range lower limit) / (value upper limit - value lower limit) + range lower limit. Do you need a specific example?

session_342.speaker: Yin Hao

session_342.speaker: Yin Hao's Assistant
session_342.text: Ladder diagram: first use the MOV instruction to read PIW (analog input word), then call FC (such as SCL) for conversion; for filtering, use the averaging method—accumulate 10 cached values per scan cycle and divide by 10 to get the filtered value. Pay attention to the sampling period and hardware filtering. Do you need me to write out a ladder diagram segment?

The interval between coats is usually 4–6 hours depending on temperature and humidity; when touching it lightly with a finger leaves no residue, you can apply the second coat.

session_345.speaker: Yin Hao

For old houses, polyurethane coating is recommended because it has good elasticity and strong crack resistance, but pay attention to ventilation and protection. Coating consumption is about 1.5-2 kg/m², estimated by multiplying the actual area by the number of coats.

session_346.speaker: Yin Hao
session_346.text: I just snapped up Nippon Paint Low-Odor 120 latex paint and Davco flexible waterproof coating during Double 12. My father reminded me about anti-counterfeiting and winter construction, but I also want to know the official verification method and more comprehensive winter construction key points. Can you help me sort this out?

session_346.speaker: Yin Hao's Assistant
session_346.text: Of course. Nippon Paint's official anti-counterfeiting can be checked by QR code, phone (400-883-2888), or official website; Davco waterproof coating packaging has an anti-counterfeit label and coating code, supporting QR code or SMS verification. For winter construction: do not apply when the temperature is below 5°C; the substrate should be dry and clean; the interval between coats should be at least 6 hours; apply the waterproof coating in a cross-hatch pattern; dilute latex paint with no more than 20% water; after sanding the wall, apply primer first and then two topcoats; after application, ventilate but avoid a cross-draft; and cure for more than 48 hours. If you have specific questions later, feel free to ask.

session_346.speaker: Yin Hao
session_346.text: Can you explain more specifically the key points of applying the paint in a crisscross pattern? Also, I'm still a bit unclear about the water-to-latex paint ratio and the drying time.

session_346.speaker: Yin Hao's Assistant
session_346.text: Crisscross application: brush the first coat vertically and the second coat horizontally, with uniform thickness for each coat and no missed spots. Water dilution ratio for latex paint: Nippon Paint Odorless 120 recommends adding 10%–15% water (about 1–1.5 liters of water per bucket of paint), not exceeding 20%. Drying time: after each coat, dry for at least 4–6 hours at 5–10°C; extend if humidity is high. After the primer dries, sand it before applying the topcoat. Refer to the instructions on the product can for details.

session_346.speaker: Yin Hao
session_346.text: Understood, thank you. If the construction temperature drops below 5°C but we still need to meet the deadline, are there any emergency measures?

session_346.speaker: Yin Hao's Assistant
session_346.text: Construction is not recommended below 5°C, otherwise the latex paint will not form a proper film and the waterproof coating may crack easily. If you must rush the work, you can use heating equipment (such as a fan heater) to raise the ambient temperature to 5-10°C, but be careful with ventilation to prevent drying too quickly. You can also use winter-specific coatings (which need to be replaced in advance). The safest option is still to wait for the temperature to rise to ensure construction quality.

session_349.speaker: Yin Hao
session_349.text: Tomorrow evening I need to scrape the old wall coating and do the protective work. This is my first time renovating by myself; can you give me a clear step-by-step checklist? In particular, I need to know whether to spray water, what tools to use to save effort, how to handle the internal and external corners, and how to protect the paint and the floor.

session_349.speaker: Yin Hao's Assistant
session_349.text: You'll be short on time tomorrow evening, so you need an efficient, executable process. Recommendation: do the protection first, then scrape the wall surface. Spray water to moisten (using a spray bottle to evenly wet the wall, let sit for 15–20 minutes) to soften the putty, saving effort and reducing dust. For tools, use a scraper (scraping at a 45-degree angle); use a small scraper or trowel for inside and outside corners. Cover paint buckets and the floor with plastic protective film and masking tape to prevent splashes. Cracks need to be scraped open and cleaned before patching flat.

session_349.speaker: Yin Hao
session_349.text: I got blisters on my hands from scraping putty the day before yesterday. Will it affect my efficiency if I work tomorrow night? Also, about how long does each step take?

session_349.speaker: Yin Hao's Assistant
session_349.text: For the blister, it is recommended to cover it with a band-aid or medical tape to avoid friction. Tomorrow evening's time plan: protective covering (30 minutes) → wetting with water (20 minutes) → scraping off wall paint (1.5-2 hours / 15 square meters) → sanding (30 minutes) → cleaning (20 minutes). Total time about 3 hours. You can scrape the large flat areas first, and use the scraper to trim the internal and external corners last.

session_349.speaker: Yin Hao
session_349.text: This morning I found a 1 cm blister at the base of my right index finger, caused by scraping putty the day before yesterday. I applied aloe vera gel and a band-aid, but tomorrow I need to operate a CNC machine tool during the day and scrape wall putty at the new house in the evening. How should I care for it to avoid infection and not affect my work?

session_349.speaker: Yin Hao's Assistant
session_349.text: Your main concerns are blister rupture and infection, and hand protection for the two jobs tomorrow. If the blister has not broken, do not puncture it. It is recommended to disinfect with povidone-iodine and then apply a hydrocolloid dressing for protection. When operating the machine tool, you can wear half-finger anti-slip gloves to maintain dexterity; when scraping wall paint, choose lined anti-slip gloves to reduce friction.

session_349.speaker: Yin Hao
session_349.text: What should I do if a blister accidentally breaks while working? Do I need to remove the Band-Aid to let it breathe when sleeping at night?

session_349.speaker: Yin Hao's Assistant
session_349.text: If it ruptures: rinse immediately with normal saline, apply mupirocin ointment, and bandage with sterile gauze. At night, it is recommended to remove the dressing to let the blister breathe naturally and avoid stuffiness, but be careful not to rub it. Changing to a waterproof dressing before work tomorrow would be safer.

session_349.speaker: Yin Hao
session_349.text: Understood. Then what should I pay attention to when holding tools tomorrow? Are there any long-term prevention methods?

session_349.speaker: Yin Hao's Assistant
session_349.text: When holding tools, avoid a death grip; use your fingers rather than the heel of your palm for force, and relax your hands every 30 minutes. For long-term prevention: apply a layer of anti-slip chalk or hand cream before each session to reduce friction, and choose work gloves with silicone pads, which can greatly reduce the risk of blisters recurring.

session_349.text: Hello, I'm Yin Hao, a CNC machine operator. Today my master mentioned a new insert for machining flanges, but didn't specify the model. The flange materials I work with are mainly ductile iron or carbon steel. I'd like to know the current mainstream high-efficiency insert models, materials, nose radius, and chip breaker parameters, as well as their advantages over my current inserts in tool life, surface finish, and cutting speed. Also, where can I buy them locally in Songjiang? Do I need to adjust my existing cutting parameters?

session_349.speaker: Yin Hao's Assistant
session_349.text: Hello Yin Hao! According to your working conditions (flange, ductile iron/carbon steel), we recommend the following mainstream high-efficiency inserts: Sandvik CNMG120408-PM 4325 (coated carbide, nose radius 0.8mm, suitable for fine finishing surface quality) and Seco DNMG150608-MF2 TP2500 (medium cutting, optimized chipbreaker). Compared with ordinary inserts, tool life increases by 30-50%, surface finish can reach Ra0.8, and cutting speed can be increased by 20%. Purchase channels: tool specialty store at Songjiang Hardware City or JD Industrial Products (brand flagship store). Parameter adjustment suggestions: increase spindle speed by 15%, keep feed at 0.15-0.25mm/r, and appropriately reduce depth of cut. You can discuss these models directly with your master tomorrow.

session_349.speaker: Yin Hao
session_349.text: Thank you! This info is really helpful. When I was machining today, I ran into a surface finish problem and only got it back to normal after adjusting the tool and cutting fluid concentration. Do you think there is room for improvement in how I handled it? Also, if I try out the insert you recommended, are there any precautions for installation or matching the cutting fluid?

session_349.speaker: Yin Hao's Assistant
session_349.text: Adjusting the tool and cutting fluid on your own initiative was the right move. Room for improvement: check whether the cutting fluid concentration is within 5–8%, and make sure the blade runout after installation is less than 0.01 mm. When trying a new blade, start from the lower limit of the recommended cutting parameters and optimize gradually. For cutting fluid, an emulsion at a concentration of about 7% is recommended. Also, the chip breaker groove shape is critical for chip evacuation; if chips get tangled, switch to an MF-type groove.

Can you tell me the specific steps and key pitfalls to avoid? The wall has already been scraped down to the cement base, and I've also bought the putty powder.

session_351.speaker: Yin Hao's Assistant
session_351.text: Okay. Core steps: 1. Mix putty powder with water according to the instructions (usually 1:0.4-0.5), let it sit for 15 minutes, then mix again. 2. Apply the first coat thickly, controlling the thickness at 1-2 mm, press firmly to avoid air bubbles; use a special tool to straighten internal and external corners. 3. Wait 4-6 hours between coats (depending on humidity), and after it dries thoroughly, sand with 240-grit sandpaper. 4. After two coats, finish with 320-grit fine sandpaper, then apply primer. Prevention of common problems: mix thoroughly, apply thin coats in multiple passes, and let each coat dry completely before applying the next.

session_351.speaker: Yin Hao
session_351.text: Thanks! After the first coat is applied, if there are small bubbles, how should I handle them? And what happens if I choose the wrong sandpaper grit when sanding?

session_351.speaker: Yin Hao's Assistant
session_351.text: Small bubbles are usually caused by rapid stirring or high moisture content in the wall. For minor ones, break the bubbles with a scraper and patch them flat before applying the second coat; for severe ones, the affected area needs to be scraped off and reapplied. Choosing the wrong sandpaper grit: too coarse, such as 120 grit, leaves deep scratches and affects flatness; too fine, such as 600 grit, is inefficient and paint does not adhere well. It is recommended to use 240 grit for the first coarse sanding, 320 grit for the second fine sanding, and finally 600 grit to lightly sand away loose dust.

session_351.text: It is recommended to choose a 5-7 km recovery jog, with a pace 30 seconds to 1 minute slower than usual, and prioritize smooth breathing. Do dynamic stretching before the run (focusing on hips, knees, and ankles), and fully relax afterward. In the morning the temperature is low, so keep warm. You can check the local air quality; if pollution is severe, it is recommended to postpone.

session_360.text: I just won a technical award. My master reminded me to prepare for next year's competition for team leader, and I also plan to get the senior technician certificate. Can you tell me exactly what to do?

session_360.text: You need to improve both your technical and management abilities while planning your certification path. I can help you sort out the specific requirements for the job competition and certification. Which details are you more concerned about?

session_360.text: They all want to know, especially the exam subjects and learning resources for the senior technician certificate, and what management skills team leaders need.

session_360.speaker: Yin Hao's Assistant
session_360.text: For the senior technician certificate (CNC direction), you need to be tested on PLC programming, mechanical principles, etc. You can register for the National Open University PLC course and pair it with the textbook 'CNC Machine Tool Fault Diagnosis'. The team leader recruitment focuses on team management, communication, and coordination. I recommend the online course 'Frontline Supervisor Skills' and the book 'Toyota Production System'. I suggest focusing on PLC hands-on practice first while simultaneously using fragmented time to learn management. Do you want me to help you arrange a daily study plan?

session_360.text: Okay, help me plan how to arrange my time each day. I work during the day, and study and exercise in the evening.

session_360.speaker: Yin Hao's Assistant
session_360.text: Recommendation: get up 30 minutes earlier every day to memorize management theory, spend 1 hour after work on PLC hands-on practice (add 2 hours on weekends), and exercise for 45 minutes in the evening. Use TickTick to set staged goals: focus on PLC and theory in the first 3 months, and intensify interview simulation and management case studies in the following 3 months. On weekends, you can sign up for an offline hands-on training class to accelerate skill application. This is both balanced and efficient.

qa.answer: In September, my exercise routine shifted from focusing mainly on morning runs and core training to gradually adding cycling for commuting, then switching to rehabilitative swimming and low-intensity core exercises due to a lumbar muscle strain, and finally gradually returning to morning runs. At the beginning of the month, I kept up morning runs and core training (e.g., a 4.2 km morning run plus 15 minutes of core work on the 1st, and morning core exercises on the 4th), but afterward the frequency fluctuated somewhat. Starting on the 8th, I made cycling to work a regular workout (about 35 minutes one way), while still mixing in morning runs (e.g., a 5 km morning run on the 9th and an 8 km morning run on the 12th). In the middle of the month, I felt discomfort in my lower back, and from the 18th I had soreness, but I still completed a 5 km road run on the 19th. On the 25th, suddenly lifting something heavy caused a right-side lumbar muscle strain, so I completely stopped running and switched to recovery activities: on the 26th I did breaststroke to relax, and from the 27th I did low-intensity core exercises every day (such as cat-cow stretch, bird-dog, glute bridges, etc.), gradually adding meditation and stretching. By the end of the month, the injury had improved; on the 28th I completed a 6 km recovery morning run with a running buddy, and then continued with core rehabilitation training. Overall, my exercise pattern shifted from running alone to a cross-combination of running, cycling, swimming, and core training, forming a flexible system better adapted to my schedule and physical condition. This change reflects that I prefer to switch exercise forms flexibly according to my schedule and body feedback, prioritizing maintaining basic fitness and recovery over simply pursuing high intensity or a fixed pattern, which shows a pragmatic attitude toward health management.

session_3.speaker: Lu Mingqiang
session_3.text: I hurt my lower back today while moving a distribution box. My colleague recommended a lumbar support belt, and my father taught me the superman exercise and five-point support. But I don't know how long I should wear the belt, and whether these exercises are suitable to do right now.

session_3.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_3.text: After a lumbar sprain, treatment needs to be divided into the acute phase and the recovery phase. In the acute phase (48-72 hours after injury), apply cold compresses, and avoid hot compresses and vigorous activity. The lumbar support belt can be worn intermittently during the acute phase, no more than 2 hours at a time, and should be removed when resting. Superman exercises and five-point support are suitable for the recovery phase (after symptoms ease); in the acute phase they may worsen the injury, so it is recommended to start with gentle abdominal breathing and leg slides. How is your pain now? Is it stabbing or sore and swollen?

session_3.speaker: Lu Mingqiang
session_3.text: Right now it's mainly soreness and swelling, with no obvious stabbing pain. The sprain happened about a day ago.

session_3.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_3.text: OK, it is currently in the late acute phase. Recommendations: 1) Continue wearing the lumbar support belt intermittently, no more than 2 hours at a time, and remove it while resting in bed. 2) Switch to hot compresses to promote blood circulation. 3) For rehabilitation exercises, start with ankle pumps and supine leg presses; after the pain basically disappears, slowly try the five-point support. 4) At work, avoid bending over; squat first before lifting. If the pain worsens or you develop numbness in your legs, seek medical attention promptly.

session_3.text: Okay. You want to understand the mapping between fault codes and hardware components, and the troubleshooting order when multiple faults occur together, right? Using cases from your actual work, I can provide diagnostic logic and steps.

session_3.speaker: Lu Mingqiang
session_3.text: Yes, especially for overcurrent faults. I once encountered a burnt-out motor, but I wasn't sure whether it was a motor insulation problem or an inverter parameter setting problem.

session_3.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_3.text: For overcurrent, first check the motor winding insulation resistance (use a multimeter to measure the resistance to ground, which should be >1MΩ), then confirm whether the inverter parameter auto-tuning is complete, and finally check the main circuit rectifier and inverter modules. It is recommended to troubleshoot in this order to avoid omissions.

session_10.speaker: Lu Mingqiang
session_10.text: I just finished several relay protection setting calculation problems, but I feel the coefficient values are easy to confuse, and I'm worried about getting stuck on similar problems in the exam. Can you give me analyses of some typical example problems and tips on common mistakes?

session_10.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_10.text: Of course. For distance protection setting, the common exam points are impedance grading and time coordination. Pitfalls: 1) The values of coefficients Krel, Kss, and Kre must be selected according to fault type and operating mode; 2) The calculation of branch coefficient Kb easily ignores infeed or outfeed. I suggest you focus on mastering the standard formulas for three-zone setting and memorize them together with waveform diagrams. Would you like me to show the detailed steps of a typical example?

session_10.speaker: Lu Mingqiang
session_10.text: Yes, especially the branch coefficient. I can never figure out when to use the maximum or minimum operating mode in calculations. Can you give me a specific example?

session_10.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_10.text: Okay. Take a dual-power line as an example. When setting Zone I of protection 2, the branch coefficient Kb should take the minimum value for a fault at the end of this line (to ensure sensitivity). When setting Zone II, faults on the adjacent line need to be considered, and Kb takes the maximum value (so the protection range does not overreach). For example: assuming system impedance Zs1=10Ω, Zs2=15Ω, line impedance Z1=20Ω, calculations give Kb_min=1.2 and Kb_max=1.8. Remember the mnemonic: "Take the small value for Zone I to ensure sensitivity; take the large value for Zone II to prevent overreach."

session_11.text: In zero-sequence current protection, what effect does load current have on zero-sequence compensation? While reviewing, I found the phase relationship a bit vague.

session_11.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_11.text: Are you mainly concerned about the deviation in compensation coefficient calculation caused by the vector superposition of load current and zero-sequence current, or the error caused by load imbalance in on-site wiring?

session_11.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_11.text: Load current generates an additional zero-sequence component, causing the compensation coefficient K to deviate from the theoretical value. In the exam, you can first assume the load is symmetrical, then use a vector diagram to analyze the fault component.

session_34.text: You'd like to understand the specific causes of gas protection maloperation and the on-site troubleshooting methods, right? I can add details based on common causes and procedures.

session_34.speaker: Lu Mingqiang
session_34.text: Yes, especially external vibration and secondary circuit problems. I want to know how to quickly diagnose them.

session_34.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_34.text: Common causes of maloperation include: 1) strong external vibration (e.g., heavy hammer impact); 2) internal fault of the gas relay; 3) poor insulation of the secondary circuit or a parasitic circuit. On-site troubleshooting steps: first check the vibration source, then test the relay contact state, and finally check the circuit insulation. Do you have any relevant records in your notes?

session_34.speaker: Lu Mingqiang
session_34.text: There is a record, but it doesn't mention the specific method of insulation testing. Could you elaborate?

session_34.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_34.text: Insulation testing usually uses a 500V megger to measure the secondary wiring's insulation to ground; the resistance should be greater than 1MΩ. Remember to disconnect the trip pressure plate to prevent misoperation. In addition, the action signals of light gas and heavy gas protection are different: light gas is often due to oil level or air, while heavy gas is mostly internal faults. When preparing for the exam, it is recommended to compare and distinguish them.

session_41.speaker: Lu Mingqiang
session_41.text: Tonight at home I drew the control circuit diagram based on the actual star-delta starter cabinet at Xiuying Food Factory, but I'm still a bit unclear about the timing logic of the contactor interlock. Can you help me sort it out?

session_41.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_41.text: Okay. In star-delta starting, KM1 and KM3 are interlocked to ensure that the star contactor (KM3) and the delta contactor (KM1) are not energized at the same time. At startup, KM3 and KM2 energize first, and the motor starts in star; after the time relay delay, KM3 opens and KM1 closes, completing the changeover. The interlock contacts prevent incorrect operation.

session_41.speaker: Lu Mingqiang
session_41.text: Got it. So how do I set the setting value of the time relay? For example, the motor I saw today is about 30 kW.

session_41.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_41.text: Generally, estimate based on motor power and load type: for light load, starting time is about 5–10 seconds; for heavy load, extend it appropriately. For a 30 kW motor, I suggest starting with 8 seconds and adjusting from there. You can confirm the switchover by listening to the sound or checking the ammeter for a current drop. In practice, you can also refer to the motor nameplate or empirical formulas.

session_41.speaker: Lu Mingqiang
session_41.text: Thanks! Also, what are the common mistakes to watch out for when actually wiring? I want to prepare for the senior technician exam.

session_41.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_41.text: Common errors: 1) Interlock contacts connected incorrectly causing a short circuit; 2) Confusing normally open and normally closed contacts on the time relay; 3) Mismatched contactor coil voltage. It is recommended to check each wire against the wiring diagram, especially testing continuity in the control circuit using the multimeter's resistance mode.

However, considering your BMI of 24.8 and the lower back strain from work, it is recommended to distinguish between acute soreness and chronic strain: if there is still no improvement after resting for 2 days or if stabbing pain appears, be alert. Your rehabilitation exercise direction is correct, but you can optimize the details of force application: avoid excessive lower back extension during the superman exercise, and the glute bridge should be driven by the buttocks rather than the lower back. When lifting heavy objects in daily work, keep your back straight and knees bent, and slightly bend your knees when standing to reduce lumbar spine pressure.

session_41.speaker: Lu Mingqiang
session_41.text: I see. Are there any common mistakes in the superman exercise and glute bridges I do? Also, what is the complete process for warming up before exercise and stretching after exercise? I still want to play squash on weekends—how should I balance exercise with work-related strain?

session_41.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_41.text: Common mistakes: during the swallow exercise, the neck is overextended backward and the arms are raised too high; instead, you should look at the ground and keep your palms facing down. During the glute bridge, the lower back is lifted too high off the ground; you should keep your lumbar spine in contact with the floor. Recommended stretching exercises: cat pose 20 reps, child's pose 30 seconds to relax the lower back. Warming up before exercise (dynamic stretching + 5 minutes of jogging) and stretching after exercise (static stretching of the lower back and hips) can reduce the risk of injury. It is recommended to avoid bending and lifting heavy objects the day after playing ball, and you can wear a soft lumbar support belt for auxiliary support, and add one core stability training session per week (such as plank).

session_46.speaker: Lu Mingqiang
session_46.text: Today I reviewed busbar differential protection. I still have questions about the cases of misoperation caused by TA saturation and the application of the restraint characteristic curve. Can you help me sort out the key logic and common pitfalls?

session_46.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_46.text: The core of busbar differential protection is based on Kirchhoff's current law; under normal conditions, the differential current is zero. When the TA saturates, the secondary current distorts, which may produce differential current. Key to discrimination: the restraining characteristic curve ensures that it operates only when the differential current exceeds the restraining quantity. Common mistakes: confusing the ratio restraining coefficient with the differential threshold, and ignoring the harmonic effects during TA saturation.

session_46.speaker: Lu Mingqiang
session_46.text: Yes, when I drew the logic flow chart, I wasn't sure about the value of the braking coefficient. Can you give an example to explain?

session_46.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_46.text: For example, the braking coefficient K is usually taken as 0.5–0.7. If the braking current is 10A, the differential current must be greater than 7A for the relay to operate. When the TA saturates, the differential current may contain second harmonics, and harmonic blocking can be used. A common error is that the setting value is too small, causing misoperation. In the exam, remember to calculate using practical examples.

session_48.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_48.text: No problem. The main causes of moisture exceeding the standard include seal leakage, adsorbent failure, moisture intrusion during operation, or substandard new gas. The national standard limits: the moisture content of SF6 circuit breakers in operation should be ≤300 ppm (arc-extinguishing chamber), and the annual leakage rate should be <0.5%. Handling process: first test to confirm the exceedance, then evacuate, replace the gas, replace the adsorbent, and locate and repair leaks. Routine regular moisture testing and recording are required.

session_48.speaker: Lu Mingqiang

session_48.text: Your key points are correct, but adding seal inspection and leakage rate limits would be more professional. Vacuum circuit breakers do not have a micro-water problem because the arc-extinguishing medium is different; the concerns are vacuum level drop and switching overvoltage. session_49.speaker: Lu Mingqiang

session_49.text:

[Daily Safety Inspection Checklist]
1. Voltage testing: □ Self-check the voltage tester □ Confirm the voltage level □ Re-check before touching conductors
2. Work at height: □ Inspect the double hooks and safety harness □ Anchor point above head □ Alternate protection
3. Temporary electricity: □ Test the leakage protector with the T button □ Record results □ No alarm or nuisance tripping
It is recommended to print this and stick it inside the tool box, and tick it off and sign every shift.

session_49.text: At 8:20 p.m. on February 18, 2025, I was self-studying Power System Analysis in my study, focusing on short-circuit current calculation. I drew an equivalent circuit diagram, but got stuck on formula derivation when simplifying, especially how the symmetrical component method corresponds to a transformer short circuit in the community distribution room. Could you explain step by step based on a real scenario?

session_49.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_49.text: I understand your difficulty. The method of symmetrical components essentially decomposes an asymmetric short circuit into three symmetrical systems: positive, negative, and zero sequence. In an actual distribution room: the positive-sequence impedance is the path for normal load current, the negative sequence is like a reverse-rotating magnetomotive force, and the zero sequence requires a ground return path. I suggest you ignore the difficult formulas for now, draw the high-voltage side equivalent circuit of your community's transformer, mark the sequence impedance values, and then apply the superposition principle according to the short-circuit type (e.g., single-phase-to-ground). Tomorrow I'll give you a calculation example based on the community's 10 kV transformer, with a unit conversion mnemonic.

session_51.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_51.text: This analogy is very creative and does make the abstract process vivid. Automatic transfer failures are often caused by abnormal logic in the dual-power transfer controller, stuck relay contacts, or unstable control circuit voltage. It is recommended to troubleshoot in the order of power supply side → controller → actuator: first measure the dual incoming line voltages, then check the controller output signal, and finally inspect the contactor operation.

session_51.speaker: Lu Mingqiang
session_51.text: Understood. If both power supply voltages are normal, but the closing fails during switching, what is the most likely cause?

session_51.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_51.text: It is likely that the closing command issued by the controller was not transmitted to the circuit breaker because the relay coil burned out or the contacts were oxidized. It is recommended to use a multimeter to measure whether there is a 24V DC signal at the controller output terminals. If not, check the controller's internal program or output module; if yes, check the intermediate relay and corresponding wiring.

session_54.speaker: Lu Mingqiang
session_54.text: I'm working on the exercises for asynchronous motors in the senior technician textbook, and the problem about broken rotor bars in a squirrel-cage rotor has me stumped. Could you explain in detail the fault characteristics, diagnostic methods, and repair solutions? I'm going to consult Master Li next week, so I need to understand it clearly first.

session_54.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_54.text: Common features of broken bars in a squirrel-cage rotor: reduced starting torque, periodic fluctuation of running current, and abnormal motor vibration. Diagnostic methods: use a clamp ammeter to measure current fluctuation (if the fluctuation period correlates with the slip, it can be judged); alternatively, sprinkle iron powder on the rotor surface to observe the magnetic field line distribution (iron powder is sparse where bars are broken). The difference from stator inter-turn short circuits is that the current fluctuation frequency differs. Repair: for minor cases, weld the cracks; for severe cases, replace the rotor. Do you have an actual work case you'd like to compare?

session_54.speaker: Lu Mingqiang
session_54.text: How exactly do you do current spectrum analysis? I only have a clamp meter on hand — can it detect broken rotor bars? Also, Master Li taught a crude method using iron powder; could you explain the steps in more detail?

session_54.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_54.text: Spectrum analysis requires a spectrum analyzer; using a clamp meter alone can only show waveform jitter. Here's what you can do: run the motor with no load, clamp one phase wire with the clamp meter, and observe whether the ammeter pointer swings regularly. If the swing frequency is close to the slip frequency (about 1–5 Hz), a broken bar is suspected. Iron powder method: remove the rotor and sprinkle fine iron powder, then apply low-voltage high-current (e.g., stepped down from 380V). The iron powder will cling along the rotor bars, and the iron powder will be noticeably sparser at the broken bar. It is recommended to combine these two methods and go to Master Li next week for hands-on verification.

session_55.text: Tonight I'm studying high-voltage power distribution systems. I don't quite understand the actual electric arc phenomenon in a “broken-bar fault.” I want to know its specific color and sound, and how to distinguish it from an ordinary short-circuit arc.

session_55.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_55.text: The arc caused by a broken bar fault is usually blue-white, accompanied by intermittent 'crackling' sounds, unlike a short-circuit arc, which is continuously bright and has a continuous sound. The fault point is often at the conductor break, and the arc flickers as the line impedance changes. You can observe whether there are intermittent flashes or burn marks near the line nodes.

session_55.speaker: Lu Mingqiang
session_55.text: Understood. How do you use a multimeter or a megger to make a preliminary judgment during an actual survey? What should you pay attention to for safety?

session_55.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_55.text: You can use a multimeter to measure the phase-to-phase resistance; broken bars will cause the resistance to increase abnormally. Use a megger (megohmmeter) to measure insulation resistance; if the value fluctuates greatly, it may point to intermittent arc discharge. For safety, be sure to disconnect power, verify no voltage, attach grounding wires, and wear insulating gloves. Referring to the fault tree analysis diagram in the textbook, focus on the areas with abnormal node temperatures.

session_55.text: I just saw a push notification about the layout of charging piles in Hainan. As an electric power worker, I would like to understand the technical differences between DC fast charging and AC slow charging, and also which areas in Haikou have insufficient charging pile coverage.

session_55.text: DC fast charging has high power (60-150 kW) and requires a dedicated transformer and three-phase power access, making it suitable for highway service areas; AC slow charging has low power (7-22 kW) and can use a household 220V circuit, making it suitable for overnight charging in residential communities. At present, the central urban areas of Haikou, such as Longhua District and the center of Meilan District, have relatively dense coverage, but there are still gaps in old residential communities and the western part of the city.

session_57.text: I am self-studying the ladder diagram of a PLC self-locking circuit. Is the logic of connecting a normally open contact in parallel with the start button correct? What is the difference from traditional relay self-locking?

session_57.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_57.text: Are you comparing PLC ladder diagram symbols with actual wiring? Common issue: in a self-locking ladder diagram, the normally open contact corresponds to the physical contact of the output relay, and the start button is paralleled before the normally open contact, but you need to pay attention to the PLC internal scan cycle and the inversion of normally closed contacts.

session_57.speaker: Lu Mingqiang
session_57.text: Right, I'm worried the ladder diagram is drawn incorrectly. For example, connecting the stop button directly in series, but in the program the normally closed contact needs to be inverted—isn't that easy to miss?

session_57.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_57.text: Correct approach: use a normally closed input (X0) for the stop button, and connect a normally open contact in series in the ladder diagram (because the PLC input circuit has a normally closed external button). Common mistake: forgetting to invert the normally closed contact, causing the stop function to fail. It is recommended to verify the logic with simulation software (such as CX-Programmer).

session_57.speaker: Lu Mingqiang
session_57.text: Understood, I'll try it with simulation software. When moving from relay to PLC self-locking, what should I pay attention to regarding address allocation?

session_57.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_57.text: Address assignment: start button connects to X0, stop button connects to X1, output Y0 controls the contactor. Ladder diagram: X0 normally open contact in parallel with Y0, then in series with X1 normally closed contact (for stop), and finally output Y0. Difference from hardwiring: the PLC maintains self-locking through the program and can be modified online. It is recommended to master the basic instructions first, then gradually practice complex functions.

session_58.text: I need to help a friend appraise an old wine bottle this afternoon. Can you teach me some general appraisal methods? For example, looking at the cap seal, label font, or the liquor bubbles?

session_58.text: Of course. First look at the bottle cap: the cap of an old liquor bottle is usually rough and worn, while a new fake is smooth. For the liquor foam: after shaking, the foam lasts a long time (about 15 seconds for Moutai) and dissipates evenly. I suggest first confirming the brand and vintage, then search online for the characteristics of the same period.

session_58.speaker: Lu Mingqiang
session_58.text: My friend didn't say the exact brand, and the photo only shows the bottle body. If there's a numeric year mark on the bottom, how can I tell what range is reasonable?

session_58.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_58.text: If there is a number on the bottom of the bottle, follow common baijiu distillery markings: Moutai, for example, used 'Local State-Run' before 1980 and later changed to 'Guizhou Moutai'. You can also use the foam to tell whether the vintage matches — aged baijiu has dense foam that dissipates slowly. It is recommended to bring a bright flashlight to check the color of the liquid; aged baijiu is slightly yellow and clear.

session_59.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_59.text: Okay. In the secondary circuit, the current transformer provides measurement signals to the relay; the key is the selection of the turns ratio and accuracy class. The setting calculation needs to consider the maximum/minimum operating modes of the system. Overcurrent protection is generally based on setting above the maximum load current and sensitivity verification, while zero-sequence protection is based on the amplitude and direction of the zero-sequence current. Need me to give an example?

session_59.speaker: Lu Mingqiang
session_59.text: Yes, it's best to use an actual trip-and-repair case to demonstrate the calculation steps. I'm going to consult Master Li tomorrow, so I want to have a clear idea beforehand.

session_59.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant

For zero-sequence protection in a small-current grounded system, you can set it to 20 A (equivalent to 0.166 A secondary) with no time delay. You can draw the wiring diagram on paper and simulate the CT, relay, and trip circuit in series to verify the coordination relationship.

session_64.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_64.text: Sure. Think of R as the insulation resistance measured with a megohmmeter (resistive), and X as the inductive reactance of the motor winding to AC. This makes it more intuitive to remember.

session_64.text: Mnemonic: inside the square root, R squared plus X squared. For quick calculations, if R is much smaller than X, Z≈X; similarly for the opposite case. You can write it on a small card and put it in your safety helmet, then silently recite it twice during the lunch break.

session_65.speaker: Lu Mingqiang
session_65.text: Tonight I studied transformer differential protection, but the ratio restraint characteristic curve and the inrush current identification algorithm are still a bit unclear. Could you explain them based on our electricians' field experience?

session_65.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_65.text: The ratio restraint characteristic can be understood as follows: when a large current appears due to an external fault, the threshold of differential protection automatically rises to avoid maloperation; during an internal fault, the restraint quantity is small and the operation is sensitive. Inrush current identification commonly uses second-harmonic restraint, taking advantage of the high harmonic content in magnetizing inrush current to distinguish it from internal faults.

session_65.speaker: Lu Mingqiang
session_65.text: Got it. Then how are the restraint coefficient and knee-point current determined in the setting calculation?

session_65.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_65.text: The braking coefficient is generally set according to the ratio of the minimum operating current to the transformer rated current. The knee-point current is usually 1.0-1.5 times the rated current to ensure that the unbalanced current during normal load and external faults is avoided. You can use the example formula in the textbook and plug in the parameters you have for a trial calculation.

session_66.text: First verify the equivalent impedance value: Z_total = Z_transformer + Z_line + Z_grounding resistance. session_70.speaker: Lu Mingqiang
session_70.text: This morning the terminals in the power distribution room were loose. The relationship between the heat effect formula and contact resistance in the textbook is a bit confusing to me. Could you help me understand it thoroughly using this example?

session_70.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_70.text: No problem. The loose terminal you encountered mainly involves contact resistance Rc ≈ ρ/(πa²) (ρ is resistivity, a is the radius of the contact point). When loosening occurs, a decreases and Rc increases. According to Joule's law P=I²R, the heating power rises, and thermal expansion further loosens the connection, forming a vicious cycle. The thermal effect formula in your textbook is actually the mathematical expression describing this process.

session_70.speaker: Lu Mingqiang
session_70.text: So what effect does thermal cycling have on bolt preload? Will the exam test this kind of comprehensive question?

session_70.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_70.text: Thermal cycling causes the bolts and conductor to have different thermal expansion coefficients, reducing the preload and causing the contact resistance to increase again. The senior technician exam often uses case analysis, for example asking how to prevent this. I suggest you remember two practical points: use a torque wrench to tighten to the specified torque, and apply conductive paste to the contact surfaces. In this way, you can understand the formula and also handle prevention-measure questions in the exam.

session_80.text: This afternoon, in the meter box of Building 17, Binhai Yuewan Community, I found the incoming terminals hot and discolored, and the current was too high. session_80.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_80.text: Heating discoloration is usually caused by poor contact; thermal imaging is recommended to confirm. If overloaded, replace with a 20A circuit breaker and use 4 mm² copper-core cable; if poor contact, polish the terminals and replace with cable of the same specification. For temporary monitoring, measure the temperature every 2 hours and restrict the use of high-power appliances.

session_80.text: I'm from Hainan and want to cook an authentic pot of qingbuliang to suit my wife's taste. This is my first time making it myself, so I've bought dried coconut meat, barley, mung beans, red dates, and papaya. Can you tell me the exact ingredient ratios and preparation steps?

session_80.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_80.text: You want to make a coconut-milk-based qingbuliang similar to those from the old street-side shops, right? We need to confirm the gram ratio for each ingredient, the soaking time, the cooking heat, and whether to add condensed milk or sugar to balance the sweetness.

session_80.speaker: Lu Mingqiang
session_80.text: Yes, either coconut milk base or sugar water base works; the key is to have an authentic taste. Would papaya be suitable to put in?

session_80.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_80.text: Suggested using a coconut milk base: dried coconut meat 100g, Job's tears 50g, mung beans 50g, red dates 5 (pitted). Papaya is usually not added; you can substitute watermelon or coconut meat instead. Soak the dried ingredients separately: Job's tears for 3 hours, mung beans for 2 hours, coconut meat for 1 hour. With a regular pot: first boil Job's tears and mung beans for 20 minutes, then add coconut meat and red dates and cook for 15 minutes, finally add condensed milk and sugar to taste. Bring to a boil over high heat, then turn down to low heat. A pressure cooker can shorten the time but the texture is slightly inferior.

session_82.text: When I practice backhand shoulder rotation in squash, I always feel my power isn't flowing smoothly. My playing partner says I'm slow with the shoulder turn. Are there any systematic ways to improve?

session_82.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_82.text: Would you like to obtain the power-generation techniques and movement breakdowns for shoulder rotation on the backhand side, so as to correct the problem of slow shoulder rotation and improve shot quality?

session_82.speaker: Lu Mingqiang
session_82.text: Yes, when I train I deliberately slow down the movement to feel the core driving it, but I never quite get it right. I want actionable steps and auxiliary exercises.

session_82.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_82.text: Suggested in 3 steps: 1. Standing twist exercise: stand with feet shoulder-width apart, simulate holding the racket with both hands, and use the waist and abdomen to drive the upper body to rotate left and right; 20 reps per set. 2. Resistance band shoulder rotation: anchor the resistance band at the waist, pull it at the backhand position to simulate shoulder rotation, and feel the back muscles engage. 3. Gaze-guided method: when turning the shoulders, first keep your eyes on the landing point of the shuttle, then follow the racket head trajectory, driving the head and torso to rotate together. Practice at home for 15 minutes every day.

session_82.speaker: Lu Mingqiang
session_82.text: Got it! I'll try the resistance band exercises and gaze guidance. Also, does the shoulder turn have the same technique for the backhand serve?

session_82.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_82.text: Yes, the backhand serve also requires shoulder rotation to store power. The key is to fully rotate your shoulders during the backswing so that the shoulder on the non-racket side points at the target. At the moment of contact, release power through body rotation, with the racket head trajectory going from low to high. You can combine this with multi-ball training to lock in the movement rhythm.

session_82.text: Hello, today I watered the peppers and lettuce on my parents' balcony and applied compound fertilizer. I noticed the potting soil dries out easily. I'm in Haikou. I'd like to ask about the best watering frequency and fertilizing methods for balcony potted vegetables.

session_82.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_82.text: Haikou's climate is hot and humid. On sunny spring days, water once in the morning and once in the evening whenever the surface soil looks dry, and water thoroughly until water drains from the bottom of the pot. Lettuce needs a lot of water during the seedling stage, while peppers are slightly more drought-tolerant. Compound fertilizer is recommended every 10-15 days, diluted to 1:800. If you want to be safer, you can alternate with organic liquid fertilizer.

session_82.speaker: Lu Mingqiang
session_82.text: Thanks! Do I need to adjust the water volume on the drip irrigator I'm currently using? Also, I haven't encountered pests and diseases before. How can I prevent aphids and powdery mildew?

session_82.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_82.text: Fine-tune the drip irrigator according to the amount of water draining from the potting soil to ensure each watering soaks through completely without waterlogging. To prevent aphids, spray diluted neem oil once a week. For powdery mildew, ensure good ventilation and avoid overly wet leaves. In the early stage, spray with a baking soda solution (1 teaspoon mixed with 1 liter of water). It is recommended to check the undersides of leaves.

session_85.speaker: Lu Mingqiang

I suggest you strictly follow the double-bolt requirement during work and measure that the contact resistance is less than 0.1 ohm. This is crucial for the senior technician practical assessment.

session_86.text: Today I inspected the distribution cabinet at the Xiuying Port cold storage warehouse. All three modules of the three-level surge protector were burned black and cracked. I replaced them with modules of the same model and also suggested Old Li add a second-level lightning arrester. I want to confirm: what is the reason for the three levels burning out at the same time? Is there any possibility of hidden risks remaining?

session_86.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_86.text: The simultaneous burnout of all three levels is usually caused by excessive lightning current exceeding the surge capacity of the three-level modules, or by a missing second level causing surges to directly impact the third level. Your suggestion to add a second-level surge arrester is correct. In addition, check whether the grounding resistance is up to standard (<4Ω) and whether there are other weak points in the circuit.

session_86.speaker: Lu Mingqiang
session_86.text: I'll test the grounding resistance again later. What are the key considerations for selecting a Type 2 surge arrester? For example, how are parameters like In and Up determined? I want to write the model clearly when helping Lao Li with the approval submission.

session_86.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_86.text: Type 2 surge arrester selection: In (nominal discharge current) is recommended to be ≥20 kA (the 10/350 μs waveform corresponds to 10 kA, but selecting 20 kA is more reliable in practice), Up (voltage protection level) ≤2.5 kV, Uc (maximum continuous operating voltage) not lower than the system's maximum voltage (for a 380 V system, choose Uc ≥385 V). The installation position is at the incoming end of the main cabinet; keep the wiring as short and straight as possible.

session_86.speaker: Lu Mingqiang
session_86.text: Understood, I've noted the parameters. Also, when I measured insulation with the megger today, the reading was about 500 MΩ. Is that value normal? After replacing the third-level module, how long should the subsequent maintenance cycle be?

session_86.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_86.text: 500MΩ is completely normal, indicating good insulation in the downstream circuit. For the three-stage surge protector, it is recommended to check the appearance and indicator window every six months, with key checks after the thunderstorm season. Replace it in time when the service life expires or the number of operations exceeds the limit; generally it needs complete replacement after 3-5 years.

session_86.speaker: Lu Mingqiang
session_86.text: I'm reviewing separately excited DC motor speed control and have two questions: What is the difference between the mechanical characteristic curves of armature voltage speed control and field weakening speed control? Why can field weakening only adjust the speed upward?

session_86.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_86.text: Changing the armature voltage for speed control is constant-torque speed control; the characteristic curves are a set of parallel, downward-shifted straight lines. Field-weakening speed control is constant-power speed control; the characteristic curves bend upward and the slope increases. Field weakening can only adjust upward because the excitation current cannot exceed the rated value; otherwise the magnetic circuit will saturate and the armature current will become too large, causing commutation difficulties or even burning out the motor.

session_86.speaker: Lu Mingqiang
session_86.text: Got it. So which speed control method is more economical under actual load?

session_86.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_86.text: For constant torque loads (such as cranes), armature voltage speed control is preferred because it is efficient and smooth; for constant power loads (such as machine tool spindles), field-weakening speed control is used. The senior technician exam often tests load characteristic matching; it is recommended to understand it with example problems.

session_88.text: Rotor resistance starting limits the starting current by cutting out resistors in stages. It is recommended to first use a multimeter to check whether the resistance of each section is normal, and then check the time logic of the control circuit.

session_88.text: Logic diagram: Resistance removal is usually done by shorting out sections in time sequence (for example, with 3 sections of resistance, cut one section every 0.5-1 second). Compared with star-delta starting, rotor series resistance provides greater starting torque and is suitable for heavy loads, but maintenance is more complicated. It is recommended to focus on rotor series resistance, because the senior technician exam often tests fault analysis of it.

session_91.speaker: Lu Mingqiang
session_91.text: Hello, I'm Lao Lu, an electrician. I'm working on the electrical room renovation plan for the old supply-and-marketing-cooperative dormitory building. Today Team Leader Zhang suggested I use a thicker incoming conduit to facilitate future upgrades. I'd like to confirm: what size of incoming conduit is generally chosen for old public housing? Should it be PVC or steel pipe? Also, are there any standard recommendations for the main cable ampacity and leakage protection configuration?

session_91.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_91.text: Hello, Old Lu! I understand your concern about the safety and forward-looking nature of the renovation. For the incoming conduit, it is recommended to use a PVC conduit or galvanized steel pipe with a diameter of 32mm or more, so as to facilitate heat dissipation and future wire pulling. For the main cable, refer to the GB/T 16895.15 standard and reserve a 20% margin based on the total load. For the residual current protective device, it is recommended to use a 30mA tripping current with overload protection. Do you still need construction key points for concealed works or budget persuasion techniques for communicating with the owner?

session_91.speaker: Lu Mingqiang
session_91.text: Yes, concealed works are very important. For example, are there any special considerations for the grounding system renovation and cable routing paths? Also, when convincing the owner, how should the costs be calculated so that the owner will accept the budget for thicker conduit and higher-spec cables?

session_91.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_91.text: Okay! For concealed works: for old buildings, it is recommended to redo the TN-C-S grounding system. The burial depth of incoming conduits should be no less than 0.5 meters, the bending radius should be at least 6 times the pipe diameter, and joints should be sealed and moisture-proof. To convince the owner: use the life-cycle cost method — although thicker conduits plus larger cross-section cables cost 10%-15% more initially, future upgrades will not require tearing open walls or cutting power, saving labor and materials in the long run. You can refer to the case data in the “Technical Guidelines for Renovation of Old Residential Communities” issued by the Ministry of Housing and Urban-Rural Development.

session_91.speaker: Lu Mingqiang
session_91.text: I just bought Musk Zhuanggu Plaster and Huoluo Oil for my mother. She is 60 and has chronic knee problems. Can these two be used together? How many times a day? Should she use a hot compress? Are there any contraindications?

session_91.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_91.text: Musk bone-strengthening plasters and Huoluo oil can be used together, but it is recommended to space them 2 hours apart. First apply Huoluo oil and massage for 5 minutes, then apply the plaster. Use one plaster per day, for no more than 8 hours; use Huoluo oil 3 times a day. Warm compresses can promote absorption, but do not use if there is broken skin or an allergy. Watch for redness, swelling, or itching, and stop use immediately. In daily life, you can wear a knee pad for warmth and avoid going up and down stairs too often.

session_91.speaker: Lu Mingqiang
session_91.text: Thanks! Is topical medication enough? Do we need to take her to the hospital for a check-up? Also, are there any recommended home physiotherapy methods?

session_91.speaker: Lu Mingqiang's Assistant
session_91.text: If the pain affects walking or rest, it is recommended to take an X-ray to rule out progression of osteoarthritis. In daily life, you can practice straight leg raises and wall sits for 15 minutes a day; get calcium and vitamin D from your diet, and get more sun. Topical medication only relieves symptoms; if it keeps worsening, you need to see a doctor.

session_100.text: Based on experience, aging of the spring leaves in old relays can cause a slight 'click' noise during pickup and unstable pickup under high current. session_100.text: Common signs include: 1) abnormal vibration noise from contactors or relays when they close; 2) a slight "hissing" discharge sound near the terminal block; 3) periodic abnormal noise accompanied by current fluctuations during equipment operation.
